items.descriptionOriginal: When we think about ecological and biological disruption, we tend to focus on the big picture: destroyed habitats, melting ice caps , and animal extinctions. So it’s easy to overlook how small actions can have an enormous impact on the natural world, often in ways we never notice. A great example happened in the summer of 2023 in Carlsbad Caverns National Park in Southeastern New Mexico near the Texas border, when a park visitor dropped a bag of Cheetos in a cave. The cave, known as The Big Room, is an expansive chamber filled with stalagmites and stalactites. LEAD Technologies Inc. V1.01 How a bag of Cheetos changed a cave’s ecology It’s disappointing that someone littered in a national park, but the rangers investigated the incident at a micro level. When food is introduced into an area cut off from the outside world, it can cause significant disturbance. “The processed corn, softened by the humidity of the cave, formed the perfect environment to host microbial life and fungi,” the National Park Service wrote on Facebook . “Cave crickets, mites, spiders, and flies soon organize into a temporary food web, dispersing the nutrients to the surrounding cave and formations. Molds spread higher up the nearby surfaces, fruit, die and stink. And the cycle continues.” A bag of Cheetos in a cave. Photo credit: National Park Service “The cave has 90 to 100 percent humidity, so things get soggy pretty quickly,” park guide Ashley Parsons told National Geographic . “Life started to find a way in that area. Fungi and mold, stuff like that, started to grow around the area of impact, where the bag was. Because of that, other lifeforms—like mites, sprighairs, and other things, even cave spiders—started to congregate in that area,” Joseph C. Ward, with the National Park Service, told KCRW . After rangers discovered the Cheetos bag, they met to decide how to clean it up. They scooped up almost all of it, and a park ranger then used a toothbrush to remove rings of mold and fungi that had grown and spread from the original Cheeto drop site. The cleanup only took around 20 minutes. Carlsbad Caverns National Park. Photo credit: Canva The National Park Service used the incident as a teachable moment The Cheeto incident was a great teaching moment for the National Park Service, which wrote a reminder of the importance of leaving nature as we found it on Facebook: “Great or small we all leave an impact wherever we go. How we choose to interact with others and the world we share together has its effects moment by moment. And we feel it. Here at Carlsbad Caverns, we love that we can host thousands of people in the cave each day. Incidental impacts can be difficult or impossible to prevent. Like the simple fact that every step a person takes into the cave leaves a fine trail of lint. Other impacts are completely avoidable. Like a full snack bag dropped off-trail in the Big Room. To the owner of the snack bag, the impact is likely incidental. But to the ecosystem of the cave it had a huge impact.” Ultimately, people found the Cheetos bag, cleaned it up, and life in the cavern returned to normal. But the National Park Service used it as an opportunity to discuss an important issue: just because something isn’t happening on a human scale doesn’t mean it’s unimportant. “At the scale of human perspective, a spilled snack bag may seem trivial, but to the life of the cave it can be world changing,” The National Park Service concluded its Facebook post. “Great or small we all leave an impact wherever we go. Let us all leave the world a better place than we found it.” The post Somebody dropped a Cheetos bag in Carlsbad Caverns, and it was ‘world-changing’ for the ecosystem appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: For many of us, telling our friends and family that we love them is second nature. Every time someone leaves the house, “Love you!” Before bed at night, “Love you!” Getting off a call with them, “Love you!” That’s all well and good until that sweetly ingrained habit spills over into your work life . Especially when you’re talking to an important client, where the boundaries of professional conduct are particularly important to uphold. (Do you feel the cringe coming?) I Love You Elf GIF by MOODMAN Giphy A woman shared an oh-so-human story about absent-mindedly telling a client she loved him, and his thoughtful response has people cheering. “Accidentally said ‘Love you!’ at the end of a call with an important client yesterday,” wrote a Reddit user . “I heard him giggle as I hung up, and I was mortified. Today, I saw he emailed me this:” Accidentally said "Love you!" at the end of a call with an important client yesterday. I heard him giggle as I hung up, and I was mortified. Today, I saw he emailed me this: by u/ButterscotchButtons in MadeMeSmile The email began, “Hey—Just wanted to say that I didn’t mean to laugh at you when you accidentally signed off on our call with a ‘love you.’ I just found it funny because I’ve definitely done that before, and I know it happens.” Okay, phew, he understood that the laughing was mortifying and he wasn’t bothered by the “love you.” But then he added the absolute best thing he could have said about the situation: “I’m glad you have enough love in your life that that response comes naturally. If anything, you should be proud of that. :)” Then he mercifully resumed their professional conversation. “Have a great weekend! We’ll follow up about my call with Chris on Wednesday, as discussed.” He didn’t just ignore the elephant in the room and let it hang over her like an awkward cloud. He put her at ease, letting her know he’s done it before and it happens and is no big deal. But then he took it a step further, adding a deeper human layer to the moment by acknowledging the fact that the words flowing so automatically and easily for her meant she was surrounded by love. The client’s emotional intelligence and thoughtful response warmed people’s hearts. “What a great and respectful response. He is completely right, it’s such a beautiful thing to have that much love in your life that it comes out naturally.” “You work with good people.” “Honestly, this made my day It’s so wholesome how they responded. Shows that a little kindness (even accidental) always leaves a good impression!” “Such a classy response. Made you feel at ease while staying professional and moving the conversation forward.” “Green flags from that client.” Green Flag GIF by The Last Talk Show Giphy People also shared their own similar experiences with blurting out accidental “love you”s and it was a veritable love-fest: “I told my supervisor I loved her at the end of our weekly touch point call – she chuckled and said she loved me too. We shared a good laugh. I am happy to see empathy from a random human, it is much needed.” “I said ‘love you’ to my new boss at labcorp when she called me to tell me I passed my drug test. Same thing, hanging up, not thinking, she gave me my results and my start date to come in for orientation and I ended the call with ‘bye love you!'” “Back in the day I straight up called one of my bosses mom. It was so embarrassing I almost died.” “A surprising number of people have done this at least once. Happens when you’re distracted and tired. My ex husband (a prosecutor) accidentally ended a phone call with ‘I love you’ when talking to a rural county sheriff in the middle of the night.” Embarrassed Hide GIF by flor Giphy “I had a coworker say ‘love you,’ just as we were about to hang up. There was an awkward pause, clearly neither of us had hung up, then he added, ‘Don’t tell my wife.’ We both laughed and finally disconnected.” “I did that with my ex husband last Thursday, we both burst out laughing lol. Happily we get along great and he and his fiancée are attending my wedding next week.” “Was on phone with my boss right after he had called his wife. He ended the call with “love you.” Had so much fun telling him that while I cared for him, I didn’t think it was love.” Embarrassing moments don’t have to ruin your day—in fact, when handled like this client, they can turn into beautiful moments of human connection. This kind of relatability, empathy, and emotional intelligence makes us all feel better about our shared humanity, oopsies and all. This article originally appeared in May. This article originally appeared 1 year ago. It has been updated. The post A woman accidentally said, ‘Love you!’ to an important client. His response was perfect. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: In the era of supermarkets and wholesale clubs, growing your own food isn’t a necessity for most Americans. But that doesn’t mean it’s not a good idea to try. A household garden can be a great way to reduce your grocery bill and increase your intake of nutrient-dense foods. It can also be a good source of exercise and a hobby that gets you outside in the sunshine and fresh air more often. However, not everyone has a yard where they can grow a garden or much outdoor space at all where they live. You can plant things in containers, but that requires some upfront investment in planters. Potted plants and herbs can thrive in a container garden. Photo credit: Canva Or does it? Gardener James Prigioni set out to see if an Amazon shipping box would hold up as a planter for potatoes. He took a basic single-walled Amazon box, lined it with dried leaves to help with moisture retention, added four to five inches of soil (his own homegrown soil he makes), added three dark red seed potatoes, covered them with more soil, added a fertilizer, then watered them. He also planted a second, smaller Amazon box with two white seed potatoes, following the same steps. Two weeks later, he had potato plants growing out of the soil. Ten days after that, the boxes were filled with lush plants. Prigioni explained how to “hill” potato plants when they grow tall enough, which helps encourage more tuber growth and protect the growing potatoes from sunlight. Hilling also helps support the plants as they grow taller so they don’t flop over. He also added some mulch to help keep the plants cooler as the summer grew hotter. After hilling, Prigioni only needed to keep up with watering. Both varieties of potatoes flowered, which let him know the tubers were forming. The red potato leaves developed some pest issues, but not bad enough to need intervention, while the white potato plants were unaffected. “It goes to show how variety selection can make a big difference in the garden,” he explained. The visible plants have to start dying before you harvest potatoes, and Prigioni checked in with the boxes themselves when they got to that point. Freshly harvested potatoes are so satisfying. Photo credit: Canva “I am pleasantly surprised with how well the boxes held up,” he said, especially for being single-walled boxes. The smaller box was completely intact, while the larger box had begun to split in one corner but not enough to affect the plants’ growth. “This thing was completely free to grow in, so you can’t beat that,” he pointed out. Prigioni predicted that the red potatoes grown in the larger box would be more productive. As he cut open the box and pulled potatoes from the larger box, they just kept coming, ultimately yielding several dozen potatoes of various sizes. The smaller box did have a smaller yield, but still impressive just from two potatoes planted in an Amazon box. People often think they don’t have room to grow their own food, which is why Prigioni put these potato boxes on his patio. “A lot of people have an area like this,” he said. “I will never look at cardboard boxes the same,” Prigioni added. “There are so many uses for them in the garden and it’s just a great free resource we have around, especially if you’re ordering stuff from Amazon all the time.” Do you see a box or do you see a planter? Photo credit: Canva People loved watching Prigioni’s experiment and shared their own joy—and success—in growing potatoes in a similar fashion: “I have been growing potatoes in every box I can find for several years now. I have had excellent success. I honestly think potatoes prefer cardboard. And yes, most of my boxes were from Amazon.” “I live in an upstairs apartment with a little deck and I have a container garden with containers on every single stair leading to the deck. I grow potatoes in a laundry basket. It’s amazing how much food I can get from this type of garden!! Grateful.” “I literally got up and grabbed the empty boxes by our front door, the potatoes that have started to sprout, and soil i had inside and started my planting at 1am. Lol. I will take them outside today and finish. Thank you James!” “I grew potatoes and tomatoes on my tiny balcony in Germany (in buckets and cardboard boxes). Now I have a big garden here in America. I so love to grow my own food.” “I grew sweet potatoes in cardboard boxes. It’s so much fun.” Next time you’re stuck with an Amazon box that you don’t have a use for, consider whether you could use it as a planter for potatoes or some other edible harvest. Gardening doesn’t have to be fancy to be effective. You can find more of gardening experiments on The Gardening Channel with James Prigioni. This article originally appeared in April. This article originally appeared 1 year ago. It has been updated. The post A guy planted two potatoes in an Amazon shipping box to prove a point. Mission accomplished. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: One of the most famous portraits of Napoleon , completed in 1812, features him striking a rather odd pose . He’s slouching in a formal uniform while standing in his study, but it’s the placement of his right hand that strikes some viewers as unique . His hand is tucked into his uniform. Not in a pocket, per se, but right through the buttons , which have been opened to accommodate all five fingers. It looks a little like he’s getting ready to pull out a pocket watch or a pistol. It’s not a pose you would see commonly these days, that’s for sure. Napoleon in 1812. Photo credit: Jacques-Louis David/Wikimedia Commons The more you look at it, the stranger it becomes. What’s especially interesting is that this wasn’t the first or only time Emperor Napoleon posed like this; it was something of his signature look. Napoleon didn’t invent this pose The “hand-in-waistcoat” pose wasn’t even Napoleon’s invention . It was extremely popular at the time, especially in portraits of royalty and noblemen. Some of the most famous portraits of all time feature men with a hand tucked inside a shirt, vest, or coat. A few notable examples include: General Lafayette The 1st Duke of Wellington George Washington George Washington doing the “hand-in-waistcoat.”Photo credit: Charles Willson Peale/Wikimedia Commons The pose wasn’t just ever-present in old paintings; it eventually made its way into the early days of black-and-white photography. Here’s philosopher Karl Marx in 1875, doing the same thing with his right hand. Karl Marx posing in 1875. Photo credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall/Wikimedia Commons So why did everyone do this? So, what gives? Why the hand tuck? The simple explanation is that the pose was a sign of dignity and high class. It likely dates back to ancient Greece . “Some societal circles in ancient Greece considered it disrespectful to speak with your hands outside of your clothing,” writes Readers Digest . “Statuary from the sixth century BC, therefore, showed celebrated orators such as Solon with their hands tucked into their cloaks.” Keeping one hand in a robe also helped prevent nervous gestures while speaking, which made the pose commonplace among powerful men and great orators, such as Aeschines, who helped popularize it. In the 17th and 18th centuries, portraiture was incredibly important. It helped symbolize the power held by royalty, functioning almost as propaganda. It was crucial for figures of nobility to appear powerful in their portraits, so they adopted the ancient Greek approach to posing. “Concealing a hand in a shirt became a common pose in paintings as a symbol of statesmanlike nobility and restraint,” writes BBC History Magazine . “According to a 1737 book on etiquette, The Rudiments of Genteel Behaviour by François Nivelon, it symbolised ‘manly boldness tempered with modesty.'” Similar poses, like holding your hands behind your back, are still often perceived as displays of confidence and thoughtfulness. There are some fun theories too But there are other, more fun explanations and theories behind this iconic pose. Some theorize that sitting for portraits, especially paintings, took so long that it was more comfortable to rest one hand inside a jacket. In fact, portrait sittings could require several sessions, each lasting multiple hours. Others point to the famous idiom, “It costs an arm and a leg!” Hands and feet are notoriously difficult to paint, even for seasoned artists, so hiding one’s fingers could make a portrait easier and perhaps even cheaper. Painter Thomas Hudson was responsible for so many famous portraits featuring this pose that some theorized he was simply terrible at painting hands. Some say the hand-in-waistcoat pose signifies membership in the Freemasons, a secret fraternal society. Others suggest that, when it came to Napoleon’s role in popularizing the pose, he may have been clutching a painful stomach ulcer. After all, he later died of stomach cancer . But most of these theories are not backed by evidence. The pose most likely caught on as a symbol of power and nobility and, frankly, because people thought it looked cool at the time. Frankly, anyone sitting for a portrait needs something to do with their hands, and today you’ll often see men posing with one hand in a pocket or “candidly” adjusting a sleeve. In a weird way, it’s Napoleon’s legacy living on. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. This article originally appeared 3 months ago. It has been updated. The post Historians explain why men in old-timey portraits always had one hand in their vest or coat appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: I’ve written extensively about minimum wage , supported by fact-checkers, economists , and scholarly studies. All of them support raising the minimum wage as a solution to lifting people out of poverty and getting them off public assistance. It’s slowly happening, and there’s much more to be done. But when it comes right down to it, where the rubber meets the road is what it means for everyday workers who have to live with those wages . I honestly don’t know how they do it. Ask yourself: Could I live on this small of an hourly wage? I know what my answer is. (And note that the minimum wage in many parts of the county is STILL $7.25, so it could be even less than this). One year of work at McDonalds grossed this worker $13,811.18. u200bvia JustFrugalMe/YouTube The YouTube channel Just Frugal Me discussed the viral paycheck and noted there’s absolutely nothing wrong with working at McDonald’s. More than 2 million people in the U.S. alone work for the fast food giant. The worker’s paycheck shows they put in 72 hours over the pay period, making $8.75 per hour. Before taxes, that’s $631 for the week. Just Frugal Me’s breakdown is even more eye-opening, breaking down this person’s pay after taxes and weighing across average rent and utility costs. Spoiler Alert: the total costs for basic necessities far outweigh what this person is making even while working 12 hours per day. But they do make too much to qualify for Medicaid, meaning they will have to go out and buy their own health insurance. A photo of a McDonald's in Hartford, CT. via Mike Mozart/Flickr Even in states like California, where the state’s $20 minimum wage ensures that people earn nearly three times as much as the federal minimum wage, which remains as low as when this paycheck first made the rounds nearly 10 years ago. Still, even for a worker that maxed out at 40 hours per week and took zero vacation or sick time, that’s only a little over $41,000 per year. That’s barely half the median wage in the state of $78,000 and far below a sustainable living wage in cities like Los Angeles. The U.S. federal minimum wage is just $7.25 and hasn’t been raised since 2009. In April 2025 , the Raise the Wage Act of 2025 was introduced in the House of Representatives and U.S. Senate. The bill would increase the federal minimum wage to $17 an hour by 2030 and eliminate the subminimum wage for tipped workers and those with disabilities. But supporters should be cautious that it’s unlikely to pass the Republican-controlled Congress. If the Wage Act of 2025 were to pass, over $22 million workers would get a raise, which is 15% of the U.S. workforce. It would raise $70 billion for low-wage Americans, an increase of $3,200 per worker. “No person working full-time in America should be living in poverty,” Virginia Congressman Bobby Scott said in a statement. “The Raise the Wage Act will increase the pay and standard of living for nearly 22 million workers across this country. Raising the minimum wage is good for workers, good for business, and good for the economy. When we put money in the pockets of American workers, they will spend that money in their communities,” This story originally appeared ten years ago. It has been updated to reflect new information. This article originally appeared 1 year ago. It has been updated. The post Here’s a paycheck for a McDonald’s employee. And here’s my jaw hitting the ground. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: At 8,849 metres above sea level, there is little room for anything except the next step. On 21 May 2026, as Shradha Gupta stood on the summit of Mount Everest, the world below seemed to disappear. Around her stretched a landscape of snow, ice and distant ridgelines, while the summit itself offered barely enough space to stand. After years of balancing boardrooms, client calls and a demanding banking career with early-morning workouts and long weekends in the mountains, the 41-year-old banker from Delhi had finally reached the highest point on Earth. "I didn't know I was going to Kilimanjaro when I started hiking. When I started Kilimanjaro, I had no idea that I was going to be at Everest," she tells The Better India. Perhaps that is what makes her journey remarkable. Everest was not a childhood ambition mapped out over decades. Just three years before standing on its summit, Shradha had only recently rediscovered something she had loved as a child: mountains. Today, she has climbed five major summits across three continents, including four of the Seven Summits — Kilimanjaro in Africa, Elbrus in Europe and Aconcagua in South America — along with Manaslu and Everest in the Himalayas. But for Shradha, the story begins long before the summit photographs. It begins with a glass table, a long recovery, and a realisation that life had been passing by. The accident that made her look back Shradha has spent two decades in banking. Originally from Delhi, she left India at 17 to study engineering in Singapore and eventually joined DBS Bank, beginning her career on the trading floor. She spent 11 years in Singapore before moving to Dubai with the same bank in 2017. Today, she leads corporate business for the Middle East. For years, work had naturally occupied much of her life. Then, in 2020, an accident at home changed the way she looked at it. Shradha's first major expedition to Mount Kilimanjaro in 2023 helped her discover that she could take on climbs she had once thought impossible. A glass table caused a severe forehead injury that required reconstructive surgery. The bone had broken, muscles had torn, and her doctors had to piece everything together layer by layer. Her recovery took around 18 months. "The first one to two months was really bad. I couldn't even walk properly because it affected my balance, and it used to hurt all the time," she recalls. The experience left her thinking about how close she had come to losing the life she knew. It also made her wonder about everything she had postponed. "I think for me it ended up just being a life-changing experience," she adds. "I started thinking about how life had taken over, how work had taken over, and you just keep going year by year, and you forget about the things that are important to you and the ones that give you joy." One of those things had always been mountains . Growing up in Delhi, Shradha remembers her parents packing the family into their car during school holidays and heading towards the hills. Nainital, Mussoorie, Pithoragarh, Sangla Valley and other parts of Himachal Pradesh were part of her childhood. She had even climbed Mount Fuji with her parents as a teenager and later hiked in Malaysia while studying in Singapore. But a long gap passed before she returned to the mountains. That changed in February 2022. From weekend hikes to a much bigger dream A friend invited Shradha on a hike in Dubai with a group of women. Until then, she had associated Dubai with skyscrapers, not mountains. "I didn't even know that I could hike in Dubai," she says. "I had no idea that there were mountains like two hours away." After that first hike, she kept returning, heading almost every weekend towards the mountains around Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. The hikes became her place to switch off, move and feel like herself again. Then came an old bucket-list dream: Mount Kilimanjaro. With her 40th birthday approaching, Shradha decided she did not want to keep waiting. "I don't know how long my body and mind are going to support me. So, if I have to do this, then let's just do it. There's no point waiting anymore." There was one practical problem. Kilimanjaro could take seven to nine days, and Shradha had never been unavailable for that long in her corporate career. She leads a business dealing with large corporate clients, so being disconnected was unfamiliar territory. From Kilimanjaro in Africa to Elbrus in Europe and Aconcagua in South America, each summit prepared Shradha for the challenges of Everest. Eventually, she found an expedition during the Eid break, giving her a week away from work. In June 2023, she set off. It was also her first expedition with strangers: five women, including three Indians, an Algerian and an Egyptian, along with one husband and their British expedition leader. The mountain gave them something in common. "You're there for each other, supporting, talking about your life stories, and sharing food together." More importantly, Kilimanjaro showed Shradha that she could actually do this. "I learnt that I could climb when I almost thought it was impossible," she shares. One summit kept leading to another After Kilimanjaro, Shradha travelled to Everest Base Camp in October 2023. It was there, while watching the sunrise from Kala Patthar, that the thought first appeared. She looked at Everest as the sunlight emerged behind it and thought, "One day, I want to stand on top of that mountain." It was not yet a plan, but the idea never took a back seat. Preparing for Everest meant balancing a demanding corporate career with hours of daily training. Her next test was Mount Elbrus, Europe's highest mountain, in June 2024. If Kilimanjaro had tested her at altitude and Everest Base Camp had tested her endurance over a longer journey, Elbrus introduced her to technical climbing on ice and snow. Then came Aconcagua in January 2025, the highest mountain in South America and the highest peak outside Asia. Each expedition, she says, became a way of introducing one new variable. Higher altitude. Longer duration. More technical terrain. By then, Everest was no longer just a thought. Before attempting it, though, Shradha wanted to test herself at 8,000 metres. In September 2025, she climbed Manaslu, the 8th-highest mountain in the world, at 8,163 metres, with Elite Exped. It was her first 8,000er and a completely different world from the mountains she had climbed before. There were fixed ropes, ladder crossings, crevasses, avalanches and the extreme conditions of what mountaineers call the "death zone". "Once you're in the 8,000-metre degree, it's a completely different world," she says. "It is harsh, and almost every day it's like you're fighting for your life because you don't know what's going to go wrong." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shradha Gupta 🇮🇳 🇦🇪 🇸🇬 (@iamshradhagupta) Manaslu confirmed that she was ready to attempt Everest. But it also showed her exactly how much preparation would be required. Preparing for the mountain while holding down a career Training for Everest became another full-time commitment layered on top of her actual job. In Dubai, Shradha hikes whenever she can. During the summer, when temperatures can make outdoor training difficult, she uses Ski Dubai's indoor slope. Her routine also includes weightlifting, incline treadmill sessions, StairMaster workouts, swimming and running. At peak training, she was spending nearly two and a half to three hours exercising each day, split between mornings before work and evenings afterwards. Her Everest coach, Mike McCastle, based in Las Vegas, USA, began working with her in January 2026. Despite a shoulder injury, injured ribs and a persistent cough during her Everest expedition, Shradha continued towards the summit one step at a time. "She began fit. She finished expedition-ready," he says. McCastle's programme focused not just on cardiovascular fitness but on the demands of an expedition: loaded uphill movement, strength endurance, muscular durability, recovery and the ability to keep working after fatigue had accumulated. For him, Shradha's age was not the defining factor. "I coach the athlete standing in front of me, not the number written beside their age," he says. What stood out instead was her consistency . "She was balancing a demanding professional career, travel, stress and normal life alongside Everest preparation," McCastle says. "Consistency does not mean executing a perfect programme for months. It means continuing to return to the process when life disrupts the programme." Everest asked for everything she had The Everest expedition in 2026 did not go according to plan. With conflict in the Middle East creating uncertainty around air travel, Shradha left Dubai for Delhi in late March to complete her preparation without risking delays closer to the expedition. For Shradha, reaching Everest's summit meant pushing through one of the most physically demanding experiences of her mountaineering journey. On the mountain, she slipped on an ice wall in the Khumbu Icefall and injured her left shoulder, leaving her barely able to lift a one-litre bottle. With the route through Khumbu also delayed, she returned to Kathmandu for four days to recover before coming back to the mountain. Then came the dreaded Khumbu cough. The relentless dry cough left her sleep-deprived and progressively weaker. By the time she began her summit push, she was dealing with injured ribs, illness and exhaustion. "Nothing has tested me the way Everest has tested me," she says. "I have never been this hurt, this injured and this sick on a climb as I was on Everest." Still, she kept moving, drawing on a lesson she had learnt on Kilimanjaro: break the biggest goal into smaller steps. "My only responsibility today is to deal with today. We will deal with tomorrow when it comes." Shradha's first Kilimanjaro expedition brought together women from different backgrounds, united by the challenge of climbing Africa's highest peak. Her coach, Mike McCastle, saw the same resilience. "Mountains punish rigidity. Weather changes. Bodies change. Plans change," he says. "Shradha experienced setbacks during both training and the expedition... But she kept recalibrating." When she finally reached the summit, there was happiness and gratitude, but the climb was not over. She still had to descend, with an exhausted body and little left in the tank. She had to keep walking. There is still another mountain somewhere For Shradha's family, watching her journey from weekend hikes to 8,000-metre peaks has been its own experience. While the early expeditions worried them less, Manaslu and Everest were different. She stayed in touch with them through a satellite communicator, even as she remained aware of the risks. Before attempting the 8,000ers, she signed body-disposal forms, knowing that preparation cannot eliminate every danger. "When you're entering the world of 8,000ers, you are prepared to die," she says. "I know the risks that I'm going through. Sure, I will fight till my last breath to survive, but sometimes it may be out of my control." From weekend hikes to Everest's summit, Shradha's journey is a reminder that every big dream begins with one step. Today, she is back between Dubai and Delhi, returning to the corporate life she has continued alongside the mountains. But three years after that first hike, Everest is behind her, and the journey still feels far from over. For someone who once thought of mountains as family holiday destinations, there is perhaps no better way to look ahead than with the lesson that has carried her this far. "Whatever your dream is, it doesn't have to be mountains. It can be anything in life. Take that first step." She adds, "You may not be at your strongest. You may not be at your best. But if you want it bad enough, if you're giving it everything that you've got, the world will come together to make it happen for you." And so, after Everest, there is still another first step waiting somewhere ahead. All images courtsey of Shradha Gupta

items.descriptionOriginal: At 12:54 am on 7 March 2024, a small wild cat approached a man-made pond in a forest patch near Goa's Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary. It stopped to drink, unaware that a camera trap beside the water was recording its movements. The camera captured five short video clips, which would soon become an exciting discovery for wildlife researchers Akshita Pungaliya and Atul Borker. The visitor was a mainland leopard cat ( Prionailurus bengalensis ), a shy, elusive wild cat that had never been photographically documented in Goa, according to the researchers' published findings. The sighting became the state's first reported photographic record of the species, with the findings published in the IUCN Species Survival Commission's Cat News in 2025. But the researchers hadn't set out looking for a leopard cat. Their project began with a much simpler concern. Every February, a freshwater stream running through this forest patch would dry up, leaving animals with fewer places to drink as the hotter months approached. Akshita and Atul wondered whether a small artificial pond could make water available to wildlife during those months. They decided to create one and use a camera trap to see what happened. What they recorded would help them understand the animals using this forest, including one that had rarely been documented in the region. When the forest ran out of water Akshita and Atul have long been interested in wildlife species that receive less attention than animals such as tigers and elephants. In 2023, the two researchers co-founded Vanasa Conservation Foundation to work towards protecting lesser-known wildlife. Their work brought them to a patch of private forest land bordering Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary, where a seasonal stream offered an opportunity to understand how animals cope with disappearing water sources. "We wanted to understand if creating an artificial water source in these forest patches would actually be used by animals," Akshita tells The Better India. "We've been monitoring activity across the year, but the original plan was to provide it in the drier months." Before building the pond, however, the team wanted to find a spot that animals were already likely to visit. They walked through the forest looking for small trails, fruit remains and disturbed leaf litter. These were clues that mammals regularly passed through certain parts of the landscape. "We looked at places where we could see smaller trails made by mammals, food lying around, signs that told us this is a walking path they use," Akshita explains. Using these signs, they chose a suitable location, dug a small pond, lined it and filled it with water. The artificial pond had a capacity of 40 litres. A camera trap placed nearby would help the team find out whether animals discovered the water and, more importantly, whether they returned. As the recordings began coming in, the researchers got their first answers. The mainland leopard cat is one of Asia's most widespread wild cats, found across parts of India, Southeast Asia, China, Taiwan, Japan and the Russian Far East. Photograph: (Camera Trapped) Birds, squirrels and leopards began visiting The camera soon captured birds arriving to drink, mongooses stopping by and squirrels moving across the frame. As monitoring continued, the researchers began seeing larger visitors too, including Indian gaur and leopards. Giant squirrels also appeared in the footage. Some animals came so close to the camera that it could barely capture their bodies. Akshita recalls moments when "you can barely see the hooves." For a team hoping to understand whether wildlife would use the pond, the variety of visitors was encouraging. But what caught Akshita's attention was how some animals appeared to be returning to the same spot. "If we keep it on across seasons in the year, you see them getting used to that spot," she says. "Earlier they may have found it by chance, but now they recognise it." The repeated visits suggested that some animals were becoming familiar with the water source. Meanwhile, the camera was helping the researchers observe wildlife that might otherwise pass through the forest unseen. Across 390 camera-trap nights, they documented visits by several species. Among those recordings were the five clips of the mainland leopard cat drinking from the pond on 7 March 2024. "My co-founder and I were just really excited to see that this happened," Akshita says. Their excitement came from knowing how difficult it could be to photograph a species like this, particularly in a region with so few previous records. A wild cat that Goa had never photographed The mainland leopard cat is actually one of Asia's most widespread wild cats. It is found across parts of India, Southeast Asia, China, Taiwan, Japan and the Russian Far East, and is listed as Least Concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Yet there are still gaps in our understanding of where these cats live in India. Most records come from the southern Western Ghats, the Himalayas and the Northeast. In the northern Western Ghats, photographic sightings have been particularly scarce, with only two previously documented in the wider region. Wildlife checklists had suggested that leopard cats could occur in Goa, but researchers lacked photographic evidence from the state. The footage from Akshita and Atul's pond helped fill that gap. Part of the challenge is the animal's behaviour. Leopard cats are small, shy, mostly active at night and often move through dense vegetation, making them difficult to observe. "This cat doesn't work the same way tigers or leopards do," Akshita explains. "It's small, elusive, shy, and mostly active at night." Researchers can sometimes recognise individual cats through their coat markings, but obtaining repeated camera-trap records across large forests takes considerable time and effort. And that effort needs funding, which can be difficult to secure for lesser-studied species. "Wildlife research highly depends on funding," Akshita says. "And funding often goes towards larger species or species in conflict with humans." As a result, smaller carnivores often receive less research attention, even though they perform important roles within forests. Leopard cats, for instance, feed on rodents and other small animals, helping regulate prey populations. Understanding their movements and habitats can help researchers learn more about how these forest ecosystems function. This is why even a single confirmed photographic record can be valuable. It tells scientists that a species is present in a particular landscape and gives them a starting point for further research. For Akshita, the Goa finding also shows what can emerge from a relatively small conservation experiment. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nature's Nest Goa (@natures_nest_goa) Could more forests benefit from this idea? Creating an artificial pond like the one used in the project costs approximately Rs 30,000 to Rs 40,000, Akshita estimates. A basic camera trap can cost between Rs 8,000 and Rs 10,000, while a higher-end model costs around Rs 25,000. "This is in general a very low-cost plan," she says. The pond can provide a water source during dry months, while the camera trap helps reveal which animals visit the surrounding area. Akshita says nature resorts in Karnataka have already begun discussing similar interventions. For privately owned properties bordering forests, carefully planned projects like these could offer a way to contribute to conservation while learning more about local wildlife. But they also require an understanding of how different animals might respond. For instance, if smaller animals begin using the pond, could larger predators follow? "It could," Akshita says. "And I'm very sure a lot of bigger cats do use these areas, and maybe nature resorts don't even know them yet." That possibility makes careful monitoring important. People living or working near forests may have little idea of the different species passing through their surroundings, especially at night. And as Akshita points out, learning about those animals doesn't always require creating a new water source. "If you want to know what's in your backyard," she says, "sometimes you don't even need a waterhole. Just set up camera traps near good forest habitat." Her team's experience in Goa offers an example of why that curiosity matters. They began by noticing a stream that dried up every February. They followed the paths animals had made, created a small pond and placed a camera beside it to see who would come. The footage revealed a variety of animals visiting the water, including a leopard cat that had never been photographically documented in Goa before. Five short video clips gave researchers a new wildlife record and drew attention to a small wild cat that remains poorly studied in this part of India. And it all began because two researchers noticed that the animals in a patch of forest might need somewhere to drink.

items.descriptionOriginal: "1 Plant, 100 Uses" explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. Sugarcane is a familiar sight across India's agricultural landscape. Its sweet juice is a popular summer drink; its stalks are crushed to make sugar and jaggery, and its leaves can be used as cattle fodder. But the plant's usefulness does not end when the juice has been extracted. India produced 454.61 million tonnes of sugarcane in 2024-25, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare's Agricultural Statistics at a Glance 2024-25. Beyond sugar production, the crop also supplies raw materials for industries that use its fibrous residue and other by-products. From generating electricity and making paper to producing compostable tableware and enriching agricultural soil, sugarcane offers several uses beyond the kitchen. Even the fibrous residue left after crushing the stalks can become a valuable raw material for industries. Research by Indian agricultural institutions highlights how different parts of the crop can be put to use. Here are ways this everyday plant finds a purpose well beyond the sugar bowl. 1. Sweeten everyday foods Sugar is the most familiar product made from sugarcane. Its juice is processed to extract sucrose, then crystallised into the sugar used in homes, restaurants, and food manufacturing. Sugarcane is a familiar sight across India's agricultural landscape. Photograph: (Saveur) The crop also supplies traditional Indian sweeteners such as gur (jaggery) and khandsari sugar. Jaggery is made by boiling concentrated sugarcane juice until it solidifies and is widely used in regional sweets, laddoos, halwas, and traditional preparations. The Government of India's One District One Product portal provides further information on sugarcane-based products such as jaggery and molasses. 2. Make a refreshing drink Fresh sugarcane juice is a popular street-side drink across India, particularly during summer. Vendors crush the stalks to extract the juice, often serving it with lemon, ginger, or mint. The juice can also be boiled down to make jaggery. In traditional production, the fibrous residue left after extraction may be burnt to provide heat for boiling the juice. This allows one part of the plant to help process another. 3. Create compostable tableware The fibrous residue left after extracting sugarcane juice is called bagasse. Its fibres can be processed into plates and other disposable tableware, offering an alternative to conventional plastic products. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research's Central Institute for Research on Cotton Technology has developed a technology to produce disposable paper plates using sugarcane bagasse and banana pseudostem fibres. According to ICAR's technology note on creating wealth from agricultural waste , a production unit could manufacture between 10,000 and 30,000 paper plates a day, depending on its size. The process uses compression moulding to turn the fibres into usable products. This provides sugarcane-processing industries another way to use the residue left behind after crushing the stalks. 4. Generate electricity Bagasse can also serve as fuel. Sugar mills burn this fibrous residue in boilers to produce steam, which drives turbines to generate electricity. The electricity helps meet a mill's own energy requirements, while facilities with suitable infrastructure can supply surplus power to the grid. According to a Press Information Bureau release from the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy , sugar mills have used bagasse-based cogeneration plants to produce steam and electricity for their operations and generate additional power for sale. 5. Turn waste into paper Bagasse contains cellulose , a component of plant fibres used in paper manufacturing. After suitable processing, it can be converted into paper and other fibre-based products. The Institute of Wood Science and Technology, under the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education , explains how bagasse can be used to manufacture particle boards. It also identifies the material as a potential source of pulp for paper production. Its juice is processed to extract sucrose, then crystallised into the sugar used in homes, restaurants, and food manufacturing. Photograph: (Gardening Know How) Using this residue can create another source of raw material for industries that rely on plant fibres. 6. Feed farm animals Sugarcane can support livestock farming, too. The green tops and leaves left after harvesting can be used as dry fodder for cattle, particularly when conventional fodder is scarce. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research's study on sugarcane trash as fodder explains how the material can be chopped and mixed with green fodder and concentrate feed. Its nutritional limitations mean it should be used as part of a balanced ration rather than as a complete feed on its own. 7. Enrich agricultural soil Press mud, also known as filter cake, is a by-product separated during sugar juice clarification. It contains organic matter and plant nutrients that can be useful in agriculture. After appropriate treatment, it can be incorporated into compost and soil amendments, helping return organic matter to farmland . Its composition should be checked before application to make sure it is suitable for the intended use. This provides another route for putting sugar-industry residues to productive use instead of treating them solely as waste. 8. Make particle boards Sugarcane bagasse can be used to manufacture particle boards, which are made by processing plant fibres or particles and binding them into sheets. These boards can be used in certain furniture and interior applications. The Institute of Wood Science and Technology's research on bagasse particle boards describes the material's fibre content and its potential in board manufacturing. This application turns a residue from sugar production into a material that can serve the construction and furniture industries. Fresh sugarcane juice is a popular street-side drink across India. Photograph: (Juice at Home) One crop, many possibilities Sugarcane's value lies not just in its sweet juice but also in the many products that can be made from its different parts. Making better use of these materials can reduce waste and create additional value for sugar mills and farmers. The key is to choose suitable processing methods so that more of the crop can be used productively.

items.descriptionOriginal: Ten years after a childhood bike crash, Rika Matsuda unfolded an origami crane a stranger who witnessed the crash had given her and found a message written inside -- a Japanese expression meaning "cherish the moment," or more fully, that we should treasure each encounter because it may never come again. The man had slipped the words in quietly, without drawing attention to them, letting them wait until she was ready. What the story reveals is something almost too simple to name: that a caring stranger's gentleness, offered in a few unhurried minutes at a water fountain, can fold itself into a life and stay there. "He didn't say anything," Matsuda recalled. "He just smiled and handed me the origami crane."

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine arriving at a popular tourist destination alone. You want to explore the place, take in the landscape, and spend a few hours at your own pace. But what happens if you feel unsafe, cannot find a working public facility, or need help navigating an unfamiliar area? And who do you turn to if something goes wrong? For women travelling alone, access to assistance can shape how comfortable they feel exploring a place. Kerala is seeking to address these concerns through its Green Marshal initiative, which aims to place trained personnel at selected tourist destinations to assist visitors, monitor safety and improve the upkeep of public spaces. The first phase is expected to create around 180 jobs, bringing local workers into the day-to-day management of tourist destinations. More than a safety checkpoint The Green Marshals are being envisaged as a visible, accessible point of contact for visitors. Their responsibilities will include monitoring tourist spots, assisting travellers, identifying problems and helping ensure that basic facilities remain functional. For a women exploring an unfamiliar destination, knowing whom to approach when she needs assistance can make a difference. The presence of trained personnel could also help visitors report concerns and seek support without having to navigate an unfamiliar administrative system. The initiative comes at a time when independent travel is an important part of the tourism landscape . Women travelling alone may have to assess unfamiliar surroundings, access to facilities and the availability of help while planning their journeys. However, the effectiveness of such a programme will depend on more than deploying personnel. Their visibility, training, ability to respond to complaints and coordination with the relevant authorities will determine how useful they are when a visitor actually needs help. The tourism department has indicated that Green Marshals will receive training in environmental responsibilities, destination management and interactions with tourists. This is intended to prepare them for the range of situations they may encounter while on duty. Who looks after the destination? Safety is only one part of the programme. Green Marshals will also be responsible for maintaining cleanliness, overseeing waste management and contributing to environmental protection at the sites where they are deployed. The tourism department has indicated that Green Marshals will receive training in environmental responsibilities, destination management and interactions with tourists. Photograph: (indiaunbound) A tourist destination is not simply a place people visit. It is also a public space that requires regular maintenance. Waste left behind by visitors, poorly maintained facilities and gaps in waste disposal can affect both the visitor experience and the surrounding landscape. Their role could be particularly relevant at destinations where visitor numbers place pressure on local infrastructure and natural surroundings Can local employment strengthen tourism? The first phase is expected to generate around 180 jobs. Beyond creating employment, the initiative proposes a role for local workers in managing the places that attract visitors to their communities. People familiar with a destination may be well placed to identify maintenance gaps, guide visitors and flag emerging concerns . Yet, the programme's long-term impact will depend on how it is implemented. The destinations selected for deployment, the number of personnel stationed at each site, the availability of reporting mechanisms and the process for responding to complaints will all matter. So will clarity on how Green Marshals coordinate with police, tourism officials and other relevant agencies when a situation requires intervention beyond their remit. When in Kerala, make time for Kovalam! #DreamSeason #InGodsOwnCountry #TravelVibes #KeralaTourism https://t.co/wKrSoYu40f — Kerala Tourism (@KeralaTourism) September 9, 2026 For women, the important question will ultimately be whether assistance is accessible and effective when needed. For the environment, it will be whether regular monitoring translates into better waste management and more responsible upkeep . A destination becomes more welcoming not merely when people arrive, but when they can explore it with confidence and when the place itself is cared for. Whether Green Marshals can deliver on that promise will become clearer as the programme takes shape across the state's tourist spots. Sources: 'Kerala To Deploy Green Marshals At Tourist Destinations From October' : By Rooplekha Das, Published on 14 September 2026 'What is Green Marshals, the Kerala initiative aimed at boosting women's safety?' : By Debolina Roy, Published on 14 September 2026

items.description: Ολοκληρώσατε την πρωινή σας ανάγνωση των Nice News, αλλά εξακολουθείτε να λαχταράτε μερικά αναζωογονητικά μέσα που προκαλούν σκέψη — θα μπορούσαμε να προτείνουμε να στραφείτε σε ένα podcast στη συνέχεια; Είμαστε μεγάλοι θαυμαστές του μέσου (τόσο πολύ που κυκλοφορήσαμε μια σεζόν του δικού μας podcast πέρυσι!) και λατρεύουμε πώς αυτές οι ηχητικές εκπομπές μπορούν να ενημερώσουν, να εμπνεύσουν και να διασκεδάσουν σε καθημερινές στιγμές της ημέρας.…
items.descriptionOriginal: You’ve finished your morning Nice News read but are still craving some uplifting, thought-provoking media — might we suggest turning to a podcast next? We’re big fans of the medium (so much so that we released a season of our own podcast last year!) and love how these audio shows can inform, inspire, and entertain during mundane moments of the day. We rounded up nine engaging shows that we think are worth a spot on your playlist, whether you’re doing the dishes, walking the dog, or just looking to unwind on the couch. No Such Thing As a Fish Prepare to laugh and be amazed. The recipient of the Heinz Oberhummer Award for Science Communication in 2019, No Such Thing As a Fish features researchers from the BBC’s comedy game show QI who spotlight a trove of hilarious and mind-boggling facts they’ve dug up over the previous week. The episodes are sure to leave you smiling after each listen. “It explains what the Second World War and carrots have to do with each other or how long you have to cook a space egg,” per a statement from the Oberhummer Awards. “And while you listen, laugh, and marvel for 40 minutes, you often don’t notice how much you’ve learned.” On Humans A favorite of Nice News Assistant Editor Rebekah Brandes, On Humans seeks to answer three questions: “Where do we come from? How did we get here? And what kinds of creatures are we?” In each episode, host Ilari Mäkelä interviews scholars primarily about our origins as humans, delving into specific topics like shamans , why we laugh , and the early days of farming . The show “always leaves me feeling smarter and more curious,” Rebekah said. Good Hang With Amy Poehler Amy Poehler isn’t trying to dole out advice or “make you better” — she’s simply looking for a good time. In Good Hang , which won the first-ever Golden Globe for best podcast earlier this year, Poehler interviews celebs and other “fun people” to provide a cozy, relaxed alternative to the plethora of self-improvement-focused media out there. Start with standout episodes featuring Jennifer Lawrence, Seth Meyers, and Tina Fey. Home Cooking Pals Samin Nosrat, author of Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat , and Hrishikesh Hirway, creator and host of the podcast Song Exploder , dished up cooking advice for amateurs with a side of friendly banter in Home Cooking , which ran from 2020-2025. A self-described perfectionist, Nosrat explained to Vogue in 2020 that the show centers a different mindset around cooking: “It’s about putting something out there to make people feel comforted and like they have technical support in the kitchen and some way to pass the time by hanging out with these funny, very dorky friends.” Unconditional With Maggie Lawson Animal lovers know there’s something special about the bonds they share with their pets — and this podcast celebrates exactly that. Hosted by Psych actor Maggie Lawson, the series explores the special connection celebrities like Henry Winkler and Janel Parrish have with their pets, and features interviews with animal experts about the “healing effects” of our furry friends. “Anyone who is obsessed with their pets will feel so seen by this podcast,” said Nice News Writer Marika Spitulski, adding, “I already want to be [Lawson’s] friend and hang out with her dog Linus.” Weirdly Helpful How can we take control of our “news diet”? And what’s considered proper handshaking etiquette in our modern age? These questions and more are answered in Weirdly Helpful , a series of bite-size episodes (each around 20 minutes or less) that spotlight guests who cover unexpected but intriguing ways to make life better. “Thanks for making me feel inspired while giving me concrete steps to evolve,” one reviewer wrote. Happier With Gretchen Rubin In 2024, we picked Gretchen Rubin’s brain about practical ways to lead a happier life — and in her award-winning podcast, the author and happiness researcher shares more strategies, ideas, and personal anecdotes to inspire you to live joyfully. Try one of her “A Little Happier” episodes for a quick fix; each lays out a lesson in five minutes or less. You can also check out her “Move Happier” series, intended to be paired with 26 minutes of movement as part of her Move 26 in ’26 challenge . The Allusionist If you’re a fan of NPR’s “Word of the Week” series, we bet you’ll love The Allusionist , which won smartest podcast at the 2018 British Podcast Awards. In each episode, host Helen Zaltzman dives into the intricacies of language, including the etymology and cultural significance of some of our most used words (and profanities), with a hefty dose of humor. Start with her April 13 episode “Hues” to learn why some of Merriam-Webster’s lexicographers took decades to define certain color names. Get Birding On HBO Max, you can catch Sean Bean ruling his corner of Westeros as the Stark family patriarch in Game of Thrones . On your podcast feed, though, he’s a soothing presence pointing out birds as they fly over his garden. The English actor took over as host for Season 4 of Get Birding , inviting ornithologists into his backyard and beyond to talk all things avian. The biweekly episodes, which you can also watch on YouTube, cover everything from why birdsong makes us feel good to why birds sing at daybreak . RELATED: How to Build a Personalized Mental Health Tool Kit for Days When You’re Feeling Down When you buy books through our links, Nice News may earn a commission, which helps keep our content free.

items.title: 5 ελάχιστα γνωστά γεγονότα για το «It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown», το ιδιαίτερο που άλλαξε την τηλεόραση
items.titleOriginal: 5 little-known facts about ‘It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown,’ the special that changed TV
items.description: Είμαστε μόλις μερικές εβδομάδες μακριά από τα φαντάσματα, τους καλικάντζαρους, τις μάγισσες και τα γλυκά που κάνουν το Halloween τόσο πολύ διασκεδαστικό. Αλλά για πολλούς, οι διακοπές δεν θα ήταν ολοκληρωμένες χωρίς να παρακολουθήσουν ένα από τα πιο εμβληματικά αφιερώματα της τηλεόρασης: It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown. Αυτό το κλασικό Peanuts, βασισμένο στο κόμικ του Charles M. Schulz, είχε κοινό κοινό…
items.descriptionOriginal: We’re just a couple of weeks away from the ghosts, ghouls, witches, and candy that help make Halloween so very fun. But for many, the holiday wouldn’t feel complete without watching one of television’s most iconic specials: It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown . This Peanuts classic, based on Charles M. Schulz ‘s comic strip, has had audiences tuning in joyfully for six decades! Schulz co-wrote the episode alongside director Bill Melendez and Lee Mendelson. Its gist is a hopeful one. The character Linus believes, against all odds, that the “Great Pumpkin” will appear with presents for all. And as many times as we might have watched, some little tidbits have been missed along the way. Here are five little-known facts behind one of the greatest 25-minute animated shows ever released. View this post on Instagram ‘I got a rock’ One of the most often quoted lines from this special was Charlie Brown deadpanning, “I got a rock,” after all of his friends (including his beloved beagle, Snoopy) had their pumpkin baskets filled to the brim with candies. In an interview for The Wrap , writer Meriah Doty talks with Jill Schulz, Charles’ youngest daughter. Jill playfully shares, “Every once in a while, my sister and I thought it’d be fun to give somebody a rock. I’m pretty sure they knew we were joking.” Even more delightfully, Jill shares that her father once told her people often mailed candy to his California studio because they felt great empathy for Charlie Brown. “I remember him telling me and chuckling about it that people were feeling bad for Charlie Brown and sending the candy.” While she doesn’t remember getting to eat the candy, she notes that the Schulz family had plenty of goodies. “My parents were from Minnesota, so there was always plenty of ice cream, Hostess cupcakes, Dolly Madison—one of the first sponsors of the Peanuts specials.” Who exactly voiced Snoopy? While, of course, different voice actors have played the lovable beagle Snoopy over the decades, the director Bill Melendez himself voiced Snoopy’s little sounds in It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown . In an interview with Emmy TV Legends , Melendez explains that it was a “happy accident.” After messing around with different voices and speeds, he insisted that “barks” and “arfs” simply wouldn’t do. They needed a “unique sound for Snoopy.” He tried different sounds and asked the editor to “run it fast,” and that’s what ended up in the show. “From then on,” he jokes, “I got stuck with it. The Screen Actors Guild said, ‘You can’t make these sounds unless you’re a member of the Screen Actors Guild.’ So here I am, a member of the union.” First aired in Canada The Vintage Vault, a YouTube channel dedicated to fun facts about TV shows from yesteryear, shares that this delightful Halloween special first aired in Canada. In a voiceover, they explain that the show originally aired on October 26th, 1966. “CBC Television aired it before CBS got their hands on it the very next day, October 27th. That’s right, Canadian kids saw Linus waiting in that pumpkin patch a full 24 hours before American audiences did.” They add that this was especially unique at the time. “In an era when U.S. networks treated their content like Fort Knox gold and wouldn’t even share outtakes with their own affiliates, letting Canada premiere a Peanuts special was basically unheard of. Makes you wonder if the Great Pumpkin is actually Canadian, eh!” It inspired so many other specials In a Facebook post, CBR (formerly Comic Book Resources) notes how incredibly inspirational the Halloween special has been. “Sixty years ago, It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown helped change Halloween television forever. It helped establish a television tradition that countless shows would eventually embrace. From The Simpsons to South Park , Halloween specials have become an annual event. And the Peanuts gang helped make it possible.” The Simpsons indeed made this a tradition with their “Treehouse of Horror” episodes, which continue to this day. The soundtrack was recorded in just one day The Vintage Vault also reports that the song we know so well was recorded in a single day, a few weeks before the show aired. They share, “The music was recorded in one day, October 4th, 1966. Mark that date in your mental calendar. That’s when Vince Guaraldi and his sextet walked into Desilu’s Gower Street studio in Hollywood.” They highlight the studio’s significance, revealing its connection to another beloved sitcom of its era: “The same studio where I Love Lucy was filmed and where the entire score was recorded in a single marathon session. The same walls that once echoed with Lucille Ball’s comedic genius now became the birthplace of one of the most iconic soundtracks in animation history.” The post 5 little-known facts about ‘It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown,’ the special that changed TV appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Parrots are incredible mimics. They can learn, remember, and near-perfectly imitate human language to the tune of hundreds or even thousands of words. But few people realize their vocal abilities go far beyond “Polly want a cracker.” Sometimes, domestic parrots can be quite adept at sound effects and even, yes, lowbrow comedy. Cruz the African grey parrot masters the “fart sound” Cruz is an African Grey Parrot who has become a massive social media star over the last few years, amassing nearly 400,000 combined followers between Instagram and TikTok. Why such a devoted following? It’s not just because he’s a mouthy little guy with an impressive vocabulary. Cruz has earned fans primarily with his sense of humor and signature sass. A few years back, he even learned to imitate a human fart sound—quite convincingly—which helped catapult him to new levels of fame. Note that he’s imitating a fart and not actually passing gas. Fascinatingly, parrots and birds in general do not fart. Popular Science writes that birds don’t carry the right bacteria in their guts to produce gas. Their digestive cycle is also incredibly short, meaning food doesn’t stay in their stomach for long, and they poop every 15 minutes or so. There’s just no time for gas to build up. But that hasn’t stopped Cruz from becoming obsessed with the sound. View this post on Instagram Cruz has learned that butts and farts earn him lots of laughs Cruz the African Grey has an appreciation for all kinds of toilet humor. In one recent video , he makes up a song about his owner’s “fat butt,” singing it over and over again as she laughs hysterically. Cruz also likes to follow up his fart noises with different punchlines. In one of his most-viewed videos of all time, he “lets one rip” and then says, “Wow.” Parrots aren’t just exceptional mimics; they’re extremely intelligent, too. Studies peg them as being about as intelligent as a 5-year-old human . So while they might not understand exactly what a fart is or what human laughter means, they are smart enough to pick up on the energy. They enjoy the burst of positive, bonding energy that comes from making their owners laugh, which explains why Cruz keeps dipping his toe in the potty humor well over and over. That crude and silly sense of humor? Yep, pretty on par with a 5-year-old. View this post on Instagram Parrots are intentional about what they repeat Parrots don’t understand the whole of human language, syntax, grammar, and contextual meaning. But they are hyper-aware of what happens when they say a word or make a sound, and they can understand how their noises provoke a reaction in context. They can learn a shocking amount just through natural interactions with humans. But with training, researchers have found that parrots can correctly identify hundreds of shapes and objects, do some limited counting, and understand basic descriptors like “bigger” or “different.” One famous African grey parrot named Alex learned on his own to say “I’m sorry” after he’d done something wrong. Not because he was actually contrite, but because he’d picked up on how humans used the phrase to de-escalate tense situations. View this post on Instagram Whatever the reason for Cruz’s fascination with farts, butts, vulgar sayings, and toilet humor, his hundreds of thousands of fans can’t seem to get enough. He’s a smile and a laugh waiting to happen, and a must-follow for anyone who wants to inject something positive into their social media feeds. One commenter summed it up perfectly: “If ever I’m in a bad mood I just have to listen to Cruz and I’m instantly cheered up.” The post Woman’s African grey parrot is obsessed with butts and fart noises. It’s the joy we all need. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: On March 11, 1999, Fred Rogers was inducted into the Television Academy Hall of Fame. By then, his long-running PBS series Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood had won nearly every award possible, including four Daytime Emmys . But arguably, Rogers got something he’d cherish even more than a prestigious award that night: a reunion with one of the many kids whose lives his kindness had changed. Welcome to the neighborhood In 1981, Jeff Erlanger, then a 10-year-old from Wisconsin whose spinal surgery left him a quadriplegic, was invited onto the show by Rogers himself. During the segment, Erlanger explained how he managed his disability: both the logistical things, like using his wheelchair, and the emotional challenges. In typical Fred Rogers fashion, he listened carefully, asked meaningful questions, and gave Erlanger the same thoughtful attention he gave every kid who appeared on the show. There was no attempt to make Erlanger’s disability into a lesson or spectacle. The conversation was merely about getting to know him as a person. Then, they sang one of Rogers’ popular songs together: “It’s You I Like.” The segment closed with Rogers saying, “I hope you’ll come back to visit again.” The unscripted, touching conversation remained one of the beloved TV hosts’ favorite moments on the show. They stayed in touch over the years as Erlanger grew up to be a disability advocate. Nearly 20 years later, the connection was still strong Still, Rogers had no idea that nearly two decades later, he’d reunite with a now-29-year-old Erlanger. The instant recognition and elation on Rogers’ face when he saw the grown-up Erlanger said it all. As one viewer wrote, “The fact that Mr. Rogers recognized this young man immediately is proof of the caliber of human that was and will always be Mr. Rogers.” Another seconded, “You know he is a truly loving person when a child he hasn’t seen in years, and even though he became an adult, still recognizes him without even a single moment of hesitation.” “On behalf of millions of children and grown-ups, it’s you I like,” said Erlanger, harkening back to the song from all those years ago. The audience gave them both a standing ovation. They both left a legacy Both Rogers and Erlanger have passed on, but not before making the world a better place. Rogers spent his career reminding generations of children (and adults, really) that they are worthy of love just as they are. Meanwhile, Erlanger used his own experience to advocate for greater understanding and inclusion for people with disabilities. Who’s to say if Rogers helped Erlanger find that path? But it’s certainly a nice thought. Even now, as folks watch this reunion again and again, Rogers and Erlanger get another chance to make the world better. items.descriptionOriginal: Brendan Fraser might be making the greatest career comeback ever , having won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his dramatic, transformative role in “ The Whale .” But the OG Fraser fans (the ones who watch “Doom Patrol” solely to hear his voice and proudly pronounce his last name as Fray-zure, for this is the proper pronunciation) have known of his remarkable talent since the ’90s, when he embodied the ultimate charming , dashing and slightly goofball Hollywood action lead. Let us not forget his arguably most well-known and beloved ’90s character , Rick O’Connell from the “Mummy” franchise . Between his quippy one-liners, Indiana Jones-like adventuring skills, and fabulous hair, what’s not to like? During a double feature of “The Mummy” and “The Mummy Returns” in London, moviegoers got the ultimate surprise when who should walk in but Brendan Fraser himself, completely decked out in Rick O’Connell attire. The brown leather jacket. The scarf. Everything. Stephen Colbert and Brendan Fraser at the Montclair Film Festival 2022. Photo credit: Montclair Film/Wikimedia Commons What Fraser said to the crowd that night “I am proud to stand before you tonight,” he told the audience. “This is a film that was made in Britain. You should know that! Even the second one, too. Be proud. Thank you for being here.” He continued, “We didn’t know if it was a drama or a comedy or a straight-ahead action or romance, a horror picture, more action, all of the above. No idea until it tested in front of British audiences. Thank you for that.” Fraser then asked the crowd if anyone hadn’t actually seen the movie yet, before shouting, “Outstanding!” when somebody raised their hand. He then quickly made a polite plug, encouraging people to go see “The Whale” before whisking himself away, saying, “I won’t take up any more of your time.” Uh, yeah…I don’t think any time spent with Brendan Fraser is a waste. Do you? Watch: Mummy 4 is officially happening The answer to whether we’ll see Fraser back as Rick O’Connell is now a resounding yes. The Mummy 4 was officially confirmed in early 2026, with Fraser and Rachel Weisz both set to reprise their roles , and a release date of October 15, 2027. Directors Matt Bettinelli-Olpin and Tyler Gillett are attached to direct. This article originally appeared three years ago. It has been updated. This article originally appeared 5 months ago. items.title: "I Struggled To Walk": Born With Clubfoot, 38-YO έχει κάνει ποδήλατο σε 4 χώρες και έχει κάνει πεζοπορία στα 15000 πόδια
