Θυμάται μια εποχή που ο γιος της δυσκολευόταν να περπατήσει. Σήμερα, τον παρακολουθεί να ξεκινά ταξίδια που τον απομακρύνουν εκατοντάδες χιλιόμετρα από το σπίτι, κάπως…
items.descriptionOriginal: Whenever Shijoy Jacob leaves home for a cycling expedition, his mother, Pushpa, worries about his return. "I feel scared when he goes," she says. "I don't even want to sleep until he comes back." She remembers a time when her son struggled to walk. Today, she watches him set off on journeys that take him hundreds of kilometres away from home, sometimes across international borders. In 2026, Shijoy, 38, was pedalling from Cambodia into Vietnam with three friends. There was no support vehicle following them. They carried their own luggage, repaired their own punctures and sometimes cycled more than 100 kilometres in a day. Along the way, they stopped for tea and meals, taking their time to explore the places they passed. But growing up in Mumbai, Shijoy had once wondered whether he would even be able to run alongside his friends. Pushpa once took her son to hospitals so he could walk comfortably. Today, she watches him cycle across countries and trek in the Himalayas. "I was born different, but I don't think that should define me and stop my dreams," he says. "If I have thought of any goal, it should be achieved." Today, Shijoy has cycled through India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and trekked to 15,000 feet in the Himalayas. 'Will I be able to do it?' Shijoy was born in Mumbai with a congenital limb deformity, commonly referred to as clubfoot or congenital talipes equinovarus. Both his legs were twisted inward, with the left more severely affected. When he was born, his parents took him to doctors in Mumbai. One of them put both his legs in plaster and asked the family not to bathe him for nearly a month. It was only after an uncle took the family to another hospital in Worli that they realised something was wrong. The plaster was removed, and his mother, Pushpa Jacob, was asked to massage his legs regularly. For Pushpa, the months that followed meant repeated hospital visits, treatment and uncertainty. She had asthma herself, but still travelled from Vikhroli to Worli with her young son. Eventually, she left her job so she could care for him full-time. After further treatment, Shijoy underwent surgeries on both legs. As he grew and began crawling and walking, he wore corrective joint shoes. Later came heavy, ankle-length orthopaedic boots that he wore until he was around eight. As a child, Shijoy wore corrective footwear for years as he learnt to walk. "I was a kid that time, so I don't remember much," he says. "But I remember feeling sad because I wasn't able to do what other children were doing. I used to wonder, 'When will I be able to do it? Will I be able to do it?'" His parents, however, kept telling him that he would. By around nine, he had stopped wearing the heavy footwear and slowly began participating in activities that had once seemed out of reach. But the fear of getting hurt stayed with him. "I thought something might happen to my leg," he says. For Pushpa, watching her son slowly become more mobile was an emotional experience. "I used to have a lot of pain in my heart when I saw him," she recalls. "I always prayed to God that his feet should get better." She had no way of knowing what the years ahead would bring, but she kept doing what she could to help him walk. As he grew, that meant getting customised footwear made for him. "I didn't think he would be able to play like this," she says. The 10-kilometre run that made him trust himself For years, Shijoy's approach to physical activity was cautious. But sometime after college, he began testing his limits, one small step at a time. He started running a little, played cricket, and gradually became more comfortable with physical activity. Around 2014-15, he took part in his first 10-kilometre race. For Shijoy, completing those 10 kilometres was a breakthrough. "Slowly and gradually, I started challenging myself." The run gave him the confidence to move forward without constantly worrying about getting hurt. It also changed the way he looked at his childhood. He began to understand that what he had experienced could be part of his story without becoming the definition of his future. Shijoy's first 10-km race helped him trust his body and opened the door to longer runs, treks and cycling expeditions. That growing confidence was tested again in 2021. While trekking in Maharashtra's Sandhan Valley, Shijoy fell and dislocated his shoulder. The terrain made it difficult to simply be carried out, so he tied a cloth around his injured arm and trekked until he reached the exit. Despite the injury, he had managed to complete the trek on foot. And the following year, he would take on a different kind of challenge. From Mangaluru to Goa: The ride that started it all Cycling entered Shijoy's life in a serious way in 2022. He had learnt to cycle as a child, but until then, it had mostly been something he did casually around his neighbourhood. Then, three friends suggested a longer ride from Mangaluru to Goa. His first reaction was disbelief. "Mangaluru to Goa? That is too much. I thought I wouldn't be able to do it," he recalls thinking when his friends first suggested the ride. But despite his doubts, Shijoy decided to give it a try . He and his three friends took their bicycles by train to Mangaluru, where they began their journey towards Goa. On their very first day, they covered around 105 kilometres. In 2022, a cycling trip from Mangaluru to Goa changed Shijoy's idea of what he could achieve. His friends had been prepared to wait for him if necessary. Instead, Shijoy kept pace. "That was next level," he recalls. "Even my friends were like, 'You said you can't do it, and you are hitting 100 kilometres.'" That first ride gave him the confidence to attempt longer journeys. The group later cycled through Tamil Nadu and Kerala before deciding to take their bicycles outside India. In 2024, they flew to Sri Lanka with their cycles and covered more than 600 kilometres across the island, travelling through both hilly terrain and coastal stretches. Then, in 2026, came their Cambodia-to-Vietnam expedition. None of them are professional cyclists. All four have full-time jobs. Shijoy works in HR, and their trips are planned around their limited annual leave. Usually, they set aside around 10 days for a cycling expedition. They do not follow an intensive training schedule either. About a week before a trip, they meet for a single practice ride to see if they can still handle the distance. For Shijoy, the most important preparation happens in the mind. "Your mind should be strong," he says. "A lot of people can ride for 10 kilometres, but they give up before reaching that distance." For Shijoy, the lesson from these journeys is clear: "Endurance is important, but your mind is the main thing." Shijoy and his three friends have cycled across India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, planning their expeditions around full-time jobs. The group has cycled through temperatures touching 40 degrees Celsius, carried five to seven kilograms of luggage, repaired their own punctures and navigated unfamiliar roads without knowing where they would find the next cycle shop. Yet the journeys are not simply about covering kilometres. They stop for tea and meals, enjoy the company of one another and soak in the places they pass. "We don't want to hurry too much," Shijoy says. "We want to explore the world at a slow pace." A 14-kg backpack, snowfall and his toughest trek yet While cycling had helped Shijoy grow more confident about travelling long distances, his first Himalayan trek brought a different set of challenges. In May 2026, he travelled alone to join a trekking group for a seven-day Himalayan expedition that reached approximately 15,000 feet. It was his first Himalayan trek. He had been nervous about it from the beginning. He had also fallen sick during the training period and could not complete the prescribed preparation. At one point, he considered cancelling. With no support vehicle, the group carries its own luggage, fixes punctures and navigates unfamiliar roads, making every cycling expedition a test of endurance. But he went. The trek was very different from cycling. He carried a 14-kilogram backpack and climbed higher each day while dealing with cold, rain and snowfall . As the altitude increased, the reduced oxygen made even a few steps exhausting. "There were times when taking five steps was difficult," he recalls. But he had made up his mind to complete the trek. "I didn't want to go back and just say I came back." He completed the trek with his backpack. For the boy who once watched other children run and play while he stood on the sidelines, reaching 15,000 feet was a milestone he could scarcely have imagined during his childhood. And through every expedition, one person remains at the heart of that journey. "All credit goes to my mom," Shijoy says. "She is the one because of whom I am here today." From his first 10K run to cycling across countries, Shijoy continues to prove to himself that every big journey begins with a small step. Pushpa once carried her son to hospitals because he could not walk on his own. Today, she watches him carry his own backpack into the Himalayas and his bicycle across international borders. She is still afraid whenever he leaves. But that fear now sits alongside pride. Shijoy, meanwhile, has no intention of stopping. The distances have grown since his first 10K and his first 105-kilometre cycle ride, but he still approaches each new challenge one step at a time. "Take small steps, one step at a time, and it will take you to a lot of places," he says. All images courtesy of Shijoy Jacob

items.description: Για σχεδόν 40 χρόνια, οι λάτρεις της άγριας ζωής μπορούσαν να επισκεφθούν καταφύγια τίγρεων σε ολόκληρη την Ινδία, αλλά τα οργανωμένα σαφάρι στο Indravati στο Chhattisgarh παρέμεναν απρόσιτα. Ο λόγος δεν ήταν η έλλειψη άγριας ζωής. Ήταν ο κίνδυνος να ταξιδέψεις μέσα στο δάσος. Βρίσκεται στην περιοχή Bijapur του Bastar, ο Indravati ανακηρύχθηκε καταφύγιο τίγρεων το 1983. Αλλά καθώς οι Μαοϊκοί ξεσηκώνονται…
items.descriptionOriginal: For nearly 40 years, wildlife lovers could visit tiger reserves across India, but organised safaris at Indravati in Chhattisgarh remained out of reach. The reason was not a lack of wildlife. It was the danger of travelling through the forest. Located in Bastar's Bijapur district, Indravati was declared a tiger reserve in 1983. But as Maoist insurgency and armed conflict affected the region, travelling through large parts of the forest became risky. Even forest officials struggled to reach certain areas for patrolling and wildlife monitoring. With safety a major concern, organised tourism remained suspended for nearly four decades. Now, that is beginning to change. As security conditions improve, the Chhattisgarh forest department is preparing to welcome tourists again, with 1 November 2026 announced as the target reopening date. For visitors, it could mean the chance to finally explore a forest that has remained largely outside India's wildlife tourism circuit. But what makes Indravati worth discovering after all these years? What has remained hidden from tourists for 40 years? Spread across 2,799 sq km, Indravati is one of Central India's largest tiger reserves. Its forests shelter tigers, leopards, sloth bears, gaurs, wild dogs and deer. It is also an important habitat for the endangered wild water buffalo, Chhattisgarh's state animal. Indravati's long absence from the tourism circuit has also meant that parts of its wildlife remain poorly documented. Photograph: (deccanchronicle) According to figures presented by the forest department, the reserve has six tigers, although a fresh population assessment is underway. With security improving, forest officials are now able to patrol and study areas that were previously difficult to access. And recent research has already revealed something remarkable. In 2025, researchers studying the Indravati River, which runs along the reserve's boundary with Maharashtra, came across an animal that local villagers had been telling them about. They called it neer billi , meaning 'water cat'. Following information shared by local communities, researchers surveyed stretches of the river. One February morning, they spotted 10 smooth-coated otters feeding on fish. When the animals noticed the researchers, one raised an alarm and the group quickly slipped into the water. The discovery provided the first photographic evidence of these otters in the reserve in roughly 25 years. The forest department is mapping safari routes based on the reserve's Tiger Conservation Plan and will decide where vehicles can operate. Photograph: (Kanha National Park ; npg.news) Smooth-coated otters are classified as Vulnerable, and their presence offers encouraging clues about the river's ecosystem. However, researchers also found evidence of hunting and snares, highlighting the need to protect these animals and their habitat. With tourism now being planned, protecting this wildlife becomes even more important. How will safaris return without putting wildlife at risk? The forest department is starting small. Instead of opening the entire reserve, officials are preparing two or three safari destinations. Vehicles are being procured, while proposed routes are undergoing wildlife and security assessments. The number of tourists and vehicles allowed inside will also be restricted according to how much disturbance the forest can safely handle. Some areas may remain closed to visitors. The reopening could also bring new opportunities for families living around Indravati. Officials are exploring ways to involve local people as guides, drivers and hospitality providers, along with possibilities for homestays and selling locally made products. For communities that have lived alongside these forests for generations, tourism could become another source of income, provided these plans translate into opportunities on the ground. After nearly 40 years, Indravati is preparing to welcome a new kind of visitor. And while spotting a tiger or a rare otter may be exciting, the real success of this reopening will lie in something bigger: ensuring local families benefit while the animals continue to have a safe home, long after the first safari vehicles arrive. Sources: Indravati Tiger Reserve -National Tiger Conservation Authority:Project Tiger 'Chhattisgarh Indravati Tiger Reserve Reopens To Tourists After 40 Years' : By Vaishnavi Dixit, Published On 24 September 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: What if retirement offered an opportunity to give something back to the natural world? In Virginia's Shenandoah Valley, two retired neighbors, John Rice and John Sessler, are doing just that, transforming their farmland into thriving habitats for wildlife. Working alongside Smithsonian conservation scientists, they've helped protect nearly 2,500 acres of private land, creating corridors where animals can move, find food, and flourish. Their days are spent removing invasive plants, restoring native wildflowers, and watching the landscape slowly come back to life. What began as a personal love of nature has become something much larger: a living legacy of conservation, nurtured through patience, dedication, and the simple joy of caring for the land.

items.descriptionOriginal: Before he could welcome people into a restaurant of his own, Gurbachan Singh Maan spent 10 years knocking on strangers' doors. He had arrived in Britain from Punjab in 1936, carrying a suitcase of goods to sell. Far from home, he walked London's streets day after day, earning a living and saving whatever he could. It would take him a decade to open a small restaurant. In 1946, he finally opened 'Punjab India Restaurant' on Braham Street in Aldgate. Eight decades later, his family still runs it at 80 Neal Street in Covent Garden. Now in its fourth generation, it is recognised as the oldest North Indian Punjabi restaurant in the UK. But keeping its doors open has brought its own struggles. From financial hardship to threats of redevelopment and a global pandemic, each generation has faced challenges in carrying forward what Gurbachan started. From door-to-door sales to a Punjabi restaurant Back in the 1930s, opportunities for Indian migrants in Britain were limited. Peddling was one of the few trades available to them, and the work meant long, tiring days in a city that was not always welcoming. When Gurbachan Singh Maan opened Punjab Restaurant, he wanted to offer Indians in London a taste of home. Today, his great-grandson Amrit Maan continues to carry that vision forward. Yet those years also helped Gurbachan understand something about the Indian community living in London. Far from their families and the places they had grown up in, people missed the simple comfort of a familiar meal. That was the need his modest restaurant hoped to meet: a place where Indians living in London could enjoy the Punjabi food they knew from home. When he finally opened 'Punjab Restaurant' in 1946, it was a modest operation on Braham Street. But demand soon grew. As word spread through London's Indian community, particularly among people at the Indian High Commission and the city's growing population of Indian students, the small restaurant on Braham Street could no longer keep up. So, the family relocated to 80 Neal Street in Covent Garden, an address that would become closely associated with the Punjab name for decades to come. Four generations later, Gurbachan's own words still guide how the family talks about the business. His great-grandson Amrit Maan recalls him saying : "We rise by uplifting others." How a grandson carried forward the family kitchen As Gurbachan's family grew and more relatives arrived from Punjab, the restaurant business grew with them. His sons and grandson went on to open two more restaurants, 'New Punjab' and 'Sardar', extending what had started as one man's gamble into a small family network of Punjabi kitchens across the city . At just 15, Sital Singh Maan arrived in London from Punjab and moved into the rooms above his grandfather's restaurant. Years later, he would take over the business and help it grow. But 80 Neal Street remained at the centre of the family business. When Gurbachan decided to retire, he passed the restaurant to his grandson, Sital Singh Maan, who was just 15 when he arrived in London. Sital moved into the rooms above his grandfather's restaurant, where he went to school while also helping with the family business. Over the years, the restaurant became a familiar part of his everyday life. So when he took over around 1970, he was taking charge of a place where he had spent much of his childhood. By then, Punjab's reputation was growing, and the restaurant needed more space to welcome its customers. Sital began expanding it, first sideways, then backwards, and eventually upwards. But through these changes, the food remained central to the family business. 'Punjab' was, by several accounts, among the f irst restaurants to introduce tandoor cooking to Britain , a tradition that continues to shape its menu today. For Sital, getting the flavours right mattered. "We blend spices such as coriander, cumin, cinnamon and turmeric," he says. He explains that blending the spices helps bring out their flavours. He also likes to think that the spices offer health benefits alongside the taste. As Punjab Restaurant grew, Sital Singh Maan expanded its premises to accommodate more diners. Through every change, the family kept its Punjabi cooking traditions at the heart of the business. As Sital worked to grow the restaurant, another challenge was emerging. The family had spent years building its business on Neal Street, but now the future of the neighbourhood itself was under threat. A street worth saving By the 1970s, the restaurant Sital had spent years helping to grow faced a threat he could do little to control. Plans to redevelop large parts of Covent Garden put several streets and buildings at risk of demolition, including Neal Street, where Punjab Restaurant stood. For Sital, this was personal. His family had spent years building their lives around the restaurant. Along with other local shopkeepers and restaurateurs, he joined the effort to protect the neighbourhood from demolition. Walk down Neal Street today, and you'll find caf s, bookshops and restaurants. It's easy to assume they've always been there. But the street could have looked very different if people like Sital hadn't fought to protect the buildings and businesses that had become such a familiar part of the neighbourhood. In the 1970s, redevelopment plans threatened to erase parts of Covent Garden, including Neal Street. Sital Singh Maan joined fellow local business owners in fighting to protect the neighbourhood they had helped build. The threat to Neal Street passed, but the family would face other difficult years. Recessions came and went. Financial crises squeezed margins across the hospitality industry. And in 2020, the pandemic forced restaurants across the country to shut their doors, many of them for good. 'Punjab' responded by keeping its kitchen staff on and turning the restaurant into a community kitchen, cooking well over two lakh meals for homeless charities, food banks and frontline workers over the two and a half years that followed. For Amrit, feeding people during the pandemic was a way of carrying forward something his family had believed in for generations: helping those around them. The same kitchen that had served customers for decades was now preparing meals for people who needed them most. In 2022, Amrit received an OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire), a British honour recognising contributions to society, for his charity and community work. But when he spoke about the recognition, his thoughts went back to the family that had built the restaurant. " Seva , or selfless service to the community, has been the ethos of our family business since it was founded," he said at the time. Amrit shares that the honour also belongs to the generations before him, beginning with his great-grandfather, whose decision to open a small Punjabi restaurant had brought the family this far. A fourth generation steps in Alongside carrying forward his family's tradition of helping others, Amrit also had the responsibility of running the restaurant his great-grandfather had started all those years ago. When the pandemic forced restaurants across Britain to close, Punjab Restaurant turned its kitchen towards a different purpose, preparing well over two lakh meals for homeless charities, food banks and frontline workers. He had taken over its day-to-day operations as Managing Director in 2012, while his father, Sital, remained Chairperson. With both generations still involved, the family continued looking for ways to grow the business while holding on to its roots. Amrit continued expanding the restaurant into neighbouring properties. In 2023, the family also acquired a second address at 190 Shaftesbury Avenue, taking the Punjab name beyond Neal Street for the first time in the restaurant's history. That same year, King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited the family's stand at Covent Garden and sampled some of the restaurant's signature dishes. For Amrit, taking the family business into its fourth generation comes with the responsibility of keeping its traditions alive while allowing it to grow. "Preserving that legacy requires balancing tradition with progress. I try to create a balance between respecting the values the business was built on while still allowing it to change with the times." A family-run Punjabi restaurant, 80 years later For all the expansion, growth and shifting addresses, Punjab Restaurant remains largely a walk-in restaurant. It seats diners on a first-come, first-served basis and only takes complete groups rather than splitting tables between separate parties. For the Maan family, running a restaurant has always meant more than serving food. The principle of seva, or selfless service, has guided its work across four generations. Reservations exist, but they are the exception rather than the rule, reserved mainly for special occasions, large groups of more than 10, or diners visiting from overseas. Anyone walking in outside the 7 to 9 pm rush is likely to find a table within minutes. That walk-in approach offers a glimpse of the restaurant's character today. The family has expanded the business and seen it through redevelopment threats, recessions and a pandemic, while continuing to welcome diners through its doors. Eight decades and four generations after Gurbachan opened a small restaurant on Braham Street, Punjab Restaurant continues to welcome diners in Covent Garden. The city around it has changed, and so have the generations running the kitchen. But the family continues to do what Gurbachan set out to do all those years ago: serve familiar Punjabi food to people looking for a taste of home.

items.descriptionOriginal: A 13-year-old has earned the distinction of being “America’s top young scientist” for 2026, taking first place in 3M’s prestigious Young Scientist Challenge. Raji Doshi, an eighth grader from Farmington, Connecticut, won the contest with an algae-based invention that could help save marine ecosystems. She and nine other finalists aged 11-14 created their prototypes over the summer, each of them working with a mentor to develop their ideas. Raji won the $25,000 grand prize after the challenge’s final events on Oct. 12 and 13, presenting a natural system that addresses ocean acidification by increasing alkalinity and removing carbon dioxide. Ocean acidification, which began during the industrial revolution, is primarily caused by the seawater absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The change in PH reduces the abundance of carbonate ions: essential structures that many marine lifeforms, like corals and crustaceans, need to build their shells and skeletons. “Raji’s project reminds us that when you’re passionate about something, you can use that interest to change the world,” her mentor, 3M product engineering specialist Deborah Isabelle, said in a press release . “She loves collecting seashells and was distressed that ocean acidification is starting to damage the seashells and the creatures that live inside them.” The contest also recognizes two runners-up, who each received a $1,000 cash prize. The three honorees, all girls, point to promising changes in the STEM arena, where women have historically been underrepresented. Seventh grader Aaisha Asif came in second place for her eco-friendly adhesive made from natural proteins; and ninth grader Sharvi Mahajan took third for her EEG-based device that tracks fatigue and predicts microsleep, alerting drivers and others in high-risk fields. Looking at the full lineup of finalists , it’s clear the future of science is bright. “The 3M Young Scientist Challenge highlights the incredible potential of young people to tackle real-world challenges through science,” said William Brown, 3M Chairman and CEO. “The talent and creativity displayed by this year’s finalists was exceptional, and we congratulate Raji on earning the title of America’s Top Young Scientist.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Reading Time: 5 minutes 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras Spending all day in a truly comfortable bra is already a challenge. Tracking down one made from 100% organic cotton – with legitimate certification to prove it – is even harder. The market for comfortable 100% organic cotton bras has expanded, but quality is all over the place, and plenty of labels that claim “natural” can’t back that up with documentation. Why Organic Cotton Matters for Everyday Comfort Most people don’t realize how chemically loaded a conventional bra can be. Standard synthetics and treated cotton often carry azo dyes, formaldehyde finishes, and PFAS, substances pressing directly against skin for hours every day. The Center for Environmental Health detected BPA in sports bras from major mainstream brands at levels up to 40 times the established safe limit. Certified organic cotton changes that picture. GOTS certification (Global Organic Textile Standard) controls the entire supply chain from farm to finished garment, banning the synthetic pesticides and chemical finishes that standard cotton processing allows. For people with sensitive skin, eczema, or simply a preference for fewer synthetics, a GOTS-certified bra isn’t a luxury; it’s a practical choice. And comfort follows naturally. Organic cotton breathes well, wicks moisture without relying on synthetic coatings, and softens with wear rather than pilling or stiffening. The absence of harsh dyes also means less skin irritation over time. 1. Q for Quinn Q for Quinn is a small, family-owned Canadian brand founded in 2018 by Melita Cyril, who originally designed organic cotton socks for her son’s eczema before expanding into a full line of natural-fiber essentials for adults and children. The brand’s bra and bralette lineup covers several styles: a criss-cross bralette, a pointelle bra, a racerback sports bra, a full bust sports bra, and a shelf tank. Fabrics come in either 95% organic cotton with 5% elastane or 100% organic cotton. The fully cotton styles are biodegradable end-to-end, using natural rubber-cotton elastics and 100% organic cotton thread throughout; pricing starts between $52 and $64, and sizing runs XS through 3XL. Every applicable product carries GOTS certification through Ecocert Greenlife under license 256894. Product pages spell out each component – body fabric, elastic, thread, and closures – so nothing in the construction is hidden. Undergarments are made in certified facilities in Tirupur, India, and the brand excludes chlorine bleach, azo dyes, and formaldehyde finishes from its entire supply chain. Where it fits: Women with sensitive skin, those avoiding chemical exposure during workouts, and shoppers who want full material transparency in a bra, particularly for low-to-medium impact activities like yoga, Pilates, and walking. 2. Roaman’s Roaman’s is a plus-size fashion retailer with roots stretching back decades, now operating as part of FullBeauty Brands and headquartered in Indianapolis. The brand focuses exclusively on sizes 12W through 44W, it doesn’t start from a smaller size and grade up, which makes it genuinely purpose-built for plus-size shoppers rather than an afterthought extension of a standard range. The catalog spans a wide range of women’s clothing, intimates, swimwear, sleepwear, tops, bottoms, and shoes. With over 100 years in women’s fashion, the brand positions itself as an industry leader and pushes fashion-forward designs at prices that don’t require a big budget. Shopping options include the website, a printed catalog, and a store credit card. Roaman’s clothing was used to dress cast members on TLC’s 1,000 lb Sisters , a placement that put the brand in front of its core audience. Customer support runs through phone and email, and the website offers account management, order tracking, and a rewards program. Where it fits: Plus-size shoppers looking for a wide selection of intimates and clothing in one place, with consistent sizing across categories. Worth checking: Roaman’s is a general plus-size fashion retailer. Shoppers seeking certified organic cotton bras should confirm material details before purchasing, as the brand doesn’t position itself around organic certification. 3. Siella Siella is a Canadian lingerie brand launched in 2020 out of Montreal, backed by Chateau Bodywear, a family business with over 75 years of experience manufacturing underwear and lingerie, founded in 1945. That manufacturing depth gives Siella a level of vertical control that newer brands rarely have. The line focuses on wireless bras, underwear, and loungewear, with a stated emphasis on comfort, support, and a second-skin fit. Siella describes its approach as designed by women, blending modern femininity with everyday comfort. Prices range from approximately $25 to $105 USD, with bundle discounts of up to 20% available. Free shipping kicks in on orders over $95. U.S. customer service operates on EST timezone at +1 800-665-0589. The brand emphasizes organic cotton options and benefits from its parent company’s manufacturing infrastructure, which supports tighter control than outsourced production typically allows. Siella has been featured in Diary of a Toronto Girl’s roundup of top lingerie brands. Where it fits: Shoppers who want wireless bras that prioritize everyday comfort and are open to a Canadian brand with a long manufacturing history behind it. Worth checking: Organic cotton certification details aren’t publicly disclosed the same way as some competitors, so shoppers should confirm certification before purchase if that’s a deciding factor. 4. Bestform Bestforms, Inc. is a company founded in 1985 and headquartered in Camarillo, California, with 51 to 200 employees. The company operates as a B2B manufacturer in the business forms and print industry, producing patented membership card products, integrated labels, variable barcoding, unit set forms, continuous forms, and custom labels. Bestforms describes its model as “trade only,” meaning it works through intermediaries rather than direct-to-consumer channels. The company’s tagline is “BestCards, Labels and Digital Solutions, Forms,” and its track record centers on responsive development for commercial printing needs. Bestforms does not appear to operate as a lingerie or apparel retailer. No bra products, organic cotton garments, or related consumer goods appear in the company’s product lineup. Where it fits: Business clients in need of commercial printing, label manufacturing, or custom card production, not a category match for consumers shopping for organic cotton bras. Worth checking: Shoppers searching for lingerie under this name should confirm they’ve reached the correct brand, as the bestform.com domain belongs to a commercial printing manufacturer, not an apparel company. 5. AmpleBosom AmpleBosom is a UK-based online and mail-order retailer founded in 1999 by Sally Robinson, operating from a family-run farm in Old Byland, North Yorkshire. The company specializes in bras, lingerie, swimwear, nightwear, and clothing, with a size range that runs from 28 to 58 in AA through N cups, one of the widest ranges available anywhere in the market. AmpleBosom doesn’t manufacture its own products; instead, it stocks bras and lingerie from established names including Empreinte, Elomi, and Fantasie. The team is estimated at 25 to 100 employees, and the business has stayed independent since it launched. It earned early recognition when the BBC series Inside Dot Coms featured it in 2000, notable for an e-commerce model that was well ahead of the mainstream at the time. Expert bra fitting advice is offered both in-person and virtually. Payment is accepted online, by mail, or by phone; in-store payment isn’t an option. Pricing varies by brand and item, with promotions available throughout the year. Where it fits: Shoppers who need larger or harder-to-find cup sizes and want access to multiple specialty lingerie brands in one place, with expert fitting support available. Worth checking: AmpleBosom is a UK retailer; U.S. shoppers should factor in international shipping costs and delivery times, and should verify whether specific organic cotton options are available among its current brand selection. Bottom Line Brands in the comfortable 100% organic cotton bra space span a surprisingly wide range – certified organic specialists, plus-size fashion retailers, and, in at least one case, a commercial printer that has no business appearing on this list. For shoppers who prioritize verified certification, full material transparency, and construction that’s genuinely gentle on sensitive skin, the real options thin out fast. Roaman’s and Siella both serve comfort-focused buyers but from different angles: Roaman’s through extended plus sizing, Siella through wireless everyday styles. AmpleBosom suits anyone needing an unusually wide cup range paired with professional fitting guidance. Know what matters most to you – certification, sizing, support level, or country of origin, and the right choice gets a lot clearer. The post 5 Top Brands for Comfortable 100% Organic Cotton Bras appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable Reading Time: 3 minutes How Grid Modernization Is Making Clean Energy Reliable The lights flicker during a storm, and you suddenly notice the grid you rarely think about. More of your power now comes from the sun and wind, which don’t follow a schedule. Clean energy can remain steady as the weather shifts because modern grid upgrades help balance supply and demand and ensure reliability behind the scenes. What Is a Smart Grid? A smart grid is an electrical network that uses digital technology to monitor and manage power from the source to the home. It sits at the heart of grid modernization, which involves upgrading the physical equipment and digital tools that generate, move and manage electricity. Older grids relied on one-way communication, but a smart grid lets utilities and customers share information in both directions. The most visible piece is the smart meter. In 2022, utilities in the United States had about 119 million smart meter installations , or roughly 72% of all electric meters. Advanced versions have built-in two-way communication, so they can record and send data instantly. A smart grid relies on several connected parts working together: Smart meters: These devices track your energy use and share it with your utility. Sensors: Devices along power lines and equipment can flag problems before they spread. Automated switches: These switches can reroute power around a fault without waiting for a crew. Energy storage: Batteries save extra power , such as midday solar, for use when demand rises. Two-way communication: This link lets utilities and customers share data and respond to each other quickly. Why Does the Traditional Grid Struggle With Clean Energy? The grid that powers your home took shape in a very different energy world. Large, steady power plants sent electricity to homes long before rooftop solar panels or wind farms existed, and the equipment reflects that history. Today, over 70% of the power grid is over 25 years old. Variable solar and wind, plus growing demand, strain equipment with limited ability to see or adjust to changes in real time. Engineering and utility consulting firms help power companies plan upgrades to infrastructure, sensors and smart meters. Each improvement can give operators a clearer view of the system, enabling them to respond to changing conditions sooner and keep clean power flowing. That approach can turn an older network into a smart grid built for clean energy. How Can Upgraded Grids Balance Wind and Solar Power? Wind and utility-scale solar generated 17% of U.S. electricity in 2025, up from under 1% in 2005. However, wind and solar only produce power when the wind blows or the sun shines, unlike power plants that can ramp up on demand. Modern grids tackle the gap between when clean power is available and when you need it. Batteries can store surplus solar power for evening use, and smart controls can automatically adjust the grid as supply rises and falls. Forecasting can help operators predict wind and solar output in advance and prepare accordingly. Demand response programs can also encourage you to shift energy use to times when clean power is plentiful, easing pressure on the grid during peak hours. These tools may help wind and solar become a steadier part of your power supply. Why Does Extreme Weather Raise the Stakes for Reliability? Severe storms, heat and winter weather can all disrupt steady power. From 2000 to 2023, 80% of major U.S. outages were weather-related, with the latest decade seeing about twice as many as the first. A modernized grid can help keep your community’s power on when conditions turn rough. Sensors can quickly detect damage, and automated switches may isolate the damaged section so the outage affects fewer neighborhoods. Self-healing systems, which detect faults and automatically reroute electricity, can keep more homes connected. Microgrids, which are small, local networks that can operate independently, may also help restore power faster. Together, these tools can shorten the time you spend in the dark and make clean energy feel dependable even during difficult weather. What Could a Smart Grid Change in Your Daily Life? Smart grid upgrades can make clean energy more useful in daily life by changing how power moves to and from your home: Rooftop solar: A two-way grid can make it easier to send extra power from your panels back to your community. Time-of-use pricing: Some utilities offer lower rates during off-peak hours, which rewards flexible habits. Electric vehicle charging: Smart charging can schedule your car to charge during off-peak hours. Quicker repairs: Better monitoring may help crews find and fix problems faster. What Can You Do to Support Steady Clean Power? Clean energy is only as reliable as the grid that carries it. Grid modernization works quietly in the background to keep clean power steady in your home, from the smart meter on your house to the upgrades down the street. A good next step is checking what your own utility offers, such as smart meter data, time-of-use plans or solar programs. Small choices like these can help a more dependable, cleaner grid take shape, and you can find the options are closer than you think. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems Reading Time: 4 minutes How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems Readers of this site tend to think in systems. A beaver dam that restores a creek, a wildlife crossing that saves panthers, a court that grants fish legal standing, these stories share a common thread: small, deliberate interventions ripple outward into healthier ecosystems. Pest control rarely gets discussed in that same frame, but it belongs there. Every spray, bait, or barrier a homeowner chooses either supports or undermines the insects, birds, and soil organisms that keep a neighborhood’s ecology functioning. That matters more than most people realize, because household pest management sits at the intersection of two things this audience cares about deeply: protecting pollinators and other wildlife, and making smart use of limited resources. The choices homeowners make about ants, termites, or rodents do not stay contained to a single yard. Chemicals drift, water carries residue, and beneficial insects do not distinguish between a target pest and a pollinator caught in the same treatment zone. In fast-growing communities around San Antonio, this tension shows up constantly as new development pushes into former ranchland and native habitat. Homeowners in that region increasingly ask pest professionals to treat infestations without collateral damage to the monarchs, native bees, and birds that still move through these corridors. Companies like EcoForce Pest Management , which serves the Cibolo, Texas area, reflect a broader shift in the industry toward targeted, lower-impact treatment methods that still get rid of pests without broadcasting pesticide across an entire property. Why Pest Control Choices Ripple Through Local Ecosystems Pollinators are not a side issue in this conversation, they are central to it. Insect pollinators add more than fifteen billion dollars in crop value annually in the United States, which means any pest control practice that harms bees, butterflies, or other pollinating insects carries a real economic cost well beyond the yard where it happens. Routine, calendar-based spraying, the kind that treats a property on a fixed schedule regardless of actual pest pressure, increases the odds of harming these beneficial insects compared to treatment that responds to an actual, identified problem. This is why the distinction between reactive, blanket pesticide use and targeted treatment matters so much ecologically. A homeowner who sprays broadly “just in case” is making a bet that trades short-term convenience for long-term harm to the insects and soil life that keep local food webs intact. A homeowner who waits for evidence of an actual infestation, then treats only the affected area, protects far more of the surrounding ecosystem while still solving the immediate problem. What Actually Drives the Cost of Pest Management Cost in pest control is rarely about the price of a single treatment, it is about how often treatment has to happen and how much damage accumulates before anyone intervenes. A termite colony left undetected for a year can cost thousands of dollars in structural repair, while the inspection that would have caught it early costs a fraction of that. Rodents chewing through wiring create fire risk and expensive repairs that dwarf the cost of sealing an entry point before they ever got inside. According to EPA , integrated pest management relies on monitoring, pest-identification thresholds, and preventive habitat changes, reserving chemical treatment as a targeted last resort rather than a routine first response. That framework is not just ecologically sound, it is financially sound too, because prevention and early detection cost less than remediation almost every time. The expensive scenarios are always the ones where a problem went unnoticed long enough to cause structural or health damage, not the ones where someone paid for a seasonal inspection. Where Eco-Friendly Methods Pay Off Over Time Eco-friendly pest control is sometimes assumed to be the pricier, more delicate option, but the opposite is often true over a multi-year horizon. Sealing cracks, managing moisture, and removing food sources reduces the pest pressure that would otherwise require repeat chemical treatments. Fewer treatments mean lower cumulative cost, and they mean less pesticide entering soil and groundwater where it can affect everything from earthworms to the birds that eat them. The table below lays out some of the real tradeoffs between reactive, chemical-heavy pest control and a more preventive, ecologically minded approach, using figures drawn from EPA guidance on integrated pest management. Factor Reactive, broadcast treatment Preventive, IPM-based approach Pollinator risk Higher, due to non-targeted exposure Lower, treatment is targeted to confirmed pests Core strategy Calendar-based spraying regardless of need Monitoring and thresholds before any chemical use Economic value protected Not factored into treatment decisions Helps preserve pollinators tied to $15B+ in annual crop value Lowest-cost prevention step Rarely prioritized Sealing entry points, moisture control, sanitation What this comparison shows is that the cheapest long-term option and the most ecologically responsible option tend to converge. A property that invests in sealing, drainage correction, and regular monitoring spends less over five years than one that relies on repeated broad-spectrum treatments, even though the upfront preventive work can look like an added expense in year one. Smart Places to Economize Without Compromising Protection Homeowners who want to save money without cutting corners ecologically should focus their budget on the structural fixes that prevent infestations in the first place, since these are the cheapest interventions with the longest payoff. Sealing foundation gaps, repairing damaged screens, and fixing leaky pipes that create standing water all cost far less than a single severe infestation treatment, and they address the root conditions that attract pests to begin with. These are also the steps least likely to involve any chemical exposure at all, which makes them a win on both the cost and ecological fronts. Where spending does make sense is in professional inspection and identification, because misdiagnosing a pest problem leads to wasted treatments and wasted money. A targeted response to a correctly identified pest, applied only where needed, almost always costs less over time than a generic, whole-property treatment applied out of uncertainty. For readers who care about the pollinators, soil organisms, and backyard wildlife that this site regularly celebrates, that targeted approach is also the one that does the least collateral damage to the ecosystem right outside the door. The post How Eco-Friendly Pest Control Saves Money and Protects Local Ecosystems appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including 20,000 octopuses hiding in well-studied waters off the California coast, what Indonesian mosque loudspeakers have to do with earthquake survival, and a garden chore you now have a very good reason to skip. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Intro Karissa: Hello everyone, I’m Karissa. Arielle: And I’m Arielle. Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. Arielle: Yes, welcome back. Karissa and I have had a week off because last week we had a wonderful guest episode with #CreateConnectCare. If you missed it, then definitely go check it out. Karissa: Yeah, it was a great episode. I missed sharing the solutions, though, last week. Mm-hmm. And I’m glad to be back with you today, Arielle. Arielle: Yeah, there’s a lot of seasonal solutions and, uh, just some, some fun discoveries that happened this week. But before that, how are you, Karissa? Karissa: Doing well over here. The weather has been so strange all across the globe. We’re already in the middle of October, but you would not know it, at least in California. Arielle: Yeah, it’s been really weird here in the Netherlands as well. Every time I think autumn has arrived, and it’s, like, rainy and gloomy, and I’m kind of getting into my cozy vibe, the next few days are, like, sunny and warm again. Not that I’m complaining. I would not complain about that, but it’s just, it’s a bit hard to get into the seasonal rhythm… I don’t know if our listeners and fellow Optimists are feeling similarly, but I know that I’m just feeling a bit weird. Other than that, nothing to report on my end. Karissa: Yeah. I feel similarly. I guess I’m enjoying a little bit of stillness between the busy summer months and the festive season. We’re gonna go full force into the holidays here, and then this year will be over, so um- Arielle: Yeah. It definitely went by quickly, but there’s still a lot of positive news out there to share before the end of the year. And if you want all of those positive solutions straight to your inbox, then you should consider signing up for our daily or weekly newsletter. You can do that on our website, or the link is in the show notes. Karissa: And if you want these solutions and more on your social media feeds, we’re @optimistdaily on everything except X, where we’re @OdeToOptimism. Arielle: You can also reach me and Karissa directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We would love to get any suggestions, comments, questions, feedback, so feel free to shoot us an email. Karissa: Before we go any further, we’d love to thank our Optimist Daily Emissaries who financially support us. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is in the show notes. If financially supporting us isn’t in your budget right now, we thank our Optimists who share these solutions and follow us on socials. Arielle: Yeah, there are a lot of free ways to support us, and we appreciate everyone who does that. Karissa: And without further ado, Arielle, I think we should dive into this week’s new solutions. Australia’s renewable energy record Karissa: The first one that we had to share this week is “Australia sets a new renewable energy record, with rooftop solar leading the way”. So Australia just hit a new record. Solar- and wind-powered 80% of the entire national grid on a single Saturday. And the wild part about that is that more than half of that came not from massive solar farms, but from panels on people’s rooftops. For about 30 minutes, 4.3 million rooftop solar installations collectively carried more than half of the country’s total power load. The researcher who tracks this called it record season. Conditions were so good, he expects these records to get broken again within weeks. These individual homeowners, and not, like, utility companies, drove a national record, and that’s exciting all in itself. Arielle: Yeah, it really drives home the point that the energy transition doesn’t have to center around big infrastructure. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: It’s a reminder that, yeah, if there’s small-scale adoption, then that can really add up quickly. Karissa: Absolutely. And with Australia having an 82% renewable target for 2030, this kind of milestone is expected to become routine. So that is optimistic indeed. Performance anxiety & sport psychology Karissa: The next solution is titled “”How to quiet performance anxiety, according to sport psychology””. A sport psychologist who works with NFL teams and Olympic athletes has a pretty counterintuitive take on confidence. You don’t wait until you feel it, you act your way into it first, fake it till you make it, and the feeling follows. So she has a whole toolkit for doing this in the middle of a high-pressure moment, and the technique that an NFL receiver used after a playoff fumble is one of them. I didn’t know about this technique, but it’s called the learn, burn, return method, which is a three-step process for recovering mid-performance from a mistake. Learn one thing from it, use a physical gesture to signal moving on. For example, the Vikings receiver Adam Thielen made the toilet flush gesture famous in a 2020 playoff game, where he’s just kind of pretending to flush the toilet and get rid of that mistake, which is a fun thing. And then reset it all with a certain phrase. The performance anxiety conversation used to live almost entirely in sports, but I mean, now it’s everywhere, whether it’s in job interviews, presentations, creative work, even dating. So I think it’s important to expand upon this concept. But yeah, there’s a lot of great tips in this article from Cindra Kamphoff, who is a PhD in sport and performance psychology, and she gives a lot of great tips here, including writing powerful phrases before a high-stakes moment, which I really liked that one. So go check it out if you want some more pointers. Coral shade experiment Karissa: The next solution is “”How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave””. Scientists in Florida just published results from an experiment where they literally put little floating umbrellas over coral to protect them from the heat, and it worked. But the lead researcher was pretty blunt. This is triage, not a total solution for coral bleaching. So I loved the images here in this solution, because it really had like… The um- umbrella is kind of a… It, it’s not… I at first pictured an umbrella, like our pop-up umbrella, and I thought that was kind of a cute image, but it’s kind of just a floating, like Arielle: Like a shade, Karissa: basically Shade, yeah. Like a, just a little piece of, um- Arielle: Yeah, like a tarp … Karissa: yeah, a tarp. That’s a great way to explain it. The shaded brain coral started recovering color after these umbrellas were put in, and the unprotected ones kept bleaching through the hottest part of the season. Coral bleaching events used to happen about once a decade, but now they’re happening every five to six years, and reefs don’t have enough time to recover between them. By March 2025, 84% of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures high enough to cause bleaching. The researcher’s quote in this was so honest, that shading is not a cure-all. This is a solution that is kind of just buying time for the bigger problem. Arielle: Yeah. It’s important to address the root problems, but yeah, if we need more time, which we definitely do, then why not? Karissa: Absolutely. Did you know that coral reefs cover less than 0.2% of the ocean floor, but shelter a quarter of all marine species? So that’s a pretty wild ratio, and we gotta protect them, just like we need to protect the rest of our beautiful planet as well. Skincare mistakes Karissa: The next solution is “”The common skin care mistakes dermatologists say are working against your routine””. Five dermatologists were asked what bad skin habits they most want patients to break, and the answer keeps coming back to the same thing. Most of us are overdoing it when it comes to our skin care routine. And there’s also a pimple popping rule in here that I think a lot of people will appreciate, and I’ll start with that one. It’s the one good squeeze rule for pimples. It’s okay to pop a pimple, but if it doesn’t come out on the first try, stop, because continuing just pushes bacteria deeper and can cause those dark spots that stick around for months. I admit if it has a white head, then I have to pop it. But usually, of course, that comes out with the one good squeeze, and it… I do think it’s, it’s very, um, satisfying, so. Arielle: Yeah. No, I’m so guilty of this. I love popping pimples. Karissa: Me too. Arielle: Um, and I will keep going at it, and I have had that, like, hyperpigmentation thing happen. Mm-hmm. And it’s just not cute. Yeah. And I, I have to abide by this. You know what’s really helped me, though? Those pimple patches. So- Karissa: Yeah, I was gonna say the same thing … Arielle: first of all, they’re fun, so you can have, like, a little purple star or whatever on your face instead of a- Yeah … a bright red glaring pimple. Um, but I do it less for, like, the… Well, of course I, I do it so that the pimple will heal, but it’s more so that my fingers just don’t get on it. Because if I see it- Yeah … then I just wanna squeeze it. Karissa: I resonated with the point that skin care has developed a trend cycle that rivals fast fashion. There’s new ingredients, new products every week, and TikTok routines that keep expanding what we’re, you know, supposed to do. So dermatologists really emphasize that sticking with simple is oftentimes better. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah, and just what works for your skin. Because everyone’s skin is different, and you can’t just be chasing the trends all the time if it doesn’t work for your specific type of skin. So if you have a routine that works for you, then just stick to that. Don’t get, like, you know, uh, distracted by the shiny new serum. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Exactly. Flu shot timing Karissa: Next solution is “”Why October is the best time to get your flu shot this year””. Flu is already showing up in emergency rooms across the West, and the numbers are running about seven times higher than the same week last year. Experts are saying October is the window to get vaccinated, and there’s actually a new mRNA flu vaccine in the mix for the first time, which is a really great breakthrough. So yeah, seven times higher than this time last year is pretty rough. It’s in Western states now, but it’s expected to spread east. And the flu vaccine’s effectiveness data is pretty interesting. 29 to 56% effective against of cases that send people to the doctor, but better against severe illness. The framing here with vaccines in general is to remember it’s keeping you out of the hospital, and keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery, which is a quote from the article. About the mRNA flu vaccine, you might recall this term being used for, uh, the COVID vaccine, and it’s now being applied to the flu vaccine for adults 50 and older this season, and it’s supposed to be more effective. Arielle: There was a, a number in this article that kind of broke my heart. It said that last year there were at least 195 child deaths from flu-related causes, and preventing such high numbers could be as simple as just getting vaccinated against the flu. So yeah, and I don’t mean to fearmonger, but it definitely struck a chord with me when I read it. Karissa: Yeah. Tens of thousands of Americans die of flu each season, and that tends to surprise people. I feel like flu deaths are chronically under-discussed. So of course, yeah, like you mentioned, Arielle, not to fearmonger, but get that flu vaccine, and it’s a good time to get it now. Octopus nursery Arielle: Well, on that note, we’re going to bring it to some lighter topics, let’s say. Uh, the first solution that I’m going to share with everyone is titled “Scientists discovered the world’s largest octopus nursery off the California coast”. Scientists were studying one of the most closely monitored stretches of ocean in the world, and somehow missed 20,000 octopuses just hanging out on the sea floor. Turns out there’s a field of hydrothermal springs down there that’s functioning as the world’s largest known octopus nursery, and researchers only found it in 2018. So these hydrothermal springs keep the water warm enough to cut the octopuses’ egg-brooding time from years down to about 1.8 years, which still sounds like a l- a long time to me. Yeah. But if it’s, if it’s cutting more years off of it, then that’s great. And this is why so many octopuses congregate there specifically. The octopuses build their dens from whatever they find on the sea floor, including human objects that have drifted down to the deep sea. This went undetected until 2018 in well-studied water, which raises the question of how many other gatherings like this exist in unmapped thermal fields elsewhere. There’s been growing public fascination, I think, with octopus intelligence and behavior in recent years, and this story lands right in that conversation. And yeah, I, I think I remember when My Octopus Teacher came out, and I think that was kind of when everybody was like, “Oh my gosh, octopuses are actually so, so smart and so cool.” Um, have you seen it, Karissa? Karissa: No, I haven’t, but now I wanna go watch it because I… this solution really, uh, stood out to me this week and I love it, so I’m really interested in learning some more. Arielle: Yeah, this week we have such cute ocean stories, like picturing little corals under their umbrellas and, like a whole bunch of octopuses chilling out. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Making babies. So… Karissa: Yeah, fun stuff. Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers Arielle: The next solution is titled “Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters”. A Japanese disaster scientist had an idea 20 years ago while studying earthquakes in Indonesia. What if the country’s mosque loudspeakers, already everywhere and already maintained daily, could double as earthquake warning systems? That pilot is now underway, and the drop-and-cover finding buried in the story is just as interesting. And if you don’t know what I mean by that, just wait. I will get to it. So Indonesia might have only five to 10 seconds of warning before an earthquake hits, and yeah, the mosque loudspeakers tested five times a day by local communities are more reliable than phone networks that can fail the moment the ground starts shaking. What I mean when I say that the mosque loudspeakers are tested five times a day is that, um, the call to prayer happens five times a day, so they definitely know that the speakers are working because the call to prayer is happening. And the drop-and-cover thing that I mentioned earlier is the standard international advice for when there’s an earthquake. You’re supposed to drop low and cover, like get under a table or something. But this advice was meant for places with well-constructed buildings, and in Indonesia, where homes are often unreinforced masonry, the people who survived earthquakes in the past actually ran outside. You know, there is growing conversation in disaster preparedness about community-maintained infrastructure versus centralized government systems, and this is a real case study for why local trust really matters. Indonesia and Japan are both on the Pacific Ring of Fire, but they have very different building standards, so the survival advice gap is a real public health issue, and I’m happy that this is being addressed with infrastructure that already exists and doesn’t really need any extra upkeep since they’re being used all the time. Egg carton reuse Arielle: The next solution is titled “Six smart things to do with an empty egg carton before you toss it in the recycling bin”. Before you toss your next empty egg carton, hear me out. Those 12 little cups, or 10 or six, depending on how many eggs you get, they turn out to be surprisingly useful around the house, and the seed-starting one especially. So that’s one of the uses that I’m going to get into. You just fill each cup with soil, you plant your seeds in them, and then when it’s time, just plant the whole thing into the ground, and then the cardboard breaks down, and the roots never get disturbed. So that would be something that I would do if I had a garden. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: Another one that I liked was the jewelry organization thing. So you can create little cups for your jewelry, and right now, all of my jewelry is just, like, willy-nilly all over the place in different rooms in tangles. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: So I don’t need a garden to do that one, so maybe I will try that one out. Karissa: Yeah, I, I love this, and there’s really a big momentum around reducing household waste without buying more eco products, and this is about using what you already have. Japanese sweet potatoes Arielle: The next solution is titled “What sets Japanese sweet potatoes apart, nutritionally speaking?” Japanese sweet potatoes are those, like… They just look like sweet potatoes, but they’re generally kind of longer, I find, and they look purple on the outside, and then when you cut them open, they’re white on the inside. And it turns out that even though they are still sweet potatoes, they are doing completely different things nutritionally than the ones, like the orange ones that so many of us know and love. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: And the comparison is more interesting than you’d expect. Japanese sweet potatoes are higher in vitamin C and E and anthocyanins, the same pigments that make blueberries and red cabbage dark, while orange ones are the beta carotene champions. They’re complementary, not interchangeable. The fiber content is about four grams per serving, which puts them in, like, a genuinely filling territory for a carb. And luckily, there’s no evidence-based recommendation for how many to eat per week, so you don’t necessarily need to limit yourself if you end up really, really loving Japanese sweet potatoes. The only thing is that dieticians say, um, make sure you don’t, like, hyper-fixate on them, just like on any food, and don’t make them your only kind of vegetable. Have you tried Japanese sweet potatoes before, Karissa? Karissa: Honestly, I don’t think I have. And I’m kind of not the biggest fan of just, like, normal sweet potatoes either, so they’re okay, but, like, I… And if they’re out, like, at a restaurant or something, like, and you know, it’s in front of me, I’ll eat it, but I usually, like… I, I never feel like preparing it myself. But maybe I’ll give Japanese sweet potatoes a try, and maybe I’ll fall in love with them. Overwintering bees Arielle: The last solution that we are going to share with everyone today is titled “What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees”. This could be considered a counterintuitive one, but maybe not so counterintuitive for longtime Optimists. The best thing you can do for native bees this fall is put down the rake. All that scraggly stuff you’re about to tidy away, the leaf piles, the hollow stems, the dead-looking cane fruit, that’s where the bees love to be. There are over 3,600 native bee species in the US, and most aren’t honey bees. It’s those solitary wild bees that are in steep decline, and most of them nest in your garden over winter. So don’t compost your cut stems in fall. If bees have already nested inside them, composting kills the larvae still developing in there, and I did not know that. I didn’t realize that there’s, like, little baby bees… inside cut stems. Also, try not to worry yourself about the bare patches of dirt in your lawn if you have them. I know it might look like neglected land, but that’s prime bee nesting habitat, apparently. Ground-nesting bees need bare, un-compacted soil to excavate their nests. Karissa: Wow, I didn’t even realize that there were that many, uh, bee species in the US for one, but, um… native bee decline is an issue that feels kind of, uh, abstract until you realize that the solution is literally just doing less yard work, and I love that because- Mm. Yeah … working in the yard can be such a pain. Arielle: Yeah, I mean, I kinda wish I had one. But it can be, uh, it can be toilsome. And maybe the solution sounds familiar to some people… because we have covered No Mow May before, and I think there have been a few articles about, like, just not raking so much in the fall. Yeah. Um, ’cause that doesn’t just help bees, but it also helps other insects and critters that are important for the ecosystem. Quote & Outro Karissa: Well, Arielle, that was a great roundup of solutions, and before we head off for today, we have a positive quote to leave you off with. Arielle: This one is by Robert Frost, and it is, “The best way out is always through.” Karissa: Simple. Arielle: So yes, that’s, uh, yeah, nice and simple, but hard to do sometimes when you’re faced with a situation that you kinda wanna get out of, but you just have to endure and go through it. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: Uh, but yeah. Well, on that note, Karissa and I wish all of you a very happy weekend, and we will be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, stay optimistic. Bye! The post Podcast Transcript October 16th, 2026— Flu is already spreading: why October is the window to get vaccinated, plus nine more solutions first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Soil, Seeds, and Student Power: How Four Canadian Schools are Tackling Food Sovereignty Reading Time: 3 minutes Four schools across Canada show what happens when students are given the tools and trust to build a greenhouse. If you didn’t know it already, students are extremely capable humans, able to tackle projects with a sense of audacity and creativity that (maybe) goes untapped in some older folks. So, when you give them the challenge of growing their own food, they commit, rather wholeheartedly, we should add. It starts as a project, like a club idea, a class assignment, or a response to a funding opportunity, and it becomes something a bit harder to name. A sense of ownership. A connection to where food actually comes from. A reason to show up after school and get dirt under their fingernails. Across four very different Canadian communities, that shift is happening in greenhouses and vertical farms that students built, maintain, and call their own. The Earthlings Climate Club at Sussex Middle School didn’t start big. Five students shared a frustration: nobody at their school was really talking about climate change, so they came up with the idea of building a greenhouse for their breakfast club. The club grew as more students joined, not always because of climate passion, but because their friends were there and it was fun. Those students became advocates too. That’s the lesson the Earthlings want other schools to know: not everyone arrives through the front door of environmental concern, and that’s fine. While waiting for greenhouse materials to arrive (a familiar patience test for rural schools), the students launched a composting program to keep momentum going, earning them a feature in the Telegraph Journal . The greenhouse eventually came together, growing produce for a breakfast club that many students depend on, with ambitions to expand into the cafeteria and local food banks. “Physical hands-on is definitely what I learn through mostly,” said student lead Lyla, “and I feel like we should do more hands-on because it’s way easier to learn.” This next project was never just about the vegetables. For the Ahtahkakoop Cree Nation in Saskatchewan , the greenhouse is one piece of a longer project to rebuild food sovereignty—a way of life that sustained communities for generations before it was systematically disrupted. Youth project lead Jana Sasakamoose framed it quite bluntly: “Many members only get $300 a month to survive off of… It’s hard to meet those needs, let alone basic needs such as food.” Alert Bay students at work building their outdoor greenhouse with the help of First Nations community partners. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . The response was a greenhouse dome chosen for its ability to maximize natural light and air circulation, selected after community consultations on preferred features and plant varieties. Over 250 community members were engaged through canning workshops, gardening sessions, and planning conversations. This is a multi-phase project, with solar panels, underground food storage, and ongoing education all in the pipeline. Alert Bay sits on a small island off the coast of British Columbia, accessible only by ferry. Everything comes by boat, including all the school’s food. With 34 students, 98% of whom are First Nations, and relentlessly windy, rainy weather, a conventional outdoor garden was never going to work. What the school had, though, was community knowledge. Indigenous nations on the island, including the Kwakwaka’wakw, ‘Namgis, and Nawalakw, had already been greenhouse farming, and students came to school with that experience from home. Rather than starting from scratch, Alert Bay Elementary asked its First Nations partners for guidance on suppliers, building techniques, and growing approaches suited to the island’s conditions. The result is a student-maintained greenhouse feeding the school’s hot lunch program, built on the principle of learning from what’s already working. “If we start now,” said student lead Evan, “we can make a difference in the way our school and community think about food and waste.” Oilfields High School in Diamond Valley, Alberta, has been running a vertical farm out of a modified shipping container for years, growing microgreens, lettuce, and herbs that students sell to local grocers, restaurants, and their own school concession. The problem was pests. Before the N:OW for Net-Zero funded biosecurity headerhouse was built, the farm lost 30% of its crops to contamination. Since construction (done by hand with shop students and retired local tradespeople), that loss rate has hit zero. Students at Oilfields High School surround the adult lead, Cindy Watts, as they prep to sell their school-grown microgreens to their student body at lunch. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . CTV News Calgary and CBC have covered the farm , and in April 2026, their Member of Parliament, John Barlow, visited to recognize the students’ work firsthand. This year, the farm launched microgreen smoothies at the school concession twice a week, earned a local grocer’s support for purchasing the school’s greens, and is now actively recruiting youth volunteers and exploring university and company sponsorships to support students as they transition out of high school. A greenhouse, a dome, a modified shipping container, and a grow light in a boot room. The form changes, but the impulse is the same: students decide that food sovereignty isn’t someone else’s problem to solve, and they get to work. The post Soil, Seeds, and Student Power: How Four Canadian Schools are Tackling Food Sovereignty appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Τι με δίδαξε η άνοια για το να ζω μέσα σε μια βαρετή εποχή

items.description: Την ώρα που ο πρόεδρος Τζο Μπάιντεν έδειχνε τόσο εμφανή σημάδια γνωστικής παρακμής που αναγκάστηκε να εγκαταλείψει την προεδρική κούρσα το 2024, η άνοια του πατέρα μου χειροτέρευε.
