items.descriptionOriginal: J ust as President Joe Biden was showing signs of cognitive decline so conspicuous that he was compelled to drop out of the presidential race in 2024, my own father’s dementia was worsening. He lived with us, and yet he lived in another reality entirely. One where he no longer understood that the food on his plate was his, and the food on my daughter’s was hers. One where he grew agitated when we wouldn’t let him walk in a rainstorm. One where he no longer knew my name. Being in the bizarre world of his deteriorating mind was not unlike reading the headlines each day as the months, and then years, went on. My once sweet and Buddhist dad’s abandonment of norms, his misplaced anger, his seemingly selfish relentlessness, were a product of his disease — the nerve cells in his brain were no longer communicating properly. His context for just about everything fell away. Courtney and her father at Thanksgiving. Credit: John Cary The country’s deterioration was different, a deliberate poisoning more than an organic disease, but the parallels were there. It felt pathological how callous and hard our country had become. But there was also something happening underneath my dad’s deterioration. My whole family was learning to collectively care for him — taking him on drives and scream-singing Tom Petty when he would get sundowners (a medical term for late-day confusion in dementia patients), reading Pema Chödrön aloud to him in the backyard, letting him have our ice cream cones when he would reach for them. And our neighbors were in on the tenderness. They’d call when he wandered too far or help him back home when they found him sitting in their unlocked cars. In our local park, when my dad started helping himself to a plate of sandwiches meticulously arranged on a picnic table, the Japanese family they belonged to welcomed this unkempt, white, six-foot-two stranger to their outing as if he were a long lost relative. Likewise, there has been something happening underneath the deterioration of our country. While the headlines reveal the truth of the matter — data centers bulldozing their way into rural communities, masked federal agents yanking delivery workers off their bikes, industry lobbyists buying legislation that allows them to poison our water and air — there are also young people planting community gardens to tackle gun violence in Milwaukee, Wisconsin; caregivers riding their kids to school in bike buses in Montclair, New Jersey; and folks of all ages gathering for the Black Joy Parade in Oakland, California. While some national figures are trying to flood the zone with so much chaos that we can’t keep up, other Americans are working hard to bring running water and indoor plumbing to those who still don’t have it. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] We’re witnessing a reweaving of local fabric, and a renewed curiosity in one another. Parents watching the resurgence of blatant misogyny are intentionally raising boys who embrace their tender feelings and connections. Famously red Texas has had more data center protests than any other state , so perhaps there is more possibility for labor and climate collaboration than we have understood. Leaders in a wide range of faiths weathered the bitter cold of Minneapolis to join local solidarity protests against ICE raids after the tragic death of Renée Good. It seems we are curious again about what role faith might play in our ethical lives together, how we can build a culture of mutual aid in our very unequal communities, and even how we might better understand the economic pain of those who have been abandoned and stereotyped by mainstream media and the political elite. If the last decade or two has been about expanding our horizons, it feels like this one is becoming about humbly narrowing the aperture on our lives and trying to get right with our neighbors, housed and unhoused alike. At a time when A.I. threatens to unravel us in so many ways, economist E.F. Schumacher’s wisdom from his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful: Economics as if People Mattered feels worth reviving: “I have no doubt that it is possible to give a new direction to technological development, a direction that shall lead it back to the real needs of man, and that also means: To the actual size of man. Man is small, and, therefore, small is beautiful.” In the end, this is what saved my family as we took care of my dad; the small moments in the midst of the chaos where we could register his essence intact, where we could devote ourselves to the sacred practice of showing up for him even when it was hard, when we could rest in the awe of it all. It didn’t cure his illness, but it reminded us of us — the fabric, the tenderness, the main thing. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime I wish that same reminder for our country in the months and years ahead — a way to keep our eye on the systemic harm, while keeping our hands in the dirt of our own communities. There are people in our midst who have lost their way through deep delusion, but there are also better angels: The family that offers a strange old man a sandwich; the organizers fighting for clean water for everyone, no exceptions; the daughters of the revolution baking casseroles for the undocumented families hiding in an attic room of their Minneapolis neighbors’ homes. May we never turn away from the systemic injustice, but may we also turn towards the small and beautiful. It’s all real and deeply interconnected, and deserves our fierce attention. The post What Dementia Taught Me About Living Through a Callous Time appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: I f you’re anything like us, you’re not exactly in a congenial mood right now. With the U.S. midterm elections fewer than three weeks away, you might be feeling combat-ready. And who could blame you? Seemingly on the ballot: the very future of the republic, steered by leaders who will shape policy about the climate, A.I., immigration, affordability, wars and many other critical issues. There’s a lot at stake. And yet, for many of us, the way we feel goes beyond those stakes. One part of our brain chugs along analytically, taking stances on legislation, policy and governance. Meanwhile, another part seethes with contempt for those who disagree: They must be stupid, immoral, blind to the facts. Multiply by 340 million, and election season becomes a volatile brew. But there’s hope. While social media algorithms, elected officials, and yes, even our own friends and colleagues, encourage us to close ranks and shut out dissenting voices, others are working in the other direction: reaching out, listening deeply, locating points of connection where they exist, and turning toward those they disagree with, rather than away. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] From now through Election Day, these are the people we’ll journey with. We’ll meet liberals and conservatives who are joining forces despite their differences to oppose data centers and border walls. We’ll talk to students who are turning their college campuses into spaces that welcome an array of opinions, and others participating in cultural exchanges far from their hometowns and comfort zones. We’ll listen in on conversations between “deep canvassers” and the voters they’re hearing out. And we’ll learn how polarization takes hold of the brain — and how, little by little, we can loosen its grip. The Depolarization Project isn’t a call to meet in the middle — it’s an experiment in curiosity. What forces fuel our sense of tribalism? Why do opposing perspectives register as a threat? Can we be open to differences of opinion without compromising our values? Is there hope for those of us who harbor a secret desire to bridge the divides? We know many of you may be skeptical. We hope you’ll take this journey with us regardless, and learn whether we can we fight for what we believe in without closing our minds and our hearts. Illustration by MUTI The post Welcome to the Depolarization Project appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Scientists Develop a Seaweed Coating to Extend the Freshness of Fruit Reading Time: 3 minutes A new seaweed coating can keep strawberries fresher at room temperature than even a refrigerator, offering a lower-carbon way to fight food waste. A new seaweed coating can keep fresh fruit lasting longer than even a refrigerator can. Researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC) developed the edible dip. In tests, coated strawberries stayed fresh at room temperature for four days or more. Uncoated strawberries left at room temperature molded within just two days. Even refrigerated, untreated berries started molding by day four regardless. Coated strawberries kept in the fridge lasted a full six days, the longest result recorded in the study. The seaweed coating relies on agar, a substance pulled from red algae. Agar is already a common food additive and a popular vegan substitute for gelatin. On its own, though, agar simply forms a thick, unremarkable gel. Doctoral student Ivy Chiu led the study alongside senior researcher Tianxi Yang at UBC. The two published their findings in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry in August 2026. Their team says no one had combined these particular ingredients into a coating like this before. Everything changed once researchers added zinc and tannic acid to the mix. Zinc is an essential nutrient, and tannic acid occurs naturally in grapes and tea. Together with agar, these ingredients self-assembled into tiny, evenly spread microparticles. That self-assembly surprised even the research team studying it. The particles form a thin, clear film that seals in moisture and blocks gas exchange. The coating also carries antibacterial and antioxidant properties that further slow spoilage. A seaweed coating enhanced with zinc and tannic acid self-assembles into a thin, clear film of evenly spread microparticles that seals in moisture, blocks gas exchange, and delivers antibacterial and antioxidant properties that slow food spoilage in ways the research team itself did not anticipate. Photo by Clare Kiernan, courtesy of the University of British Columbia . Researchers describe watching the mixture transform from a cloudy liquid into a uniform layer. The process happens within minutes once all three ingredients combine in solution. Dipped fruit emerges with a coating so thin it dries almost invisible. Cut apple slices treated with the seaweed coating stayed fresh for about 24 hours. Untreated slices, by comparison, began visibly decaying within 12 hours. Coated grapes lasted almost 14 days, a full week longer than untreated fruit. Across all three fruits, the coating roughly doubled shelf life compared to no treatment. Weight loss at the four-day mark dropped from 30% down to 13%. Treated fruit also kept more of its vitamin C and antioxidant content. Safety testing found no signs of toxicity in human intestinal cells. Researchers say the coating is safe to eat and washes off easily. It also preserves the fruit’s normal nutritional value throughout storage. A lifecycle analysis compared the coating’s environmental footprint to standard refrigeration. Emissions from the seaweed coating came in lower than or equal to those from cold storage. Researchers say these modest savings could add up across an entire supply chain. Reducing spoilage matters most in a food system that wastes enormous amounts of produce. Nearly half of all food produced in Canada is lost or wasted every year. That waste costs the Canadian economy an estimated $58 billion annually. Fresh fruits and vegetables are especially prone to this kind of loss. They lose moisture quickly and become vulnerable to mold soon after harvest. Long supply chains that rely heavily on refrigeration add further cost and emissions along the way. Cutting down on refrigeration could also ease strain on energy grids. Maintaining cold temperatures from farm to store demands significant infrastructure and power. A coating like this could reduce that demand at several points along the supply chain. They are also testing the seaweed coating across a wider range of fruits and vegetables. The team describes their invention as a practical strategy for building more resilient produce supply chains. Cutting food waste at this scale could ease pressure on refrigeration-heavy supply chains everywhere. A simple seaweed coating might not replace the fridge completely. But it could give fresh produce a longer, greener path from farm to table. The post Scientists Develop a Seaweed Coating to Extend the Freshness of Fruit appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A bleached coral, stripped of its color and slowly starving, can come back to life in just seven weeks -- if it is placed in contact with a healthy twin. Researchers at Stanford University recently discovered that when genetically identical coral fragments touch, their tissues fuse into what scientist Danny Collins calls "a nutrient highway," and within as little as 36 hours, life-giving algae begin flowing from the healthy fragment into the dying one. The discovery began with a happy accident: a healthy coral slipped against a bleached one in a tank, and someone was paying close enough attention to notice what happened next. The finding won't save coral reefs overnight -- the technique only works between genetic clones, and the ocean keeps warming, which causes coral to bleach. But the findings do open a door. Collins and his team are now exploring whether the algae themselves can be extracted and introduced to bleached corals at scale, without needing the physical bridge at all. While he is clear-eyed about the limits: the real solution is being able to stop coral bleaching in the first place, the horizons feel brighter: "bleached corals aren't a lost cause," he offers.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every fall there’s a pull to tidy things up. Cut back the perennials, rake the leaves, clear the beds, put the garden to rest. It feels satisfying, honestly, and spring does seem to start from a cleaner place. The thing is, all that leaf litter, those hollow stems, those patches of scraggly dead plant matter? That’s where the bees are. Over 3,600 bee species are native to the United States, and most of them are not honey bees. It’s the native wild bees, including mason bees, leafcutters, mining bees, long-horned bees, bumble bees, and hundreds of others, that are in steep decline. Most are solitary: each female builds her own nest, lays her eggs, stocks them with food, seals them up, and dies. As Matthew Shepherd , Director of Outreach and Education at the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation , explains, the offspring “complete most of their life stages in the cell, remaining there until the following year, when they emerge at the same season their mother was active.” That nest is almost certainly somewhere in your garden. Sam Droege , Wildlife Biologist at the USGS, says wild bees are nesting above ground and in the ground somewhere nearby no matter where you live. Ecological landscape designer Kim Eierman puts it plainly: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Most of what they need is already there, and the beauty of this solution is that all you have to do is less. What to do with the fallen leaves Move them rather than bag them. Bumble bee queens hibernate by digging a few inches underground or into leaf mulch, so piling leaves onto flower beds or into a back corner of the yard makes them a winter home. Leaf piles also give fireflies and other small garden creatures a place to wait out the cold. Shepherd’s guidance: remove leaves from anywhere they’re a slip hazard or blocking a drain, but keep them on flower borders, along the base of a hedge, or tucked into a back corner. A rake or broom does the job without the disturbance a leaf blower causes. Think twice before cutting everything back Pruning everything to the ground in fall can cost wild bees their winter home. “Avoiding the typical fall cleanup on plants and keeping stems of perennials and annuals creates nesting opportunities for tunnel-nesting bees such as small carpenter bees and leafcutters,” Shepherd says. The birds appreciate it too; they’ll forage on the seedheads through winter. If a tidy front yard matters to you, Droege has a workable compromise: cut back to about a foot tall instead of to the ground. “A plant needs to be damaged or dead for bees to be able to use it,” he says, so a shorter cut still creates usable nesting structure without looking neglected. If you’re already mid-cleanup, don’t compost what you’ve cut. “If any bees are already nesting in the stems, composting them will cause the end of that cycle,” Droege says. A loose pile left on the ground or behind the shed keeps the cycle going. Eierman adds that pithy stems from elderberry, raspberry, hydrangea, and Joe Pye weed are especially useful to cavity-nesting bees and can be bundled and left in place through winter. Leave brush piles, snags, and cane fruit stems Pruned branches can go into a brush pile rather than the compost. Loose piles don’t do much; Eierman notes they need to be “fairly tight and dense, providing cavities that shelter bees from rain.” Dead or dying trees are candidates for keeping if they’re well away from the house. These are called snags. They develop hollow passages over time as beetles tunnel through the dead wood, and cavity-nesting bees use those passages the following season. A snag that’s too tall to feel comfortable about can be cut back to a manageable height without losing what makes it useful. For cane fruits like raspberries, blackberries, and boysenberries, Droege says the same logic applies. “Cane fruits only fruit in year two,” he says. “Instead of cutting them to the ground, trimming them to a foot tall provides the best nesting material for a whole series of native wild bees.” Leave bare patches of soil undisturbed Most native bees nest in the ground and need bare, uncompacted soil to excavate their nests. “Don’t try to repair all the bare ground — leave the open areas, as bees like to nest there,” says Droege. Sandy or loamy soil in a sunny spot is ideal, but even a few square feet counts. If a bare patch feels too sparse, Eierman says planting very sparsely may still leave enough exposed soil between plants; just skip the mulch or landscape fabric, as both block bees from getting in. Treat it as wild habitat rather than an incomplete garden bed: no tilling, no cleaning up, not even in spring. Keep some flowers going through fall Most bees have wrapped up their nesting cycle by the time temperatures drop, but sweat bees and mining bees are still out foraging late in the season. Goldenrod and asters are the flowers they’re looking for. Having something in bloom through fall, and building toward a range of bloom times from spring through the end of the season, gives different species something to work with at different points in the year. “Expanding your garden for next spring and reducing your lawn is the biggest thing you can do for wild bees ,” Droege says. Eierman says it best: “You may have hundreds or even thousands of individual bees using your landscape. The good news is that you don’t have to do much to give them a place to live.” Leave the leaves. Don’t compost the stems. Keep a corner wild. That’s most of it. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post What to leave alone in your garden this October to help overwintering bees first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve bought a Japanese sweet potato, cut into it expecting orange, and found creamy white instead, you’ve already spotted the first thing that sets it apart. The skin is reddish-purple, the flesh is ivory, and the flavor is sweeter and earthier than the orange kinds most of us grew up with. The nutrition is different too, so the difference isn’t just skin deep. What Japanese sweet potatoes bring to the table They have about 26 grams of carbohydrates per 103-gram serving, nine percent of the daily value for adults. But unlike a plain starch, they come with fiber, potassium, and vitamin C alongside. Registered dietitian Danielle Smiley of NutriDS, LLC notes they’re well-suited for people who are physically active: the carbohydrates fuel effort and help with recovery. Registered dietitian Alyssa Smolen puts the fiber at about four grams per serving, which is enough to keep you full for a while. She suggests building them into a meal with a protein and some healthy fat rather than eating them on their own. What about orange sweet potatoes? Orange sweet potatoes are high in beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A. Japanese ones run higher in vitamins C and E and carry more anthocyanins, the same pigments behind the color in blueberries and red cabbage. Research on different varieties shows considerable variation in carotenoids, flavonoids, and other plant compounds depending on flesh color. If you eat both types across the week, you get more of that range. They’re doing different things, basically. How often to eat them There’s no target number. “There isn’t an evidence-based recommendation that says someone should eat a certain number of Japanese sweet potatoes per day or week,” Smiley says. Most healthy adults can have them regularly, even daily, as part of a varied diet. A small to medium potato is a reasonable portion, though how much you need shifts with activity level. “An athlete, for example, may need substantially more carbohydrates than someone less active,” she adds. What matters more is variety overall. Leaning heavily on any one food, even a good one, tends to crowd out the grains, legumes, and other vegetables that supply things Japanese sweet potatoes don’t. They’re a solid addition to what you’re already eating, not a replacement for any of it. items.descriptionOriginal: A British child who became the fastest 9-year-old girl to run a 5K earlier this year has her sights set on beating her personal record — tomorrow. Lily Janmohamed, now 10, is on track to beat her previous time of 19 minutes, 45 seconds at the Battersea Park Run in London. She became the fastest 8-year-old girl in the world to run a 5K, or 3.1 miles, on April 26, 2025, with a time of 20 minutes, 16 seconds, beating the 2015 record of 20 minutes, 30 seconds set by Gabrielle Hall. Then she smashed that personal best on March 14 of this year — the effort is believed to be a world record but Guinness World Records doesn’t track 5K times for 9-year-olds, per SWNS. Lily, from Stanmore, England, told the outlet she’s determined to beat her record at the Oct. 17 event and is hoping for 19 minutes, 25 seconds. She trains three times a week, and recent workouts suggest a new PR is possible. “My record will be hard to beat but I’m up for the challenge,” she said. “I’ve been training really well and I feel strong, I just hope the weather is good.” (If it’s not, she said she’ll punt her record attempt to the park run on Oct. 31.) Lily continued: “I can’t promise a personal best but I can promise to try my hardest.” Faizal Janmohamed / SWNS Parents Faizal and Shahliza Janmohamed said they’re both incredibly proud of Lily, who is using the upcoming event as an opportunity to rai se money for Scope, a U.K. charity that provides support and resources to young people with disabilities. “Lily has gained so much confidence through running. It’s lovely to see that she is doing this to help other children and not just to achieve a personal best,” dad Faizal said, adding: “The way she combines her natural ability with her determination and love for running is amazing to see.” “Lily is a superhero to us,” mom Shahliza shared. “We are endlessly proud of her dedication, hard work, and the heart she is putting into this. Whatever she achieves, we just want Lily to run her best.” Faizal Janmohamed / SWNS The young athlete’s dream is to eventually run for Team England and represent her country, but for now, she’s proud to have been made athletics captain at her school, St. Albans High School for Girls, this year. “Running makes me feel so free and strong, like I can do anything,” Lily said. “I love chasing new goals and getting better each time.” This article was originally written by Kate Pounds for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Silk Bicycle Tires Outperform Nylon in New Thai Research Reading Time: 3 minutes Silk bicycle tires have moved from laboratory concept to working prototype, with Thai researchers reporting major gains in durability, puncture resistance, and environmental impact compared to conventional nylon-reinforced tires. Researchers built silk bicycle tires by reinforcing natural rubber with silk textile instead of the synthetic fibers typically used in tire casings. Bicycle tires rely on an internal fabric layer, sandwiched within the rubber, to provide strength and structure. Nylon has long served as the standard material for this reinforcement layer. The idea traces back to earlier work by a Kasetsart University research team, including materials scientist Wirasak Smitthipong. Their 2016 study first tested silk textile as a natural rubber reinforcement and compared it directly against nylon. That early research found silk composites matched or exceeded nylon in several mechanical properties. Bombyx mori silk, produced by domesticated silkworms, offers unique advantages. The fiber consists of a strong core protein called fibroin, wrapped in a natural adhesive coating known as sericin. This combination gives silk an unusual balance of strength and flexibility rarely found in synthetic alternatives. Building a working bicycle tire prototype tested these lab findings under real-world conditions. Results showed silk bicycle tires achieved 129% greater durability than their nylon counterparts. Puncture resistance improved even further, jumping 157% above nylon-reinforced tires. Environmental performance told an equally compelling story. Life cycle analysis found that silk bicycle tires cut global warming potential by more than 80 percent compared to nylon versions. That reduction stems largely from silk’s natural, renewable origin versus nylon’s petroleum-based production process. Nylon manufacturing depends entirely on fossil fuels and energy-intensive chemical processes. Silk, by contrast, comes from silkworms that convert mulberry leaves into fiber through a biological process that requires far less industrial energy. This fundamental difference explains much of the environmental gap between the two materials. Thailand’s deep silk-farming tradition made it a natural place to develop this technology. Thai silk production supports rural farming communities across the country, particularly in the northeast region. A shift toward industrial silk applications could open new markets for these existing agricultural networks. Bicycle tires represent just one potential application for silk-reinforced rubber composites. Earlier research pointed toward uses in soft robotics and flexible inflatable tubing, where the combination of strength and pliability proves equally valuable. The same core material properties that improve tire performance could translate to these other fields. Silk bicycle tires are one application of a broader advance in silk-reinforced rubber composites, with the same combination of strength and pliability that improves tire performance showing equal promise for soft robotics and flexible inflatable tubing. Photo by Atlantic Ambience on Pexels. Puncture resistance matters especially for cyclists navigating debris-strewn roads or unpaved trails. A 157% improvement suggests silk bicycle tires could substantially reduce roadside repairs and replacement costs over a tire’s lifespan. Fewer replacements also mean less rubber waste entering landfills. Durability improvements matter beyond simple convenience. Tires that last longer require less frequent manufacturing, compounding the environmental benefits beyond material substitution alone. Each additional month of tire life reduces the total resources consumed per mile ridden. Cost remains an open question for silk bicycle tires reaching consumer markets. Silk has historically carried a higher price tag than synthetic fibers like nylon, reflecting its more labor-intensive production process. Whether performance gains can offset this cost difference will likely determine how quickly the technology reaches commercial cyclists. Natural rubber itself adds another layer of sustainability to this innovation. Combining silk with natural rubber, rather than synthetic rubber compounds, creates a tire built almost entirely from renewable, biodegradable materials. This contrasts sharply with conventional tires, which typically blend synthetic rubbers with petroleum-derived reinforcement fibers. Scaling from laboratory prototype to mass production presents the next major hurdle. Manufacturing processes would need to adapt to handle silk textiles at commercial volumes while maintaining consistent quality. Thai silk producers and cycling equipment manufacturers may find common ground in addressing this challenge together. The broader tire industry has faced mounting pressure to reduce its environmental footprint, from raw material sourcing to end-of-life disposal . Silk bicycle tires offer one concrete example of a wider shift already underway in materials labs worldwide, where researchers are reimagining silk as an environmentally friendly substitute for synthetic fibers, rather than a fabric reserved for clothing. As sustainability demands grow across manufacturing sectors, this Thai-led research suggests silk could carve out a meaningful niche in engineering as much as in fashion. The post Silk Bicycle Tires Outperform Nylon in New Thai Research appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published in the Daily Yonder. For more rural reporting and small-town stories visit dailyyonder.com . For Michael Sayen, visiting the local library after hours is a great way to get work done, or seek respite from the weather, regardless of what day it is. “We just had Labor Day, the library is closed all day. But if you have extended hours, you can come in and do the work, or cool down from a hot day or whatever you need to do,” Sayen said the day after Labor Day while working on a novel at the Wyoming, Minnesota branch of the East Central Regional Library (ECRL) in Chisago County. Sayen, who lives in nearby Forest Lake north of Minneapolis, adds that he has found after-hours access useful for filing time-sensitive job applications or court documents. Michael Sayen uses a computer at the Wyoming Giese Memorial Library to work on a novel. Sayen is a user of the Extended Access program at the Wyoming Library. Credit: H. Jiahong Pan/Daily Yonder The Wyoming branch library is home to a new ECRL initiative called “extended access,” which allows users to access a library branch when it is unstaffed. “We hope that it allows more people to use the facility, in particular those who may not be able to get to the library during otherwise limited hours due to work and family schedules,” ECRL executive director Carla Lydon wrote in an email. ECRL is one of a handful of rural library systems across the United States to offer such a service, increasing library access at a time when libraries are struggling for funding. How it works Extended access goes by many names depending on location. The Summit County Library in Utah calls it extended access hours . In Nevada County, California, the program is called Open+ Access . At the Independence Public Library in Kansas, it’s called Open Access . And at the Timberland Regional Library, which serves five counties in western Washington state, it’s called Expanded Access . To access an unstaffed library, a person first needs a library swipe card from the local library, which will unlock the doors. For the ECRL, any library card associated with any of Minnesota’s 12 regional libraries will do. After getting a library card, users must also sign up for the extended-access program. Some libraries allow people to do so online, while other libraries require them to register in person. Some libraries also require users to participate in an in-person tour, so they can familiarize themselves with its safety features. There also are some restrictions — for example, to have extended access to the Timberland Regional Library, users must be at least 14 years of age. For the Independence Public Library, at least 16 years of age. And, for Nevada County, Summit County, and ECRL in Minnesota, extended access is only available to members who are at least 18 years of age. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] However, even after enrolling in open or extended or expanded access, users don’t necessarily have access to the library 24 hours a day. Many libraries require visitors to leave unstaffed locations as early as 8 p.m. each night. At Summit County, unstaffed libraries aren’t accessible on Sundays, even with extended access privileges. At ECRL, signing up requires one to visit the Wyoming branch when it is staffed. The process takes about 15 minutes, and involves signing a form, sitting through a presentation on what the program is about, as well as reviewing the library’s safety features, including locations of the defibrillator, first aid kit and emergency exits. People using extended-access libraries are able to do the same things they could do when staff are present, such as read and borrow books, make copies and use computers. Some services are not available, such as sending faxes, that require cash transactions with library workers. Ryan Stigile, a pastor who lives in Wyoming, Minnesota, enjoys using extended access because it provides another space for him to get his work done, particularly in the evening. “Just being able to have an extra space to work in a community that does not have a ton of evening options available,” Stigile said while working on his computer at the Wyoming library. “We don’t have any coffee shops, so it’s this or McDonald’s.” The Giese Memorial Library, referred to as the Wyoming Library, is the first of the East Central Regional Library branches to offer extended access hours, where users can visit while it is unstaffed. Credit: H. Jiahong Pan for the Daily Yonder ECRL did face scrutiny over safety, security and behavioral issues that may play out when people are unattended. But so far, they say they haven’t encountered any problems. Still, to address the security issues that may come up, ECRL staff installed security cameras. Using a library card to unlock doors adds another layer of security. “If we have issues, because you have to sign in and are on camera, we are able to identify the issue and revoke the privilege quickly,” Lydon added. The program is getting popular at ECRL: 55 users have registered for extended access, and they have used it more than 800 times so far this year. Lydon reported usage has grown 66 percent since ECRL moved out of the testing phase in April. Meanwhile, the Timberland Regional Library has 12 branches with extended access, as well as more than 4,100 users who have access to the libraries. From September 2023 to August 2026, more than 63,000 people swiped their library cards when the libraries were unstaffed. Inadequate funding challenges expansions For ECRL, renovating the Wyoming library to allow after-hours access cost about $70,000, which included installing security cameras. It costs ECRL about $12,000 annually for the technology needed for extended access to work, which includes the software that allows users to scan their cards to enter. At this time, the Wyoming library is the only library in the ECRL system that has extended access. ECRL plans to expand the service to other branches as funding allows, but its board hasn’t committed funding to expand the service. In fact, ECRL had to reduce library hours in three counties earlier this year due to funding challenges. One of the counties affected, Aitkin County, is considering a two percent allocation increase from this year’s levels, but the increase would not restore operating hours to 2025 levels. Aitkin County is also not considering allocating more funds to increase operating hours. ECRL does not plan to cut hours further next year. Getting extended access established in ECRL branches outside of Chisago County may also require the cooperation of the cities where the libraries are located. In Aitkin and Pine counties, the cities own the buildings where the branches are housed, and the city governments would have to approve the necessary modifications. Even with libraries available for the public to use while unstaffed, extended access is not affecting jobs at the East Central Regional Library, Lydon explained. “Staffed hours remain as they were prior to implementation, and we expect that to continue,” Lydon wrote. Meanwhile, Timberland Regional Library, which received 94 percent of its funding this year from property tax levies and does not receive federal funding, is facing potential budget cuts, according to Chris Chrzan, Timberland Regional Library’s public information officer and board clerk. “Due to legal limits on annual property tax increases in Washington state, revenues have not kept up with expenditures for many years,” Chrzan said. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime On the ballot this fall in the five counties Timberland Regional Library serves is a measure to increase the tax rate per $1,000 in assessed property value from 22 cents to 35 cents, potentially raising $14 million next year . The library system has already cut $3.69 million from books, staff salaries and library programs to address a budget deficit, according to the Grays Harbor and Aberdeen-based Our Daily World. Though expanded access at Timberland Regional Library preserved library access, the system also wants to increase staffed hours for visitors. “While ‘Expanded Access Hours’ is useful for maintaining access to library facilities and some core services outside of staffed hours, our patrons tell us often how important it is to have regularly staffed hours at their local library,” Chrzan wrote in an email. “Our ability to continue to provide regularly staffed hours across the district in light of ongoing financial challenges is part of the conversations we are having with community members now.” This article first appeared on The Daily Yonder and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License . items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News What the New EU Packaging Rules and PFAS Ban Mean for Consumers Reading Time: 3 minutes The new EU packaging rules and PFAS ban officially came into force on August 12, 2026, marking a major shift in how packaging is made and sold across Europe. The EU packaging rules and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) ban are part of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR). The law now applies in all 27 member states, replacing a patchwork of national rules that companies had to navigate one country at a time. For everyday shoppers, the most visible change under the new EU packaging rules and PFAS ban involves food safety. Packaging containing high levels of PFAS, a group of manufactured chemicals sometimes called “forever chemicals,” can no longer be sold for food contact use in the EU. These substances resist breaking down and can build up in soil, water, and the human body over time. PFAS have long been used to make packaging grease- and water-resistant. That includes everyday items like takeaway boxes, pizza containers, microwave popcorn bags, and bakery paper. Under the new EU packaging rules and PFAS ban, manufacturers must now find safer alternatives for these common products. Think of it like swapping a leaky faucet for one that seals properly. The chemicals were doing a job, keeping grease off your fingers, but they left a hidden cost behind. Removing them cuts off a steady drip of harmful substances into the environment and into people’s bodies. The rules also aim to fix a bigger, slower-moving problem. Without action, packaging waste across the EU was on track to grow by 19% by 2030. Plastic packaging waste alone could have climbed by nearly 46% over that same period. To put that in perspective, Europeans already generate more than 35 kilograms of plastic packaging waste per person each year, according to the EU statistics agency Eurostat. That is roughly the weight of a large suitcase, multiplied across hundreds of millions of people, every single year. The scale of that waste stream is one reason officials pushed to get the EU packaging rules and PFAS ban into force as quickly as possible. Businesses stand to gain from the change too. A single EU-wide rulebook removes the guesswork that came with 27 different sets of national requirements. Companies that sell packaging across borders can now design products once and market them anywhere in the bloc. The EU packaging rules and PFAS ban replace 27 sets of national laws with one harmonized framework for businesses. Photo by Norma Mortenson on Pexels. Jessika Roswall, the European Commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy, called the regulation an investment in Europe’s future. She said it would help reduce waste, boost recycling, and make food packaging safer by limiting harmful substances like PFAS, while also cutting the EU’s reliance on newly extracted raw materials. She added that adjusting to the new EU packaging rules and PFAS ban comes with some costs, but that officials worked closely with market operators to keep implementation practical. More changes are still ahead. Starting in 2028, a harmonized labeling system will roll out across the EU to make sorting packaging for recycling easier for consumers. Officials expect that system to save the packaging industry several billion euros over time by streamlining recycling and composting operations. By 2030, additional measures will kick in. These include limits on excess empty space inside packaging, restrictions on certain single-use plastics, and new reuse targets for businesses. Packaging makers will also be required to use recycled plastic in new products and ensure that all packaging can actually be recycled. The European Commission has said it is working closely with national governments, industry groups, and civil society to roll out the rules smoothly. In March 2026, it published detailed guidance to help businesses understand exactly how to comply with the new PFAS restrictions tied to the regulation. Officials acknowledge the transition brings some short-term costs for manufacturers. But they argue the long-term payoff, such as safer products, cleaner supply chains, and a more predictable market, will outweigh those early adjustments. The shift also reflects a broader European goal: reaching climate neutrality by 2050 through a more circular economy, where materials get reused rather than discarded. Packaging touches nearly every product people buy, which makes it a practical place to start. For consumers, the EU packaging rules and PFAS ban may go largely unnoticed at first glance. A pizza box or coffee cup will look much the same as before. What changes is what is missing, and what that absence means for public health and the planet over time. The post What the New EU Packaging Rules and PFAS Ban Mean for Consumers appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When a 94-year-old woman in Melbourne discovered that the new vacuum cleaner she wanted was sold out, she faced a disappointing trip home. But a stranger standing nearby overheard her predicament and quietly offered to drive two hours to another store, collect the vacuum, and deliver it to her door. The stranger even assembled it for her, and the two later shared coffee. Only afterward did the woman learn that her unexpected helper was Michele Timms, a highly celebrated professional basketball player and coach. Yet it wasn't her fame that made the encounter extraordinary. It was the simple kindness of someone who saw a human being facing a dead-end and tapped into her capacity to widen the road for her.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a half-second every time you finish a carton of eggs. The lid flops open, the last two slots are empty, and you’re already reaching for the recycling bin. Before you do: cardboard egg cartons are more useful than they get credit for, and once you’ve used one as a seed tray or a paint well, you’ll find yourself pausing the next time. 6 smart uses for that empty egg carton Turn it into a bird feeder Cut the upper lid off the carton, poke a hole in each corner, and thread string or twine through. Fill the cups with birdseed and hang it near a window. You’ve got a feeder in about five minutes. It won’t last the whole season, but it’ll hold up long enough to draw a good crowd, and when it gives out, it composts. Use it as a compost booster If you compost, egg cartons belong in the pile. The ratio you’re aiming for is roughly three to four parts brown material to one part green. An egg carton counts as brown, same category as newspaper or dry leaves . Tear it up, layer it in with coffee grounds , vegetable scraps, and garden trimmings. It’ll break down on its own and bring a waterlogged or nitrogen-heavy pile back into balance. Store holiday ornaments without buying new containers The cups are almost exactly the right size for round ornaments and baubles. Stack several cartons in a bin, label them. More reliable than tissue paper, takes up less room, and you’ve already got them. Keep small jewelry from getting tangled Those same cups work well for earrings, rings, and brooches the rest of the year. They’re flat enough to slide into shallow drawers. If you’re packing up to move, they’re a practical way to keep jewelry findable without everything ending up in a pile at the bottom of a box. Set up a painting station for kids Use the cups as paint wells: a different color in each one, no tray to wash afterward. Toss the whole thing when you’re done. Cut the cups apart, and kids can paint them into flowers, caterpillars, or whatever creature they’ve decided is their thing this week. No special supplies, minimal cleanup. Start seeds for the garden Fill each cup with potting soil, drop in a seed, and you have a seed-starting tray that costs nothing to make. When the seedlings are ready to go outside, you plant the whole cup straight into the ground. The cardboard breaks down underground without disturbing the roots, which keeps transplant shock low. Flowers, herbs, and lettuce all work well. If you’re just starting to grow things and not entirely sure you’ll stick with it, this is as low-stakes as it gets. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The hardest part of any early warning system isn’t the science. It’s finding infrastructure that reaches everyone, holds up under pressure, and gets maintained over years by the people who depend on it. In Indonesia, a team of Japanese and Indonesian researchers think that infrastructure already exists. It broadcasts the call to prayer five times a day. With the largest Muslim population in the world, Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of mosques, nearly all equipped with loudspeakers that reach the surrounding community. A five-year pilot project running until 2030 is testing whether those speakers can double as earthquake alert klaxons, connected to a seismic sensor network that sounds an alarm before the shaking arrives. Several mosques have already been hooked up. The project was conceived by Dr. Inoue Hiroshi of the Disaster Prevention Research Institute at Kyoto University, who came up with the idea while researching deadly earthquakes in Sumatra nearly two decades ago. “Every community has a mosque,” he told the Guardian . The rest of his argument was practical: “The advantage of a mosque speaker is that they’re existing and well maintained. For any disaster infrastructure, maintenance is the big challenge… but the mosque speaker is maintained by the people.” Mobile phones are the default tool for modern disaster alerts, but phone networks can fail in an earthquake. Mosque loudspeakers, tested five times a day by the communities that run them, are harder to knock out. The seconds that matter in an earthquake Earthquake early warning is different from tsunami warning. Tsunamis build over time and can be tracked; communities might have minutes or hours to act. Earthquake waves move through the ground at extraordinary speed. A village 31 miles (50 kilometers) from the epicenter might have only five to ten seconds, according to Andi Eka Sakya , senior researcher at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency and Indonesian co-lead on the project. The system isn’t issuing public warnings yet, but that’s what the team is working toward. Dr. Inoue’s interest goes back to a 2009 earthquake in western Sumatra that killed at least 1,000 people. “I thought if Indonesia had the same service and people received the warning before the shaking came, then many people among those few hundred wouldn’t have died,” he says. Drop and cover doesn’t always apply What to do with five to ten seconds turns out to be its own research problem. In Japan, official guidelines center on drop and cover: get under a table, stay indoors, ride it out. That advice was written for well-constructed buildings. In Indonesia and many developing countries, homes are frequently built from unreinforced masonry, which collapses under earthquake stress. In some documented cases in Indonesia, two-story buildings have had the first floor crushed while the second floor stayed relatively intact. The people who survived ran outside. “The way people react is they quickly escape out of the room,” Inoue says. “They know how to survive.” Standard international guidelines don’t account for that. Project researchers are running simulations and human experiments to develop guidance grounded in how Indonesian buildings actually fail. Survival advice calibrated for the wrong type of building can kill people. Other countries are exploring the same approach Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Emergency Situations announced a pilot program this year to install alarm devices in 272 mosques, warning communities about floods, mudflows, landslides, and avalanches. The United Nations Development Programme , which partnered in the initiative, put it plainly: mosques “are traditionally perceived as authoritative social institutions with significant influence on local communities.” A broadcast from a trusted institution reaches people differently than one from a government system most residents have never interacted with. The Indonesia project is also adding school loudspeakers, radio, and television as backup layers. But the mosque network is the foundation. It was already there, maintained every day by the communities that need it most. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Το εναρκτήριο φεστιβάλ στη Φινλανδία, που ονομάζεται επίσημα Hiljaa Fest (μετάφραση σε "Quietly Fest"), άνοιξε το Σάββατο στο Εθνικό Πάρκο Valkmusa, abou…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome to “Quietchella,” where wind, moss, and moths are the headliners, good old-fashioned peace and quiet are the supporting acts, and tickets are open to anyone ready to slow down and leave no trace. The inaugural festival in Finland, officially called Hiljaa Fest (translating to “Quietly Fest”), opened Saturday in Valkmusa National Park , about a 90-minute drive east of Helsinki. It bills itself as not only the “world’s quietest festival” but also the first Festival of Nature Listening. Visit Kotka Hamina Although there’s no official “lineup,” the park is home to 40 types of mire (wetland) habitats, myriad bird and butterfly species, and wooden boardwalk trails — i.e., plenty of opportunities to hear crackles, creaks, tweets, and whistles. “Every performer appears on their own terms, in their own habitat, and according to their own schedule,” the playful festival announcement reads. Running through the end of October, Hiljaa Fest is a way for visitors to explore the park with a new perspective. Four “stages” each offer a unique experience: Räme Stage, near the entrance, is the festival’s aromatic opening area, with twisted pine trees and fragrant Labrador tea plants. Neva Stage (“the main stage”) boasts colorful cranberries, cloudberries, peat moss, and sundew — a tiny carnivorous plant. BjornStefanson—iStock/Getty Images Plus Sundew At Simonsaari Stage, an elevated section overlooking the entire grounds, birdwatchers can listen to their favorite kind of singers. Black grouses and common cranes fly overhead while a small lizard species may be spotted sunbathing. Headlining at the final area, Moronvuori Korpisuo Stage, are the park’s rocky Moronvuori Cliffs . “Valkmusa’s beauty can be found in its small details: how the wind whispers, how the moss faintly rustles, how the birds sing to you. We have planned the first-ever Festival of Nature Listening so that visitors get to tour the national park and really listen to the music nature creates,” said creative director and wilderness guide Simo Peri. “It is a festival trip designed to nurture one’s soul and one’s mind.” RELATED: 16 Heartwarming Words and Phrases That Don’t Have an English Equivalent

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Mission Blue and IUCN Join Forces with the One Ocean Partnership Reading Time: 3 minutes The One Ocean Partnership puts coastal communities at the heart of protecting and restoring the ocean. Mission Blue and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) announced in September a new collaboration to advance the One Ocean Partnership—a global effort to accelerate locally led ocean conservation by connecting coastal communities with the science, expertise, partnerships and finance they need to scale solutions and develop regenerative seascapes. The collaboration was announced by Dr. Sylvia Earle, CEO & Founder of Mission Blue and IUCN Patron of Nature, and Razan Al Mubarak, President of IUCN, during Climate Week NYC 2026. The partnership will bring together IUCN’s network, scientific expertise, partnerships and regenerative seascape approach pioneered under its Great Blue Wall initiative with Mission Blue’s global network of Hope Spots—ocean areas of critical ecological importance championed by local leaders. “There is only one ocean, and every breath we take, every drop of water we drink and every life on Earth depends upon it. Hope Spots show what becomes possible when science, local knowledge and courageous leadership come together. Through this collaboration with IUCN and the One Ocean Partnership, we can give local champions the recognition and support they deserve, create an effective network of action, and turn hope into lasting protection and recovery of the ocean at the scale needed for enduring security for life on Earth, humans very much included.” — Dr. Sylvia Earle, CEO & Founder of Mission Blue. “Sylvia Earle and Mission Blue have shown the power of local leadership through Hope Spots. Through this partnership, we want to build on that foundation, connecting locally led conservation with the science, expertise, partnerships, and investment needed to sustain it and expand its impact. By linking Hope Spots with wider regenerative seascapes, we can help turn successful local action into lasting progress for the Ocean and the communities that depend on it” — Razan Al Mubarak, President of IUCN. IUCN President Razan Al Mubarak, Dr. Sylvia Earle and Director of the IUCN Oceans Team, Minna Epps, at NYC Climate Week 2026. Photo courtesy of Mission Blue . Together, Mission Blue and IUCN will: Connect Hope Spots and regenerative seascapes, linking local conservation efforts with regional and global ocean goals; Advance regenerative blue economy models that restore marine ecosystems while creating sustainable livelihoods; Support coastal and island leadership, bringing local knowledge and solutions into regional and global ocean discussions; Strengthen south-south and triangular cooperation between countries and communities, helping ocean leaders share knowledge and successful approaches; Connect local leaders with expertise, partnerships and finance to help turn solutions into action; and Share successful examples of ocean conservation and regeneration to inspire action in other regions. Ocean ecosystems cross political boundaries, but ocean challenges and solutions vary from place to place. By connecting Hope Spot Champions and other local ocean leaders with IUCN’s regional networks and expertise, the partnership will help communities identify shared priorities, work together, share solutions and turn global ocean goals into action on the ground. At the heart of the collaboration is a vision for a regenerative blue economy—one where economic activity helps restore, rather than deplete, the ocean. The partnership will connect ocean protection and restoration with sustainable enterprise, innovation, local value creation and investment, demonstrating how healthy marine ecosystems can support livelihoods, resilient coastal economies and long-term prosperity. The need for action is urgent. The ocean covers more than 70% of our planet and supports food, livelihoods and economies for billions of people, while helping regulate our climate by absorbing carbon dioxide emissions. Yet warming, acidification, pollution, overfishing, more frequent extreme natural events and habitat loss are putting marine ecosystems and coastal communities under growing pressure. Protecting and restoring the ocean is essential to meeting global commitments on biodiversity and sustainable development. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework calls for at least 30% of terrestrial, inland water, and coastal and marine areas to be effectively conserved and managed by 2030. Sustainable Development Goal 14 calls for the conservation and sustainable use of the oceans, seas and marine resources. Delivering these commitments will require coordinated action that is locally led, supported by science and finance, and connected across regions. Mission Blue and IUCN will work together to help turn these global commitments into action on the ground by supporting coastal communities and local leaders to protect and restore marine ecosystems, share solutions and build sustainable livelihoods. By connecting people, knowledge, partnerships and investment, the collaboration aims to help create a healthier ocean and a more secure future for the people who depend on it. The post Mission Blue and IUCN Join Forces with the One Ocean Partnership appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Solar Panel Recycling Could Turn a Waste Problem into an Economic Opportunity Reading Time: 3 minutes A new global study finds that solar panel recycling could recover billions of dollars in materials and cut emissions by 2060. Solar panel recycling could turn a looming waste crisis into a global windfall, according to a sweeping new study . Researchers modeled 1,708 recycling scenarios across 32 regions worldwide. They found that recovered materials could generate nearly $1 trillion in economic benefits. Global solar installations are growing rapidly, faster than almost any other energy source today. Some researchers expect photovoltaic power, known as PV, to become the dominant electricity source by 2050. That growth means millions of aging panels will soon need a destination. The study, published in the journal Nature, projects between 297 and 402 million tonnes of discarded panels by 2060. Middle-income countries such as China are expected to generate much of that waste after 2040. Left unmanaged, this waste could pose serious environmental risks. Today, most retired solar panels end up in landfills once they stop working. There, they can leak toxic metals such as lead and cadmium into soil and water. Proper solar panel recycling could prevent much of that pollution before it starts. A few companies and countries are already testing what large-scale solutions look like. Veolia runs dedicated PV recycling facilities in France and Michigan. China, the world’s largest solar panel producer, now requires manufacturers to help collect and treat retired panels. Several Chinese solar manufacturers have also launched their own pilot recycling projects. These early efforts show that industrial-scale solar panel recycling is technically possible today. Scaling that capacity worldwide remains the bigger challenge ahead. Solar panels contain valuable materials, including silicon, silver, copper, and tellurium. These metals could be recovered and reused to build new panels. Silicon and silver hold the most value, though current technology struggles to recover either at high purity. Recycling most panels today still costs more than the recovered materials are worth. The study estimates that global recycling will not break even before the mid-2030s. Even so, researchers project cumulative net benefits of $529 to $935 billion by 2060. Beyond financial gains, better recycling could meaningfully shrink the industry’s carbon footprint. The study estimates emissions cuts of up to 3.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. That reduction is more than two-thirds higher than sticking with current waste practices. These benefits are not currently shared equally worldwide. Wealthier regions such as the European Union, United States, China, Japan, and South Korea already have strong recycling infrastructure. Many lower-income regions lack the technology and instead rely on outsourcing their waste. Solar panel recycling could cut up to 3.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent compared to current waste practices, but the benefits remain unevenly distributed, with wealthier regions already equipped with strong recycling infrastructure while lower-income countries are left outsourcing their growing panel waste. Photo by Hoan Ngọc on Pexels. Combining region-specific recycling technology with some outsourcing produces the largest global benefits overall. But outsourcing waste to places with cheaper technology can also widen existing inequality. A declining subsidy model, which phases out support as recycling matures, could help balance these outcomes. The research team included scientists from universities in China, Australia, and Sweden. Their model tracked material prices, trade flows, and subsidy policies across every region studied. This broad approach let them compare dozens of possible futures rather than a single forecast. Recovering materials through solar panel recycling could also ease pressure on global mineral supply chains. Silver, copper, and tellurium all face rising demand from other clean energy technologies. Reusing what already exists could reduce the need for new mining in sensitive landscapes. Researchers point to international frameworks, including the Paris Agreement, as tools for spreading technology and funding to lower-income regions. Coordinated support could help more regions build their own solar panel recycling capacity instead of depending on others indefinitely. Policymakers now have a clearer roadmap than before this study appeared. Investing early in recycling infrastructure could pay off well before most panels reach retirement age. That head start matters most for regions currently left out of the recycling economy. Solar power’s rapid growth is already reshaping how the world generates electricity. Solar panel recycling could soon reshape what happens once those panels wear out. Planning for that shift now could turn tomorrow’s waste pile into today’s opportunity. The post Solar Panel Recycling Could Turn a Waste Problem into an Economic Opportunity appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: W hen students in Singapore looked around their school cafeteria, they could see a problem shared all over the world: Single-use Styrofoam was ubiquitous. They soon learned that the school’s 2,000 students used 72,000 pieces of Styrofoam and other types of plastic every year. To find a solution, they joined the Unplastify Challenge , a global movement initiated by the Latin American social enterprise Unplastify and funded by the National Geographic Society, a nonprofit that seeks to foster environmental stewardship. What makes the program unique is its audience, design and scope. Teenagers, usually 15 to 16 years old, design and implement solutions to “unplastify” their schools, communities, neighborhoods and homes. In Singapore, the students decided to campaign for multi-use lunch boxes, winning them first place in the Unplastify Challenge 2026, the 12th such event of its kind. A garbage-strewn beach in Bali, Indonesia. Unless effective action is taken, it’s predicted that global plastic production will more than double over the next 15 years. Credit: Mariia Ploshikhina / Shutterstock In the eight years since it began, Unplastify has worked with over 3,000 students at 400 schools in 25 countries, mostly in Latin America, but also in Africa, Asia, North America and Europe. Together these students have come up with over 1,000 strategies, leading efforts to avoid an estimated 72 tons of plastic. In Chile, students have designed a biodegradable alternative to plastic glitter, thus avoiding four kilos of plastic in a single year. In Costa Rica, students have replaced plastic sponges with natural luffa. In Turkey, teenagers have researched biodegradable alternatives to medical equipment such as plastic gloves, eventually extending their work into health clinics. In Brazil, young people have worked with the supplier of their school uniforms to eliminate polyester, which is a petroleum-based plastic fiber. In Columbia, students have collaborated with grocers and butchers to replace plastic wrap with banana leaves. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Instead of just raising awareness, Unplastify equips teenagers with the knowledge to have real-world impact — through project-based learning and hands-on action. Unplastify offers online training materials that help young people identify a problem, but the students themselves decide which issue they want to focus on and then come up with actionable ideas. Teachers mentor them to translate the ideas into implementation. Along the way, the teenagers learn how to do research, prepare and hold a presentation, organize teams, design branding and create social media content. “They learn project management with the excuse of unplastifying,” says Unplastify co-founder Augustina “Tati” Besada. Besada first understood the scope of the plastic problem when she ran the community recycling nonprofit Sure We Can in Brooklyn, New York, in 2016 to 2017. “Recycling doesn’t work,” she recalls realizing. Taking into account “how difficult it is, how work intensive, how expensive, and why it doesn’t work at scale, it doesn’t solve the problem,” she concluded, starkly aware of the fact that less than 10 percent of the world’s plastic gets recycled. “All these materials end up somewhere, especially in the ocean,” she states from Unplastify’s coworking space in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Besada saw the consequences firsthand. In 2018, she sailed across the Atlantic from New York to Gibraltar on a six-month journey, taking water samples along the way. The test results were devastating: “Even in the most remote corners, every single sample we took contained plastic.” The answer, she concluded, was “to tackle the problem upstream, at the source.” Credit: PeopleImages / Shutterstock In Chile, students have designed a biodegradable alternative to plastic glitter. In Columbia, students have collaborated with grocers and butchers to replace plastic wrap with banana leaves. Together with architect Rocío González, she founded Unplastify that same year, pursuing the mission to find solutions while working with the generation that bears the brunt of the plastic crisis: young people. Without action, global plastic production is expected to more than double from 130 million to 280 million metric tons over the next 15 years, according to research by The Pew Charitable Trusts . An industrial designer by training, Besada views plastic pollution as a design problem. “Let’s look at the big picture and see where we can intervene in order to change the dynamics of the system,” she says. During the Unplastify challenges to date, 43 percent of the participants have focused on alternative materials or products, for instance biodegradable glitter, beeswax instead of paper wrap and plastic-free phone cases. Thirty-eight percent have initiated awareness campaigns, which might include organizing beach cleanups. Fourteen percent have come up with entrepreneurial projects. A group in Chile, for instance, worked with local stores to sell olive oil in bulk instead of smaller containers. “They found a supplier, designed a huge container and a very nice oil dispenser, and they started testing in different stores, eventually starting a business,” Besada says. Five percent of the students have engaged with policy aspects, aiming to change regulation, for example working with superiors to install water refilling stations instead of having single-use water bottles for sale. Besada admits that the majority of young people are initially unaware of the plastic problem or don’t care about it. “What gets them engaged is the process of what they can do,” she says. “They engage with other students, other schools, other countries, other cultures, other languages.” The Unplastify Challenge award values not only impact, communication and creativity, but also collaboration. That’s why Besada pushes back when students initially propose an obvious substitution. “They would say, ‘Let’s replace plastic cups with paper cups,’” she explains. “I’m like, ‘Okay, that’s not a solution. That’s another single-use product.’” Instead, students have to ask a harder question: How do you get an entire classroom, school or neighborhood to accept alternatives? Credit: monticello / Shutterstock “Let’s look at the big picture and see where we can intervene.” –Augustina Besada That may mean designing reusable containers, persuading a cafeteria manager, finding suppliers or presenting a budget to the school administration. “You need to argue,” Besada says. “They have to prepare for that meeting.” Some students who have taken the challenge discover a pathway towards a career; several chose to study political or environmental science to continue their fight for a plastic-free future. However, Besada is convinced that the problem cannot be solved on an individual level alone. Unplastify also works with companies and governments, supporting regulations at municipal and national levels, including negotiations around the United Nations Plastics Treaty , an international effort to end plastic pollution. Take Argentina’s largest airport operator, which manages 24 airports. Unplastify talked with 75 stakeholders, including retailers, airlines, lounges and food operators. Over three years, the operator reduced its plastic footprint by 28 percent, according to Besada. She explains that she uses a similar strategy as she does with the teenagers: She asks the business partners to identify the greatest plastic and water challenges, and encourages them to come up with solutions themselves. Her broader goal comes down to questioning the idea that plastic is inherently cheap. “Cheap for whom?” she asks. The costs of plastic are often hidden — in waste management, environmental damage and health risks, among other impacts. Conventional calculations don’t necessarily capture all of them. Unplastify’s strategy is deliberately pragmatic: Identify where plastic and water are being used unnecessarily, determine what can realistically change, measure the results and build from there. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime At the airports, for example, Unplastify found that replacing every plastic coffee cup with a paper one would cost more. But realizing that half the patrons drink their coffee in place, one part of the solution was to encourage customers to choose reusable cups, which reduces plastic and saves the operator money. Besada’s larger prescription has three parts: Don’t treat recycling as the answer; take ownership rather than waiting for governments or corporations; and think systemically — change the surrounding system so that better choices become easier for everyone. In her own life, she started with eliminating plastic bottles, then moved on to clothing, and is currently searching for a plastic-free kettle. “Go one by one,” she says. “One plastic at a time.” Asked where she hopes Unplastify will be in 10 or 20 years, she doesn’t describe a larger organization, more schools or a bigger budget. “Hopefully, we don’t exist anymore,” she says. “Because we solve the problem.” Delfina Bellagamba. Photo courtesy of Equipo Unplastify Reflections from Delfina Bellagamba, a participant in the Unplastify Challenge from La Plata, Argentina: I had never really wondered where my waste ended up. Thanks to taking part in the Unplastify Challenge, however, I came to see the scale of the plastic problem. We tend to view plastic use from an individual perspective, where each of us thinks that our impact is not so great. But by participating in the challenge, I realized that we are all repeating the same behavior and that the impact is greater than I thought. I concluded that we have to act together to change this situation. Through Unplastify and Young Leaders [an advanced mentoring program by Unplastify], I have learned teamwork, to speak in public and to quantify positive impacts, as well as how to use my voice as a young person in decision-making spaces, such as the student councils at my school. Both experiences have shaped me and helped give me the foundation to be who I am today. The post Teenagers Worldwide Are Tackling the Plastics Crisis appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
