items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Texas Grants Right to Repair Electronics, Becoming Ninth State to Pass Consumer Protection Law Reading Time: 3 minutes The right to repair electronics became law in Texas on September 1, requiring manufacturers to provide parts, tools, and manuals so residents can fix phones and laptops instead of discarding them. The Texas Right to Repair Act , known as HB 2963, took effect last month, granting residents a legal right to fix many of the products they already own. Under this law, manufacturers of covered devices must give consumers and independent repair shops access to the same parts, tools, and repair manuals that company-authorized shops have always received. The legislation passed the state legislature with striking unanimity, clearing the House 130-0 and the Senate 31-0. Texas now becomes the ninth state in the nation to guarantee right to repair electronics protections for consumers, joining California, Colorado, Connecticut, Kansas, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, and Washington. Environment Texas Executive Director Luke Metzger noted that fixing a phone or laptop in Texas has become significantly easier under the new framework. For years, manufacturers made independent repair difficult by withholding the parts, tools, and documentation people needed, often forcing consumers into expensive authorized repairs or premature replacement purchases. Right to repair electronics now ensures Texans have what they need to fix devices they already own, reducing toxic electronic waste while saving consumers and boosting local repair shops. The law covers phones, laptops, tablets, cameras, and speakers, though it excludes video game consoles, home appliances, medical devices, motor vehicles, farm equipment, and industrial or aerospace equipment. Under its terms, manufacturers of consumer electronics costing more than $50 wholesale must offer documentation, tools, and replacement parts on fair and reasonable terms with non-discriminatory pricing. Requirements scale with device cost: manufacturers must retain and provide repair documentation for three years after a product’s introduction for items priced between $50 and $99.99, extending to seven years for products priced $100 or higher. TexPIRG’s Right to Repair Campaign senior director Nathan Proctor framed the change in straightforward terms, noting that fixing something broken represents basic common sense. With Texas’s addition, more than one-third of Americans now live in a state offering right to repair electronics protections, marking substantial national momentum for a policy movement that gained little traction just a few years earlier. The environmental stakes behind this legislation are considerable. TexPIRG estimates Texas generates roughly 621,000 tons of electronic waste annually, much of it consisting of old phones, laptops, and tablets discarded simply because repair proved too expensive or too difficult to access. This waste frequently ends up in landfills, where toxic materials including lead and mercury can leach into surrounding soil and water, threatening the health of nearby communities, wildlife, and ecosystems. Right to repair electronics aims to reduce the roughly 621,000 tons of e-waste Texas generates annually, much of it containing toxic materials like lead and mercury that can leach into soil and water when devices are discarded rather than repaired. Photo by RETURN E-Waste on Pexels. Metzger connected the legislation directly to this waste problem, noting that expanded repair access means reduced waste overall. When the bill passed the previous year, advocates specifically pointed to Texas’s e-waste burden as exactly the kind of toxic problem this legislation was designed to address, a solution now formally written into state law. Right to repair electronics in Texas drew support from an unusually broad political coalition, uniting Environment Texas and TexPIRG alongside the conservative Texas Public Policy Foundation, Repair.org, and independent repair shops across the state. This cross-ideological alignment reflects how repair access increasingly appeals to both environmental advocates concerned about waste and consumer-rights groups focused on cost savings and market competition. Environment Texas and TexPIRG indicated they will continue pushing for robust enforcement of the law’s provisions, while advocating for future legislation extending right to repair protections to additional product categories currently excluded, including home appliances and medical devices. This incremental expansion mirrors patterns in other states, where initial consumer electronics legislation often serves as a foundation for broader repair rights covering more product types over time. As more states adopt similar frameworks, right to repair electronics is steadily shifting from a niche policy concept into mainstream consumer protection, driven by a straightforward proposition that resonates across the political spectrum: people who own a device should have a genuine path to fixing it, rather than facing pressure toward premature disposal and replacement simply because manufacturers control access to essential repair resources. Αυτό το ένστικτο -- να αναζητήσει τον ωκεανό στη μέση της θλίψης -- την οδήγησε πίσω στο Wednesday Ocean Waders, μια ομάδα που ξεκίνησε το 2021 όταν μια δασκάλα γιόγκα και ο γιος της ανάρτησαν στο…
items.descriptionOriginal: Two days after her daughter died, Keri Jones walked back to the beach. Not because she had somewhere to be, but because she needed, as she put it, to give herself to the water. That instinct -- to seek the ocean in the middle of grief -- led her back to the Wednesday Ocean Waders, a group that began in 2021 when a yoga teacher and her son posted on a community page inviting strangers to wade into the dark at 7am. Seven people showed up that first morning; now the group's informal membership tops 2,100. The town of Torquay, on Victoria's surf coast, has nearly doubled in population over the past decade, and that growth has quietly generated an epidemic of disconnection -- new arrivals with no roots, post-pandemic isolation still thawing. WOW became an accidental antidote: cold water, coffee afterward, and what founder Jo Halley describes simply as a kindness she has "never experienced in a group like this in my life." When Shaan died, the waders formed a circle of remembrance on the sand, laid a heart of flowers, and held the grieving mother. Keri, still working through loss, says of the community: "You can't really measure something like that." She's right -- and yet somehow, standing waist-deep in the ocean before dawn, they have.

Η προκύπτουσα πανοραμική θέα (ραμμένη μεταξύ τους από si…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you’ve ever wondered what it would be like to wake up on Mars, you’re in luck. NASA’s Curiosity rover recently snapped pics of dawn on the red planet, showing us the beauty of the morning light roughly 140 million miles away and offering scientists a deeper look at Mars’ wind-carved cliffs. The resulting panoramic view (stitched together from six pictures) is the most detailed image ever captured of the cliffs, according to a statement from the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory. It shows a serene scene of distant crags illuminated by early light, highlighting features that the Curiosity mission team has “long been waiting to see up close.” Gale Crater, Aug. 11, 2026, 8:30 a.m. local Mars time. The Curiosity rover captures the Sun rising on crags known as yardangs, a scene that scientists have long been waiting to see up close. 1/2 https://t.co/NJQH9yNEYR — NASA Mars (@NASAMars) October 6, 2026 “Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance,” NASA explained, noting the team expects to receive even more images from the rover that could help them determine how the cliffs were formed. Called yardangs, the cliffs extend for about 10 miles across the 3-mile-tall Mount Sharp, a mountain that Curiosity has been climbing for over a decade. In August, the same month that the photos were taken, the rover marked 0.6 miles in elevation in total, the most ever ascended on Mars. NASA/JPL-Caltech/ESA/DLR/FU Berlin/MSSS Ann artist’s concept of Mount Sharp, with its yardang layer indicated by the black circle NASA explained that Mount Sharp is made of layers that each records a distinct period in the planet’s history. Scientists studying the layers have been able to glean insight about the lakes and streams that covered Mars billions of years ago, leaving salty minerals behind after drying up. One theory is that after this ancient material stopped settling on the peak, wind may have stripped some of it away, creating the layer of cliffs. “The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Curiosity project scientist Ashwin Vasavada. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.” NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Over the next year, Curiosity will drive through layers of the mountain that are enriched with sulfates and carbonates, indications of water having dried on the surface. Scientists aim for the rover to reach the base of the yardangs at some point in 2027, where it will use its robotic arm to collect samples offering “one-of-a-kind data” on these enigmatic terrain features. Κατά τη διάρκεια της εβδομάδας που έληξε στις 26 Σεπτεμβρίου, το 3,4 τοις εκατό των αναπνευστικών δειγμάτων που εξετάστηκαν από κλινικά εργαστήρια ήταν θετικά για γρίπη, σύμφωνα με στοιχεία του CDC. Αυτό είναι περίπου επτά φορές το ποσοστό στο ίδιο σημείο πέρυσι, όταν το 0,5 τοις εκατό ήταν…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Flu season usually builds in late fall, but this year it’s getting a jump start. During the week ending September 26, 3.4 percent of respiratory samples tested by clinical labs came back positive for flu, according to CDC data . That’s roughly seven times the rate at the same point last year, when 0.5 percent tested positive. The early uptick is concentrated in Western states. In Washington, the share of emergency department visits diagnosed as flu climbed from 0.25 percent in late August to 1.34 percent in the week ending October 3, a more than fivefold increase in six weeks. California and Arizona are seeing elevated activity too. “This particular year, it appears to be starting early — like right now,” said Dr. William Schaffner , a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health, who says patients at clinics in his area are already testing positive. Where flu is showing up so far Flu starting in the West isn’t unusual or predictive. “There’s nothing unusual about flu starting in the West Coast and moving east,” Schaffner said. It can start almost anywhere; recent seasons have come out of the Southeast or Midwest first. An early start also doesn’t mean a bad season. The CDC’s 2026-2027 outlook projects moderate severity, though with only low-to-moderate confidence. H1N1 is leading the season so far Seasonal flu comes in three subtypes: two influenza A strains (H1N1 and H3N2) and one influenza B lineage called Victoria. Of the influenza A samples subtyped during the week ending September 26, 96 percent were H1N1. Last season a fast-spreading H3N2 variant dominated, and the CDC classified 2025-2026 as highly severe for children, with at least 195 child deaths from flu-related causes. Schaffner describes influenza A and B as siblings: “They’re very related, but they each have their own individual characteristics.” Influenza A tends to drive the biggest outbreaks early; influenza B strains “kind of smolder along” toward the end. The 96 percent figure is where things stand now, not a forecast for the full season. Flu is, as Dr. Paul Offit , director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, puts it, “a moving target.” The virus mutates constantly, especially in hemagglutinin, the surface protein it uses to latch onto human cells and the main target of flu vaccines . When circulating strains diverge significantly from those in the vaccine formulation, “that usually predicts a more difficult season,” Offit says. Whether this year’s shot is a close match won’t be clear for weeks. Why October is the right time to vaccinate The CDC recommends annual flu vaccination for everyone six months and older. Flu hits hardest in children under five, adults 65 and older, people with chronic health conditions, and pregnant people; tens of thousands of Americans die of flu each season, and serious infections can cause pneumonia, sepsis, and heart or brain complications. The shot works better when you get it at the right time. The CDC advises against vaccinating in July or August for most adults because protection can wane over a long season. With flu arriving ahead of schedule, “October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, and even more so right now,” Schaffner said. Full protection takes about two weeks to build after the shot. Effectiveness varies. In terms of flu cases that send people to the doctor, vaccines have been 29 to 56 percent effective over the past decade, per CDC estimates. They do better against severe illness. Schaffner puts the calculus directly: they work best at “keeping you out of the hospital, keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery.” The mRNA flu vaccine approved this season Adults 50 and older have a new option this year. The FDA approved mFlusiva in August, the first mRNA flu vaccine. Traditional shots contain purified viral proteins. The mRNA version delivers genetic instructions that the body’s cells use to produce those same proteins themselves, then break down. “It cannot influence human genetic material,” Schaffner said. The result, according to Offit: “you’re less likely to get symptomatic disease.” For adults 65 and older, the CDC still prefers high-dose or adjuvanted shots. Adjuvanted vaccines include an extra ingredient that prompts a stronger immune response. This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most of the deep seafloor is cold, dark, and barely mapped. The Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary covers more than 6,000 square miles of ocean along California’s central coast and is better studied than most of it. Even there, researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute somehow missed a gathering of 20,000 octopuses until 2018. The site is now the largest known deep-sea octopus congregation on Earth, which raises an obvious question about what else is down there. It sits on a field of hydrothermal springs, and that’s the key. The springs warm the water above what the surrounding seafloor offers, which speeds up metabolism and egg development in the pearl octopuses ( Muusoctopus robustus ) drawn to the heat. Normally, female octopuses in the deep sea spend years brooding their eggs. At this site, they do it in about 1.8 years. Why 20,000 octopuses gather here Pearl octopuses are pale purple, roughly grapefruit-sized, and not especially known for company. Something about the thermal conditions here has drawn more than 20,000 of them to roughly 6.2 acres of seafloor. Using underwater mapping technology, researchers counted about 6,000 in a 2.5-hectare area and extrapolated the rest. The dens they build use whatever is on the seafloor nearby: stones, shells, and whatever human objects have settled down there over time. After brooding their eggs, the females die, and their bodies become food for other animals in the area. The whole cycle keeps the local food web running on what the octopuses themselves leave behind. What protection made this discovery possible The octopus garden sits inside the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, which restricts oil and gas exploration, seabed mining , and other activities that can damage the seafloor. Hydrothermal fields in the deep sea are fragile and not well understood. Without protected status, this one could have been disturbed or destroyed before anyone knew what was living there. This congregation went undetected until 2018 in one of the most closely monitored stretches of deep ocean in the world. Hydrothermal springs aren’t unique to this part of California, and the ocean has a lot of floor. The question the garden raises is how many other congregations, in thermal fields no one has mapped yet, are still down there. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: For over 60 years, London’s Natural History Museum has put out an annual call to photographers across the globe to submit wildlife images that capture the beauty and complexity of nature. The winners of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition — which awards prizes in nearly two dozen categories — are then invited to showcase their work in a public exhibition at the museum. Judges selected the 2026 honorees out of a record 65,403 entries from young people and adults in 121 countries and territories. “This year’s winning photographs demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently,” museum Director Doug Gurr said in a Tuesday press release provided to Nice News, adding: “Together they remind us that every species plays a role in the complex web of life, and why understanding and protecting the natural world has never been more important.” Scroll to see some of our favorite winning photos from this year’s contest, from a shot of an urban-adapted coyote in San Francisco to a portrait of a scorpion burrowing in India. “Flight of the Bumblebee” by Amelie Davis | 10 Years and Under Amelie Davis / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Amelie Davis (U.K.) highlights a common carder bee suspended in mid-air as it flies in to land and feast on a flower in southern England.” “Scenes from the Swamp” by Isak Pretorius | Behavior: Birds Isak Pretorius / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Isak Pretorius (South Africa) chances across two elusive shoebill storks among wetland vegetation.” “A Watchful Eye” by Aaron Sanders | Animal Portraits Aaron Sanders / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Aaron Sanders (U.K.) glimpses a common octopus behind a curtain of kelp in the waters off southwest England.” “Labour of Love” by Oscar Whitfield | 11-14 Years Oscar Whitfield / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Oscar Whitfield (Zimbabwe/U.K.) notices the arduous exertion of this dung beetle pushing its precious cargo.” “Protective Pose” by Anton Sorokin | Behavior: Amphibians and Reptiles Anton Sorokin / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Anton Sorokin (U.S.) finds a California newt laying its eggs as it clasps vegetation that already holds another newt’s egg clutch.” “ Shifting Sand” by Sitaram Raul | Behavior: Invertebrates Sitaram Raul / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Sitaram Raul (India) encounters a scorpion burrowing into one of the shifting dunes of the Thar Desert.” “Birdsong Painted in Light” by Konrad Gräeter | 15-17 Years Konrad Gräeter / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Konrad Gräeter (Germany) highlights a male blackbird singing in a vineyard early one April morning.” “Shedding Light” by Agorastos Papatsanis | Plants and Fungi Agorastos Papatsanis / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Agorastos Papatsanis (Greece) uses ultraviolet light to reveal the glowing yellow stems of beautiful bonnet mushrooms growing from a decaying log.” “On the Outskirts” by Loren Elliott | Photojournalist Story Award Loren Elliott / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Loren Elliott (U.S.) opens a window into the lives of the often-misunderstood coyotes living in the environs of San Francisco on the West Coast of the United States.” “Escape Artistry” by Michał Michalski | Natural Artistry Michał Michalski / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Michał Michalski (Poland) uses a slow shutter speed to create the illusion of trees still swathed in autumn foliage.” “Making Morays” by Tony Wu | Under Water Tony Wu / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “Tony Wu (U.S./Japan) provides a first-time glimpse into the mating ritual of Abbott’s moray eels.” “ The Meeting Place” by James Lewin | Animals in their Environment James Lewin / Wildlife Photographer of the Year “James Lewin (U.K.) watches a young bull elephant spray a group of zebra as they congregate in the Kenyan Chyulu Hills.” Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. Click here to see all the winning images.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Primates as Umbrella Species Could Safeguard Thousands of Other Animals and Plants Reading Time: 3 minutes Primates as umbrella species offer a powerful new conservation strategy, with new research showing that protecting monkey and ape habitat in China could shield thousands of other species at once. Primates as umbrella species represent a shift in how conservationists think about protecting biodiversity. For decades, funding and effort have centered on large, charismatic animals like tigers and giant pandas. That approach assumes that saving the vast territory these animals need also protects everything else living there. An umbrella species, in ecological terms, is any species whose habitat requirements are broad enough that protecting it automatically shelters many other plants and animals sharing the same range. Tigers and pandas have long served this role. Researchers now argue primates deserve consideration too, given how much intact forest many primate species require to survive. A 2025 study published in the journal Conservation Biology , titled “Effect of primate protection on threatened and endemic vertebrates, plants, ecosystem services, and future climate refugia,” tested that argument directly. Researchers led by Yin Yang, alongside collaborators including primatologist Paul A. Garber of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, focused their analysis on China’s Yunnan province. Researchers chose China’s Yunnan province for its exceptional biodiversity. Scientists analyzed the habitats of 16 primate species living there, including the black-and-white snub-nosed monkey, the Western black crested gibbon, and several langur species found nowhere else in the country. They then compared these ranges against 601 threatened and endemic species of mammals, amphibians, birds, and reptiles. The team also included seed plants, mapping ranges for 4,010 species across the province. Their findings were striking. Designating just 30 percent of Yunnan as a primate conservation priority area would protect roughly a third of the habitat for 86 percent of those threatened animals. Seed plants would benefit almost as much, with 72% of species gaining partial habitat protection under the same plan. Beyond wildlife, this approach also offers climate benefits. That same protected zone would secure more than half of Yunnan’s annual carbon storage, according to the study’s modeling. Dense forest canopy in Yunnan province illustrates the scale of habitat that could be protected by treating primates as umbrella species for conservation. Photo by Jason Hu on Pexels. Researchers also factored in future climate scenarios when identifying priority zones. Areas expected to remain climatically stable as temperatures rise, often called climate refugia, received particular attention in the analysis. Protecting primate habitat in these zones could give many species, not just primates, a better chance of surviving long-term shifts in temperature and rainfall. This concept of primates as umbrella species is already gaining traction elsewhere. Conservation groups outside China have applied similar thinking to great apes in other biodiversity hotspots. Rainforest Trust, a nonprofit organization, has worked to protect habitat for the critically endangered Grauer’s gorilla in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The group estimates this effort could help safeguard more than 11,000 other species sharing that forest ecosystem. A similar pattern appears on Borneo. The Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation estimates that protecting Bornean orangutan habitat could benefit roughly 20,000 species across the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. Conservationists say primates make especially effective umbrella species for several reasons. Primates easily draw public attention and donor support, making them effective flagships for broader conservation campaigns. Beyond their appeal, primates play essential ecological roles, serving as both prey for larger predators and as vital seed dispersers throughout forest ecosystems, since many species eat fruit and carry seeds across long distances as they move through the canopy. A declining forest often shows signs of primate loss before other warning signs appear, Davenport pointed out. Because primates sit relatively high on the food chain and require large territories, their disappearance can serve as an early indicator of broader ecosystem stress well before other species show measurable decline. Experts agree the umbrella species approach remains a practical conservation tool. Its main limitations stem from governance and human behavior rather than any flaw in the underlying concept. That distinction matters for how conservation groups move forward. Protecting primates as umbrella species does not guarantee success on its own. Strong enforcement, local cooperation, and consistent funding still determine whether protected areas function as intended. Yunnan’s snub-nosed monkeys illustrate the stakes involved. The black-and-white snub-nosed monkey, found only in this region, depends entirely on the same forest habitat now under consideration for expanded protection. Researchers see this study as evidence that primate-focused conservation deserves more attention and funding worldwide. Protecting primates as umbrella species could allow conservation groups to accomplish far more with the same resources. Biodiversity loss continues to accelerate globally, and strategies that protect multiple species through a single, well-chosen habitat are increasingly appealing. Yunnan’s example may offer a model that other primate-rich regions, from Central Africa to Southeast Asia, could soon follow. The post Primates as Umbrella Species Could Safeguard Thousands of Other Animals and Plants appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: I n his first year at the University of California, Davis, Liam commuted three hours a day from his family’s home in the Bay Area to campus and back again. The round-trip train tickets were expensive, but not as pricey as renting an apartment in the Central Valley college town. Then, partway through the school year, conflict with his family upended Liam’s living arrangement. “I didn’t have anywhere to go,” he says. “It wasn’t like anybody was supporting me, and the money that I did have was very little.” Liam bounced from place to place before landing at Aggie House , where he spent the next nine months living a short distance from campus with roommates who were also struggling to find a place to call home. Aggie House isn’t a typical university dorm or homeless shelter: It’s a collection of low-cost apartments, created and run by UC Davis students, for classmates who are facing housing insecurity. The kitchen at the Y2Y shelter. About 3.5 million people between the ages of 18 and 25 face homelessness each year in the U.S., increasing their vulnerability to harms including trafficking, incarceration and suicide. Photo courtesy of Y2Y As high costs and low vacancies squeeze property markets across the country, housing remedies for college students exist to support young people during a particularly volatile stage of adulthood. Start-ups like Depaul USA and the Neighborhood Coalition For Shelter run initiatives such as the Dax Program and NCS Scholars that provide room, board and mentorship to college students. Yet a crucial, sometimes overlooked dimension of this assistance is the nationwide network of young adults stepping up for each other by establishing and operating housing solutions dedicated to their age group. Some cater specifically to students; others welcome anybody in their late teens to early 20s who needs a place to stay. Bound by a sense of solidarity, these spaces foster a sense of belonging and camaraderie as young people navigate school, careers and the challenges of early adulthood. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] “I think sometimes, in general shelters, it can be harder for people to understand what a student is going through,” says Hayven Angelique Pfister, a fourth-year human biology student at UC Davis and the external co-president of Aggie House. And because all the residents and volunteers there share the experience of being students, she says, “it’s easier [and] more comfortable.” A young person in the U.S. may experience homelessness due to a combination of serious family issues and broader systemic challenges . Common factors include family conflict, abuse or rejection — particularly for LGBTQ+ youth — alongside economic instability, a lack of affordable housing and aging out of public systems like foster care. The upshot is that about 3.5 million people between the ages of 18 and 25 face homelessness each year in the U.S., a situation that makes them particularly vulnerable to harms such as trafficking, violence, extremely poor physical and mental health, incarceration and suicide. Each of Y2Y’s sleeping bunks is equipped with a Plexiglas shutter for privacy, lockable storage, individual lighting and power outlets for recharging electronics. Photo courtesy of Y2Y “Young people experience a lot of trauma before homelessness, and they’re experiencing more trauma while they’re homeless,” says Darla Bardine, executive director of the National Network for Youth, a public education and policy advocacy organization focused on preventing and ending youth homelessness in America. “That’s why our perspective is: The earlier you can identify a young person experiencing homelessness and get them into help, you can hopefully prevent more compounded trauma.” The key to addressing homelessness among those under 25, Bardine says, is partnership with other young people. “They know where young people hang out,” Bardine says. “It’s easier for them to build that trusting relationship with young people because they have lived it.” Students established Aggie House at UC Davis in 2021 as part of a network of shelters on three California campuses that aim to ensure no student is left without a place to live. Many people erroneously assume that people who experience homelessness don’t work, Pfister says. “We have a lot of people who are working, who are getting financial aid,” she says. “They still can’t afford to get housing. They still can’t get what they need.” Aggie House offers accommodations for up to a year, and residents pay rent — usually $200 to $300 monthly, which is 90 percent less than the average cost of rent in Davis. Rent increases by $50 monthly to incentivize people to move on. Guests must be UC Davis students, and are vetted through an application and interview process to determine their need for housing, with many having been referred through a center run by the university that aims to ensure students’ basic needs are met. The shelter is run entirely by undergraduate volunteers on 7 p.m. to 11 p.m shifts, whose role is partly to help build social connections. A few nights a week, the volunteers take turns preparing dinner for residents. One of Pfister’s favorites she made was a sushi bake with layers of salmon, rice and seaweed. Over meals, residents and volunteers chat about pop culture, school, religion and politics. Meanwhile, over in the basement of the white-clapboard First Parish church around the corner from Harvard Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts, 22 bunks are staggered in three tiers, separated by lime green walls and white polka-dotted privacy screens. From October through April, and again for a shorter summer season, Y2Y shelter provides housing for up to 30 days for people between the ages of 18 and 24. Unlike Aggie House, Y2Y doesn’t specifically cater to students; many guests are LGBTQ+ who lost family support, or aged out of foster care. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Y2Y was founded by two Harvard students in 2015, in part to address safety concerns among youth in adult shelters, according to Caleb Oh, Y2Y’s administrative director who is studying math and statistics at Harvard University. Y2Y offers an alternative for young people who don’t get into nearby all-age emergency shelters, or feel unsafe using them. Young adults facing homelessness often avoid adult shelters and child welfare systems because of fears of exposure to substance use or sexual assault, or because of past negative experiences. “Being unhoused is incredibly frightening, incredibly isolating,” Oh says. He’s been told by people who have stayed at the youth-led shelter that the environment is less stressful than alternatives. “What Y2Y can provide,” he says, “is just being social and having a community.” At weekly youth advisory meetings, guests give feedback on the shelter, catch up and play board games. Student volunteers from universities and neighborhoods across the Boston area serve as case managers, helping guests navigate housing support programs and connecting them with other services so they have a next place to stay. This summer, four guests moved into rental units, five went on to transitional housing and four went to a different shelter with professional case management. Y2Y’s main living space. Many guests at the shelter are LGBTQ+ who lost family support, or aged out of foster care. Photo courtesy of Y2Y “I think what we get right is putting not just our guests first but attempting to let them put themselves first,” Oh says. “We are more facilitators than anything.” One of the biggest challenges for youth-led shelters is capacity. Y2Y only operates through the winter and part of the summer, when students are available to staff the shelter, and there’s a waitlist for openings. Likewise, because the shelters’ volunteers are students, they have limited bandwidth to give while balancing school. Volunteers are also learning as they go, unlike professionally trained staff at other shelters. But that youth-led perspective can also be a significant advantage. Liam says the upperclassman volunteers who supported him had navigated the same systems he then had to face. After he arrived, his student case manager helped him make sense of financial aid, enroll in health insurance, get a job, save up money and eventually find an apartment, which he now shares with roommates. He moved in about a month ago. The post Young Adults Are Building Safe Spaces for Unhoused Peers appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Crossings in Florida are Saving Panthers from Highway Deaths Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife crossings in Florida are turning deadly highways into safe passageways for one of America’s rarest cats. Wildlife crossings in Florida now exist in dozens of locations across South Florida. These structures let panthers move without crossing traffic. The results are already changing outcomes for a species once pushed to the brink, and the wildlife crossings today serve as a model other states are watching closely. The Florida panther used to roam across the entire Southeast. Today its only breeding population lives in Southwest Florida. That population now survives on less than 5% of its historic habitat. Panthers once shared their range with black bears, red wolves, and other predators across the Southeast. Hunting and land conversion eliminated most of these populations over the past century. Today conservationists work to protect the remaining core habitat in Big Cypress and the greater Everglades ecosystem. Roads make that shrinking habitat even more dangerous. In 2024 alone, drivers struck and killed 30 panthers. Each loss matters for a population this small and fragile, which is why wildlife crossings in Florida have become such an urgent conservation priority. Panthers need large territories to hunt, find mates, and raise young. When roads slice through that territory, populations become isolated. Isolated populations struggle to recover and stay healthy over time. Interstate 75, known locally as Alligator Alley, carries millions of travelers through South Florida every year. It also cuts straight through vital panther habitat. Black bears, deer, bobcats, alligators, and otters share this same landscape. Wildlife crossings in Florida benefit far more than panthers, with bobcats, deer, and black bears all documented using the same underpasses, proving that a single well-placed crossing stretches conservation dollars across an entire ecosystem. Photo courtesy of Florida Wildlife Federation . When builders planned this highway decades ago, they faced a 40-mile stretch of critical panther territory. Rather than leaving a permanent barrier, the Florida Department of Transportation added crossings into the design. That early decision is one of the clearest examples of wildlife crossings in Florida in practice. Completed in the early 1990s, the project included 24 wildlife underpasses and 12 modified bridges. Planners also added continuous fencing along all 40 miles. The fencing steers animals toward safe crossing points instead of open lanes. A Transportation Research Board study later tracked bobcats, deer, and black bears alongside panthers using these underpasses. That data confirmed multiple species benefit from a single, well-placed crossing. Shared infrastructure like this stretches conservation dollars further across the whole ecosystem. State Route 29 tells a similar story. This road splits the Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge from the Big Cypress Wildlife Management Area. One stretch, called Owl Hammock, ranks among the most dangerous spots for panthers, bears, and drivers alike. Florida’s transportation department is working on a fix there, too. Crews will build a new wildlife bridge over Barron River Canal. They will also raise the road 8 feet, add a culvert underneath, and install 2 miles of new fencing. The Owl Hammock project carries a price tag of $8.67 million. That investment reflects a broader pattern statewide. Florida now has 60 wildlife crossings and bridges in operation. Wildlife bridges like this also protect panther genetic diversity by connecting isolated groups. Without these connections, inbreeding threatens the population’s long-term health. Genetic diversity remains one of the biggest challenges to full panther recovery. Combining crossing structures with fencing has measurably reduced wildlife deaths. Researchers have documented panthers and other animals successfully using these crossings. Well-designed infrastructure can reconnect habitat while keeping both animals and drivers safer, reinforcing why wildlife crossings in Florida matter far beyond one species. Still, panthers keep dying on Florida roads, especially young cats still learning their territory. That reality shows the work is far from finished. More crossings, more fencing, and more funding are needed to keep this progress going. Congress has a chance to build on what Florida has already proven works. Reauthorizing the Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program is the next step that could extend this success well beyond Florida. Florida’s highways show that people and panthers do not have to compete for the same ground. Smart infrastructure lets both share the landscape safely. That balance took decades of planning, and it still needs steady support to last. The panther’s story is far from over. But every underpass, bridge, and stretch of fencing adds another chance for this species to recover. Florida’s roads are proving that wildlife crossings in Florida can go hand in hand with moving people forward. The post How Wildlife Crossings in Florida are Saving Panthers from Highway Deaths appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: Η Λέσλι Γκόμεζ Ριβέρα δεν άρεσε τίποτα στην καφετέρια στο λύκειό της στο Μπρούκλιν και είχε ελάχιστες ελπίδες ότι θα άλλαζε. Στη συνέχεια άκουσε για το Youth Food Advocates που υποστηρίζει τους μαθητές να υποστηρίξουν την αλλαγή. Έδωσαν στη Λέσλι τις πληροφορίες και τα εργαλεία για να κάνει κάτι γι' αυτό. Η Leslie δημιούργησε μια έρευνα με άλλους μαθητές και συνεργάστηκε…
items.descriptionOriginal: Leslie Gomez Rivera didn't like anything about the cafeteria at her Brooklyn high school, and had little hope it would change. Then she heard about Youth Food Advocates that supports students to advocate for change. They provided Leslie with the information and tools to do something about it. Leslie created a survey of other students, and collaborated with the cafeteria manager and principal. Her findings helped inspire the school to offer foods students liked to eat, student tasting and approval of new menu items, more efficient and inviting food displays, and comfortable seating. "This was one of the pivotal moments when I realized that if you want it done, you can do it yourself," Rivera said. "I felt like this was something that not only affects my everyday [life], but that the next generation … would be affected. And if I could do something about it, I would."

items.title: Πληρώσαμε φοιτητές περίπου 5 $ τη νύχτα για να κοιμούνται τουλάχιστον 7 ώρες — και οι βαθμοί τους βελτιώθηκαν γρήγορα
items.titleOriginal: We Paid College Students About $5 a Night to Sleep at Least 7 Hours — And Their Grades Quickly Improved
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Osea Giuntella, αναπληρωτή καθηγητή οικονομικών στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Πίτσμπουργκ, τη Sally Sadoff, καθηγήτρια οικονομικών και στρατηγικής στο Πανεπιστήμιο της Καλιφόρνια στο Σαν Ντιέγκο και τη Silvia Saccardo, καθηγήτρια κοινωνικών επιστημών και επιστημών αποφάσεων στο Πανεπιστήμιο Carnegie Mellon, για το The Conversation — μια μη κερδοσκοπική είδηση ​​ή…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Osea Giuntella , an associate professor of economics at the University of Pittsburgh, Sally Sadoff , a professor of economics and strategy at the University of California, San Diego, and Silvia Saccardo , a professor of social and decision sciences at Carnegie Mellon University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Paying college students about $5 a night to sleep seven hours got them a quarter more nights of adequate sleep — and better grades. That is what we found in a study we published in July 2026 . We gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit — a wearable activity tracker that looks similar to a watch — and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. We randomly chose 468 students and paid them about $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours, over the course of four weeks. We verified how much they slept using the device they wore. The students were about 19 years old, on average, and half of them were first-year students. Roughly 72% of them were women. About 55% were white, 28% Asian, 9% Black, and 4% Hispanic. Our study shows that offering an immediate financial reward can help students meet a seven-hour sleep goal, and that those effects can persist up to a month beyond when the students are paid. Not Just a Student Problem About one-third of American adults sleep less than seven hours a night, and a similar share say they wish they slept more. Among adolescents and young adults, roughly two-thirds routinely fall short of getting seven hours of sleep a night — the amount of shut-eye that health authorities recommend . One prominent sleep researcher has called sleep deprivation the most prevalent high-risk behavior. Short sleep is linked to obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, and early death . Irregular sleep predicts mortality risk even more than sleep duration does . Sleep loss shows up in decision-making, even when it comes to issues like whether people vote . Students Are Running on Empty Before we changed anything, the average student in our study slept 6.6 hours a night . Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average — a quarter after 2 a.m. Students got the recommended seven hours of sleep on a typical weeknight on only 43% of their nights, and more than 85% fell short at least once a week. They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours — the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five. And 94% said their ideal night of sleep was longer than the one they were getting. What the Money Bought The 468 students we offered nightly payments reached seven hours of sleep on 26% more nights than 380 students who were not offered the money. That is a large shift for a group in which fewer than half were hitting the mark to begin with. Students receiving the monetary incentive slept 19 more minutes per school night, roughly the difference between closing the laptop at 11:40 p.m. or at midnight. Among students receiving the payment incentive, their GPA rose by about 0.08 points that semester — roughly a quarter of the gap between students who arrived with above-average and below-average high school grades. Once the payments stopped after four weeks, students who had received the money were still sleeping about eight minutes longer per night for the remaining three to four weeks of the study. The effect was smaller than during our study, but our findings suggest that some of the change in sleep habits persisted for up to a month after the end of the incentive. The effects of the intervention on sleep and GPA were largest among first-term freshmen, whose routines are not yet necessarily fixed. Glow Images/Getty Images Universities spend heavily on helping students learn. Very few treat sleep as part of that investment. Rewards Work — if They Come Right Away Timing mattered too: Delivering the payment as a lump sum at the end of the semester, rather than every morning, produced only about two-thirds of the effect on sleep. The effects of the intervention on GPA faded over a couple of academic terms. Grades remained higher in the following semester, but two semesters later we could no longer detect an effect. Bedtime reminders and morning feedback on their own — with no money attached — had little effect. Students who received them slept only marginally more. The problem was not motivation: Nearly all said they wanted more sleep than they were getting. The challenge was following through on that intention night after night. Investing in Sleep Our results show that universities should look at how the environment they create fosters or discourages good sleep habits. Late evening deadlines to submit assignments and early classes can both make it harder for students to get enough sleep. Changing some of these features costs little compared with many academic support programs, and it may be worth testing alongside other interventions aimed directly at students. Reminders and feedback might also work better if they change over time, rather than becoming familiar and easy to tune out. Very few universities or students treat sleep as part of an investment in education, or ask whether the schedules and incentives schools create make adequate sleep harder. Our results suggest they should. RELATED: The 5 Sleep Languages: How Knowing Yours Could Help You Get Better Rest

items.titleOriginal: The common skin care mistakes dermatologists say are working against your routine
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Υπάρχει ένα συγκεκριμένο είδος βραδινής σπείρας της Κυριακής που συμβαίνει όταν έχετε αφιερώσει είκοσι λεπτά διαβάζοντας για ένα συστατικό που δεν έχετε ακούσει ποτέ και είστε πλέον πεπεισμένοι ότι ολόκληρη η ρουτίνα σας είναι λάθος. Η φροντίδα του δέρματος δεν ήταν ποτέ καλύτερη στο να μας κάνει να νιώθουμε πίσω. Πέντε πιστοποιημένοι δερματολόγοι, όταν ρωτήθηκαν ποιος…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of Sunday evening spiral that happens when you’ve spent twenty minutes reading about an ingredient you’ve never heard of, and you’re now convinced your entire routine is wrong. Skin care has never been better at making us feel behind. Five board-certified dermatologists, when asked which habits they most wish patients would break, kept arriving at the same place: most of us are doing too much, not too little. Some of what follows, you’ve heard before. Some of it will stick in a way the usual advice doesn’t. Stop chasing skin care trends “Skin care is a long game,” says Dr. Laurel Naversen Geraghty , a board-certified dermatologist in Medford, Oregon. “It’s not how much you blast your face with new ingredients; it’s the good, proven steps that you stick to over time.” That runs counter to how skin care gets marketed, where the week’s buzzy ingredient has a way of making whatever you already own feel outdated. Dr. Ava Shamban , a board-certified dermatologist in Los Angeles, keeps seeing young patients come in with reactive, inflamed skin from doing too much at once. “I’ll ask, ‘Okay, three weeks ago, what were you doing?'” The answer is almost always a new stack of products. The risk isn’t just wasted money. Layering too many active ingredients can compromise the skin barrier, leading to bumps, flakes, itchy rashes, and sensitivity that can “take time, a dermatologist consultation, and medication to calm and reverse,” Dr. Geraghty says. Her rule: don’t introduce more than one new product or ingredient at a time, and give anything at least three months before deciding it isn’t working. “Don’t give up on a proven ingredient after a few days or a week.” With retinoids, meaningful results take around six months. With peptides, two to three months. Trends come and go, but as Dr. Geraghty puts it, “your skin has to last you a lifetime.” Build sunscreen into an existing habit Sun exposure is the leading cause of skin aging and the leading cause of skin cancer. “UV light raises the risk for cancer, just like smoking and asbestos raise the risk of cancer,” says Dr. Geraghty. Every dermatologist in this article made some version of that point, with varying degrees of exasperation. Most people know they should wear sunscreen . Most people don’t do it every day. Dr. Corey Hartman , a board-certified dermatologist in Birmingham, Alabama, has a fix: put sunscreen right next to your toothbrush. “It’s something you do every single day after brushing your teeth. That way you don’t have to wonder and guess if you put it on.” Build it into a routine you’re already doing, and it becomes automatic. Aim for SPF 35 or higher and hit the areas people routinely miss: the sides of the nose, the temples, the ears, and above the upper lip. The one-squeeze rule for pimple popping This might be the hardest habit on this list. Dr. Hartman is candid: “I’m guilty of it myself.” His answer isn’t to quit entirely. It’s a limit. “You get one good squeeze,” he says. If the pimple is ready, it comes out. If it doesn’t come out on the first try, stop. Continuing only pushes bacteria deeper, delays healing, and raises the chances of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, the dark spots that can stick around long after the pimple itself is gone. After a successful squeeze, cover the spot with a hydrocolloid pimple patch. If nothing happened, use a salicylic acid spot treatment instead. Covering it either way makes the next step easier: it’s hard to keep picking at something that’s already covered. One gentle cleanser is almost always enough More cleanser doesn’t mean cleaner skin. “People get very exuberant with their cleansing technique,” says Dr. Hartman. Washcloths, silicone brushes, and mesh sponges are all too aggressive and prone to causing redness, irritation, and dryness. Double-cleansing, using two face washes in sequence, works well for people who wear heavy makeup or have very oily skin. Most people are neither. “I just think more people are double-cleansing than really need to be, and they end up over-cleansing,” Dr. Hartman says. One gentle, fragrance-free cleanser is usually all it takes. Wash your face when you get home, not right before bed If nighttime face washing keeps getting skipped because you’re exhausted, Dr. Rachel Nazarian , a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, has a practical fix: stop treating it as a bedtime task. “Rather than waiting until bedtime, shift it earlier—when you get home, change your clothes, wash your face, remove your makeup.” Do it when you still have energy, and the habit holds. Cleansing wipes aren’t a substitute. They feel like they’re doing something, but they leave behind residue that can irritate and dry out skin, and they don’t remove the dirt, bacteria, and makeup that built up during the day. You need soap and water. Stop scratching your scalp This is the one that tends to catch people off guard. Scratching an itchy scalp, even casually a couple of times a day, can cause hair breakage, according to a 2024 study in the Archives of Dermatological Research , and over time can contribute to thinning. Dr. Jeanine Downie , a board-certified dermatologist in Montclair, New Jersey, is blunt: “Then you’re adding the tension of scratching? Seriously?” The timeline is shorter than you’d think. Regular scratching can cause breakage in less than a week, and recovery takes two to three months of keeping your hands off. If your scalp is itchy, address the itch rather than scratch it. An anti-inflammatory shampoo is a reasonable first move for common culprits like dandruff or mild psoriasis . For itch without an obvious cause, a dermatologist can figure out what’s driving it and treat it at the source. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post The common skin care mistakes dermatologists say are working against your routine first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.description: Όταν φαντάζεστε τη Νεβάδα στο μυαλό σας, πιθανότατα φανταστείτε τα λαμπερά φώτα του Las Vegas Strip. Ο Kohki Yamaguchi σκέφτεται τους έναστρους ουρανούς και τα γαϊδούρια. Ο 32χρονος φωτογράφος με έδρα το Τόκιο, έχει εξερευνήσει 36 χώρες, τραβώντας συναρπαστικές φωτογραφίες από μέρη που δεν απεικονίζονται - τα σημεία που αγαπά που συνήθως δεν μπαίνουν στους τουριστικούς οδηγούς. Το ενδιαφέρον του…
items.descriptionOriginal: When you picture Nevada in your mind, you likely conjure the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. Kohki Yamaguchi thinks of starry skies and donkeys. The Tokyo-based photographer, 32, has explored 36 countries, snapping breathtaking photos of unpictured places — the spots he loves that don’t typically make it into the tourist guides. His interest in photography first piqued 10 years ago when he finished university and started taking photos of abandoned buildings. His philosophy around his craft includes noticing “what others might overlook,” his webs ite states, which ties into his travel work. In 2023, Yamaguchi decided to visit Iraq to take street photographs of people talking to each other and recalled he could “feel the humanity very strongly,” per SWNS. Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Other destinations he’s captured include the Chinese countryside and the aforementioned Nevada. “Me and a friend went there just because you can see the stars clearly at night,” he told the outlet. “But surprisingly, more than the stars, we found these random roads had donkeys walking about.” Yamaguchi said he recently looked at a graph of the world’s most-photographed areas and was shocked to see the places he’s loved didn’t make it on the list. “Those places are not just the least photographed but also just people don’t really consider that as an ideal bucket list destination,” he noted. Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Today, his photography has earned him 1.3 million followers on Instagram alone , and he said he’s grateful when people feel inspired to take their own photos after seeing his work. “I truly believe photography can enhance the way we see things and remember them,” Yamaguchi said. “I’m very happy if someone can start photography even if it’s just as a hobby.” And for all of the traveling he’s done, he most appreciates showing people the special, unpictured places in his native Japan: “Traveling to other countries and comparing them to my own country I realized — I’m not sure how to put it into one word to describe it — but how lucky I am to be from this country.” Indeed, his favorite photo he’s ever taken is of a whimsical curb in Tokyo that’s painted to resemble a piece of tamago sushi, a sweet Japanese omelet held in place atop rice with a strip of nori. “It’s something you have to be observant to spot,” Yamaguchi said. Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Kohki Yamaguchi / SWNS Here are the countries he’s visited so far: Japan U.S. Australia New Zealand Taiwan Hong Kong China Macau Thailand Singapore Indonesia Malaysia Fiji England France Poland Italy Monaco Germany Austria Netherlands Switzerland Czech Republic Belgium Turkey Greece Peru Russia (Sakhalin Island) UAE Qatar Sweden Finland Iceland South Africa Iraq Norway This article was originally written by Emily Phillips for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.titleOriginal: Can Students and Teachers Learn to Trust Each Other in the Age of A.I.?
items.description: «Ανησυχώ αν χρησιμοποιήσω μια παύλα em θα νομίσουν ότι είναι A.I.», είπα στη μαμά μου από εκεί που κάθισα στον πάγκο της κουζίνας, προσπαθώντας να δουλέψω σε ένα από τα δοκίμιά μου στο κολέγιο. Παρά τις διαβεβαιώσεις της για το αντίθετο, δεν πείστηκα. Το μόνο που μπορούσα να σκεφτώ ήταν την περασμένη άνοιξη, όταν η φίλη μου, μια μη μητρική αγγλική γλώσσα που αγαπά να γράφει, μου είπε ότι η ιστορία της…
items.descriptionOriginal: “I ’m worried if I use an em dash they’ll think it’s A.I.,” I told my mom from where I sat at the kitchen counter, trying to work on one of my college essays. Despite her reassurances to the contrary, I wasn’t convinced. All I could think about was last spring when my friend, a non-native English speaker who loves to write, told me that her history teacher accused her of using A.I. to write an essay, his reasoning being that she had included too many “big words.” He didn’t even have a conversation with my friend before giving her a zero. But is her teacher really the villain here? He and his peers have few resources to help them navigate the rise of A.I., and in lots of ways, teachers and students are in the same boat when it comes to figuring out how to adjust to this technological revolution. Somehow, in the process, students have ended up being pitted against teachers. Illustrated by Cloe Moreno One approach would be to rethink homework. Someone recently told me about a professor they know who no longer assigns essays to do at home, and the reasoning makes total sense: The educator said that the idea of walking into his classroom and immediately feeling like he distrusted his students was horrible. He said that he missed being able to look at someone’s work and simply be proud of them, and because of that he was going to have his students write essays solely in class moving forward. While this approach follows a certain logic, it feels detrimental — to students and to teachers — to scrap the whole concept of writing essays outside of class. At the same time, while, at its best, the classroom is a community space full of joyful exploration, how can we create that space if everybody enters it with mistrust? And if teachers come into the classroom automatically distrusting their students, how are we, as students, ever supposed to trust ourselves? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] I was thinking about exactly these sorts of questions when I discovered the Center for Digital Thriving , a research group based out of the Harvard Graduate School of Education that works with experts, educators and young people to create resources that support teens in their relationship with technology. Based on the principle of the Disability Rights Movement, which is “nothing about us, without us,” the Center for Digital Thriving believes that young people should not simply be spoken about, but should be able to speak, to be given a voice at the table when it comes to things that impact them so immensely. Given that 64 percent of U.S. teens use A.I. chatbots , and almost one in three of those use chatbots daily, it makes sense that research being done about teenagers and A.I. would directly involve them. Illustrated by Cloe Moreno As part of the development of every report, resource guide and lesson plan published by the Center, teenagers are being asked to share their stories and tell experts how A.I. is actually impacting their lives. A core part of this are the teen advisory boards that the Center works with. These are groups of young people who are asked to look at the Center’s research — whether on “ grind culture ” or “ thinking traps ,” and how they’re enhanced by technology — and give their insights and feedback. The Center makes sure that teenagers are directly involved in their process, enabling their research and lesson plans to be genuinely applicable. Educators, in turn, are being given resources for how to deal with A.I. and connect with their students. In one lesson plan, called Align on the Line , teachers are asked to give students a list of activities they might do in that class (for example, a literature class would have steps to writing an essay) and are asked to place them on a spectrum of whether or not they feel the activity could be done with A.I. The spectrum ranges from “totally fine” to “crosses a line,” and allows students and teachers to work with one another, instead of against, to define what they feel is acceptable. Teenagers often say they use A.I. because “it listens.” Just by listening, by being open to hearing what teenagers have to say about their lives, the Center for Digital Thriving is building trust around tech between adults and teens. The goal of the Center is not stopping the use of A.I., but simply creating communities that are informed and on the same page. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime It may seem small, but oftentimes it is the conversations and the communities formed, whether at the kitchen counter or around the seminar table, that begin to chip away reliance on A.I., a dependence which can come from loneliness and a lack of feeling understood. By showing teenagers that they are trusted and that their opinions matter, teenagers may be encouraged to rely on themselves more and A.I. less. Having a space, especially one where research is being done, where teenagers are taken seriously and asked for their insights, is a model for what it can look like to restore young people’s faith in themselves. This article was illustrated by Cloe Moreno, who contributes drawings for podcast episodes and comics that unpack the anxieties and feelings of daily life for This Teenage Life . items.title: Πώς μια ομάδα νεαρών Cherokee έγραψε ιστορία παλεύοντας για ένα ιερό ποτάμι
items.titleOriginal: How a Group of Cherokee Youth Made History Fighting for a Sacred River
items.description: Μια ομάδα κοριτσιών Cherokee, ηλικίας 10 έως 17 ετών, ξεκίνησαν να προστατεύσουν μια σαλαμάνδρα και κατέληξαν να γράψουν νομική ιστορία. Καθοδηγούμενοι από πρεσβύτερους που τους είπαν να ξεκινήσουν με το ίδιο το νερό, οι κόρες NAIWA πέρασαν ενάμιση χρόνο διοργανώνοντας δείπνα στην κοινότητα, συναντώντας τα μέλη του συμβουλίου ένα προς ένα και εμφανίστηκαν, όπως περιέγραψε η ιδρυτής τους, Jasmine Smith, «κουρασμένη, υπερβολική…
items.descriptionOriginal: A group of Cherokee girls, ages 10 to 17, set out to protect a salamander and ended up making legal history. Guided by elders who told them to start with the water itself, the NAIWA Daughters spent a year and a half hosting community dinners, meeting council members one by one, and showing up, as their founder Jasmine Smith described, "tired, overwhelmed, and emotional, sacrificing school breaks and weekends" - until the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians unanimously passed the first all-female-led rights-of-nature resolution in the United States. On the day it passed, the girls carried clay pots of headwaters into the chamber and set the water beside them as the vote was taken; afterward, they carried it back down to the river. The resolution recognizes the Longperson -- the interconnected waterway stretching 790 miles from the Great Smoky Mountains to the Gulf -- as a living entity with inherent rights, and it asks a question that outlasts any single law: "Do we see nature as something we own, or do we view it as something we have the responsibility to protect?" What these young women built was not just policy but a way of belonging to a place -- and a demonstration that a moral compass has no minimum age.

Από πού μπορεί να προέλθει η αλλαγή; Το ερώτημα είναι ένα από τα πιο περίπλοκα και πιεστικά της εποχής μας, που απασχολεί τους κατοίκους, τους υπεύθυνους χάραξης πολιτικής και τη διακυβέρνηση…
items.descriptionOriginal: Nearly half of U.S. renters and a quarter of homeowners were housing cost-burdened in 2024, meaning they spent more than 30% of their income on housing. Hundreds of thousands of others can afford no home at all. Where can change come from? The question is one of the most complex and pressing of our time, engaging residents, policymakers, and government agencies. But to Kristian Ventura and his co-founders at Actum , the answer is simple. “People want their freedom back, and the best way to do it is to eliminate the biggest burden preventing that, which is rent,” the 26-year-old told Nice News. He established the Los Angeles-based nonprofit, which launched in earnest this year, to put that belief into action: It aims to give away free permanent housing via a lottery system to anyone interested. @universalshelter Spread the good news. ♬ Runaway – Piano Rendition – The Blue Notes & L’Orchestra Cinematique Because the organization doesn’t strictly serve people “in need” by traditional definitions, the leadership team, all friends from high school, had a bit of a hurdle securing its tax-exempt status. The issue lay in the idea that anyone could apply, which made it less clear to the IRS how Actum qualified as a charity, per Ventura. “It’s supposed to be for everyone,” he explained. “That is the point. Homeless individuals are encouraged to apply. Middle class people are allowed to apply.” He added: “Our mission is that universal housing means universal.” Specifically, at least 75% of Actum’s units must be awarded to lottery applicants who make 80% or less of their area’s median income, per its eligibility requirements. The other 25% could technically go to anyone who earns above the median, though Ventura doubts the very wealthy would be interested in living in the basic units the nonprofit plans to purchase and build. As of now, Actum is still in the early stages of fundraising, with a goal of purchasing its first building, likely a duplex or fourplex, when it hits $1 million in donations. The org follows an endowment model for its donations, meaning everything that comes in is immediately funneled into an investment fund, so it can grow at a similar rate to a retirement account. And a live transparency dashboard on its website shows every transaction in real time. Courtesy of Actum Kristian Ventura (upper left), Edmarck Sosa (upper right), and Surya Singh A big part of Actum’s ethos is efficiency. “We actually only run on less than a thousand dollars a year. We have a P.O. box, a website, no paid staff, no pizza parties. We don’t need name tags,” Ventura said, alluding to what he considers wasteful behavior by some charity leaders. “If you actually strip down what a nonprofit has to do operationally, it’s very slim, and that’s what shocks people.” He and his co-leaders, founding members Edmarck Sosa and Surya Singh, met as teens in La Puente, a city in LA’s San Gabriel Valley, and each had come face to face with financial hardships growing up. Singh was born in New Delhi, and would step over children sleeping on the ground outside on his way to school, per Ventura, and Sosa is from Honduras, where his family lived in poverty. Now a rising actor, Ventura bounced around as a child — he and his mother once lived in the garage of a senior care home. After he received a scholarship from the University of Southern California, he had no place to return to during the COVID lockdown; his mom was living out of her car, and his father, who spent years unhoused in San Francisco, died in a government housing unit there in 2023. Kathlyn Almeida “Since we all come from backgrounds of poverty, we take extra efforts to make sure that people who are extremely low income, like single family parents or those living in shelters, know about our lottery,” he explained, adding: “We care about those who sleep in tents, because that’s where the founders come from.” Still, the overarching goal is bigger than just altruism, and the response to Actum’s social media content, which has racked up millions of views, has solidified that they’re onto something. “We’re trying to establish a new standard, which is, it’s technically really unfair for someone to spend 80 hours a week just for a roof over their head. There’s a problem,” Ventura said. “And that’s why we’re going viral, as people understand, ‘Wait, wait, wait. I’m not super, super poor, but I have no time for myself and I feel empty and lonely. So that’s the problem we’re tackling, is this middle class problem as well.” He shared that multiple business owners and other individuals have been reaching out wanting to get involved. “It’s people all coming together with different jobs, different kinds of walks of life, and saying, ‘I believe housing is a human right, and it’s heartbreaking it took this long.’” View this post on Instagram At the time of this writing, Actum had raised around $14,000. “In a way, it’s kind of like a global experiment. Can we actually reach the number that we need to? Can people give to the world they’re going to inherit? It’s a very straightforward model, and it kind of just depends on us. It’s up to us.” RELATED: “They’re Our Neighbors”: Social Entrepreneur Aims to Shift Public Perception of Homelessness in America

items.description: Η διαμάχη ενός εφήβου με τη μητέρα του για τον ύπνο και τη λήθη οδήγησε τον Amit Biligiri, έναν 16χρονο από την Καλιφόρνια, να κάνει μια ερώτηση που μετατράπηκε σε βραβευμένο podcast: γιατί ο εγκέφαλος απορρίπτει μια διάλεξη για τα μαθηματικά του χθες αλλά κρατιέται σε ένα χάρτινο στέμμα πριν από μια δεκαετία; Η απάντησή του, που έχει τις ρίζες του στη νευροεπιστήμη αλλά φθάνει σε κάτι mo…
items.descriptionOriginal: A teenager's argument with his mother about sleep and forgetfulness led Amit Biligiri, a 16-year-old from California, to ask a question that turned into an award-winning podcast: why does the brain discard a math lecture from yesterday but hold onto a paper crown from a decade ago? His answer, rooted in neuroscience but reaching toward something more personal, centers on a memory of sitting across from his 87-year-old great-grandfather in a Burger King in Bangalore, India, both of them wearing flimsy gold crowns, sharing fries. "I don't remember what we talked about," Amit says, "but I remember the salt on the fries, the energy of the room and the way his crown sat slightly crooked on his head." What the science reveals -- that emotion is what gives memories their staying power -- is also what the story quietly demonstrates: that the moments we carry longest are rarely the important ones by any external measure, only the ones in which we felt, without condition, that we mattered to someone. Since finishing the podcast, Amit has found his mother listening to it alone, and she tears up every time.

Αυτό που ανακάλυψε στο para powerlifting δεκαετίες αργότερα δεν ήταν απλώς η αθλητική ικανότητα που ποτέ δεν ήξερε ότι είχε, αλλά η ανάκτηση κάτι που…
items.descriptionOriginal: Julie Dickson grew up loving movement -- bikes, swimming, the easy joy of a body in motion -- until high school sorted everyone into "sporty" or not, and she quietly accepted she belonged to the wrong category. What she found in para powerlifting decades later wasn't just athletic ability she never knew she had, but the reclamation of something her younger self once took for granted: the simple right to belong in sport. "These experiences showed me something my younger self naturally knew but the uniformity of high school made me forget: I was a sporty person." As a participant in the World Dwarf Games, her silver medal in powerlifting mattered not because of the podium, but because it was wholly hers -- earned in a community where competitors cheered each other through disqualifications and everyone was chasing their own personal best, not someone else's defeat. It is a quiet reminder that the environments we move through can either diminish us or restore us to ourselves, and that it is never too late for the latter.

items.title: Η Gen Z σώζει εκατομμύρια σε ιατρικές προμήθειες
items.titleOriginal: Gen Z Is Rescuing Millions in Medical Supplies
items.description: Στις αρχές Αυγούστου, ένα φορτηγό έφτασε σε μια εγκατάσταση του OhioHealth στο Κολόμπους και πήρε περίπου 30.000 λίβρες μάσκες N95 και ζεστές και κρύες συσκευασίες, όλα συσκευασμένα, σφραγισμένα και σφραγισμένα με ημερομηνίες λήξης ακόμη ένα ή δύο χρόνια έξω. Αν μείνουν μόνες, οι ιατρικές προμήθειες αξίας 250.000 δολαρίων που εκτιμάται ότι θα είχαν πεταχτεί τελικά, θεωρούμενο απίθανο…
items.descriptionOriginal: I n early August, a freight truck pulled up to an OhioHealth facility in Columbus and took roughly 30,000 pounds of N95 masks and hot-and-cold packs, all boxed, sealed and stamped with expiration dates still a year or two out. Left alone, the estimated $250,000 worth of medical supplies would eventually have been thrown away, deemed unlikely to be required before their use-by date. Instead, the pallets were loaded and driven off toward Pittsburgh, the first leg of a journey to an under-resourced clinic on another continent. The operation was part of Project MedBridge , a medical redistribution initiative set up by 16-year-old Ben Kurian, a junior at Olentangy Liberty High School in Powell, Ohio. The idea started, as a lot of good ideas do, at the dinner table. His mother is a nurse practitioner and his family friends are doctors and nurses. Over and over he heard the same uncomfortable fact — every year, big hospitals like OhioHealth and Cardinal Health discard thousands of pounds of good quality supplies simply because they won ’ t be used before their expiration date passes, a problem greatly exacerbated by the pandemic-driven overstock . Ben Kurian (left) and Naman Soni during a Project MedBridge redistribution operation. Credit: Project MedBridge “ These are perfectly usable, sterile supplies, ” Kurian says. “ They don ’ t come out of the box, and yet no one is putting them to use, despite the fact that there are clinics with little-to-no resources in desperate need. ” When he learned that the Carnegie Young Leaders Program funds exactly the kind of social impact idea he had in mind, Kurian started cold-emailing distributors that route surplus overseas, and eventually the Pittsburgh-based nonprofit Brother ’ s Brother Foundation stepped in to handle shipping. Project MedBridge only started this year, but Kurian is far from alone in his desire to curb excess medical waste. Most of the established medical supply redistribution organizations, or MSROs, like Project C.U.R.E. and World Medical Relief (WMR), are staffed full-time by adults operating at industrial scale. But around the country, a quiet network of young people has taken up the same cause: pulling medical surplus out of the waste stream and redirecting it toward people who need it, both in faraway countries and at underserved U.S. clinics. What ’ s striking about this newer wave is that it ’ s run entirely by students, and almost entirely by volunteers — teenagers and Gen Z youth squeezing warehouse shifts in between classes and exams to right a wrong they see unfolding on their own doorsteps. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Each group has found its own way to do it. United2Heal , founded at the University of Michigan in 2007 and run by undergraduates, works hand-in-glove with WMR. Every Saturday, over a hundred members meet up — some arriving by 6 a.m. — to check expiration dates and sort through each shipment. “ Anyone who wants to come volunteer with us can, ” says Leah Beel, president of the nonprofit and a junior majoring in molecular, cellular and developmental biology. The only real limitation, she says, is how many students have cars, as they all carpool to WMR ’ s offices 40 minutes or so from the university.
