items.titleOriginal: How NYC Students Saved School Lunch
items.description: Εδώ ήταν τρεις ξεκάθαροι λόγοι για τους οποίους η Leslie Gomez Rivera απέφυγε την καφετέρια στο λύκειο της στο Μπρούκλιν: Δεν της άρεσε το φαγητό, το δωμάτιο ένιωθε ταραχώδες και υπήρχε ένα στίγμα που συνδέονταν με την κατανάλωση σχολικών γευμάτων. Προτιμούσε τη βιβλιοθήκη, όπου μπορούσε να μιλήσει με φίλους, αν και μερικές φορές αυτό σήμαινε ότι θα πήγαινε εντελώς χωρίς μεσημεριανό γεύμα. Όταν λοιπόν ο Ρίβερ…
items.descriptionOriginal: T here were three clear reasons why Leslie Gomez Rivera avoided the cafeteria at her high school in Brooklyn: She didn’t like the food, the room felt hectic and there was a stigma attached to eating school meals. She preferred the library, where she could talk with friends, although sometimes that meant going without lunch altogether. So when Rivera heard about Youth Food Advocates (YFA), an initiative that trains New York City students to research issues around school food and advocate for changes, she realized she might be able to do something to make the whole situation better. With the help of YFA, the 16-year-old developed a survey and circulated it around Midwood High. She wanted to know what her fellow students liked to eat, what they wanted on the menu, why they stayed away from the cafeteria and what might make them come back. Participants at a Youth Food Advocates leadership training. Credit: Community Food Advocates “I had the answers to [some of the questions],” Rivera recalls, “but I wanted to know what my peers thought.” Around 100 students responded out of roughly 4,000 across Midwood’s two buildings. Their answers complicated the verdict that school lunch was simply bad. Participants singled out popcorn chicken, sauces, fruit and salads as popular items. They also raised concerns about food quality and limited choices, and some wanted more of the foods they ate at home. This was back in late 2020. By then, NYC had already made lunch free for every public school student following years of advocacy that included student organizers from YFA. But free food did not necessarily equate to food students wanted to eat, or a cafeteria where they wanted to spend their lunch period. items.description: Καλώς ήρθατε πίσω στην εβδομαδιαία μας ματιά στα παρασκήνια για το τι κάνει να μιλάει η ομάδα μας. Πείτε μας τι έχετε διαβάσει στο info@reasonstobecheerful.world και ίσως το παρουσιάσουμε εδώ. Sunny outlook Πέρυσι, ο συνεισφέρων συντάκτης Peter Yeung ανέφερε σχετικά με τη δυνατότητα αλλαγής του παιχνιδιού της ηλιακής ενέργειας μπαλκονιού — δηλαδή, μικρών ηλιακών συστοιχιών που μπορούν να συνδέσουν…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Sunny outlook Last year, Contributing Editor Peter Yeung reported on the game-changing potential of balcony solar — that is, small solar arrays that can plug into regular electrical outlets. Now, as Grist reports in a story Peter shared this week, California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a bill that will allow residents to get on board — and more states could soon follow California’s example. These plug-in solar devices, Grist explains, are a way of “turning homes and apartments into a distributed network of tiny power plants.” Peter says: The balcony solar revolution continues. Light room You know how a squid can change its coloration by revealing or hiding different pigments? That’s the inspiration behind a new type of window panel that “dynamically shades in response to the sun’s rays,” according to a Be Giant story shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby. In a typical building, counteracting the heat that enters or escapes through its windows accounts for about a quarter of the energy used. Based on simulations, researchers estimate that one version of these squid-like window panels could lower buildings’ heating use by 75 percent and their total energy use by 43 percent. Becca says: Intriguing — and the artist’s interpretation at the top of the story has James Turrell vibes. What else we’re reading In a warming Arctic, Inuit bear guards protect communities — shared by Rebecca Worby from Grist Women Can Now Assess Their Breast Cancer Risk With the Help of A.I. — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from the New York Times New York expands free SUNY and CUNY tuition to those with college degrees — shared by Rebecca Worby from News10 ABC In other news… RTBC Founder David Byrne has a new book out this week! If you’re a fan of our journalism, we suspect you’ll also enjoy Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up . Publishers Weekly calls it a “wonderful and humbling celebration of the lost and found.” Read an excerpt from the book in Nautilus and pick up a copy wherever books are lent or sold .
